text: ROYAL WOMEN OF THE UR III PERIOD PART II: GEME-NINLILA Piotr Michalowski University Museum University of Pennsylvania The major source of information on the highest echelons of the Ur III state bureaucracy are the tablets from Drehem. Although large numbers of archival texts were found during the excavations at Ur, the royal chancellery was never located. Thus while the texts from the capital do provide us with important information on various aspects of the economy, Drehem remains at present the main source of archival data on the political structure of the Ur III state. One of the most productive ways in which one can study the Drehem tablets is through the comparison of personal names. The Ur III scribes rarely wrote the patronymics of individuals, and official titles were not always registered. Thus only through a careful comparison of the contexts in which names occur is one able to reconstruct the names, functions, and titles of particular individuals. The majority of names encountered in the Drehem texts are masculine. Only rarely are women mentioned. Generally, those women who can be identified by title were either wives of important officials,! daughters of kings,? or royal consorts. To this last category belong women who are described as dam or lukur of aruler.* Women who are mentioned without title, however, are difficult to identify. Often, one suspects that they were members of the royal family. Among these women was one named Geme-Ninlila. The most important reference to this woman is found ina text recording the disbursement of animals for the libation places of Shulgi, his lukur Shulgi-simti, and Geme-Ninlila.‘ Elsewhere I have suggested that Geme- Ninlila was buried in the same tomb with Shulgi and Shulgi-simti because, like the latter, she was also a lukur of the king.® Here we shall survey the published texts which mention Geme-Ninlila as well as present for the first 1. dam PN. 2. dumu-munus lugal. On the basis of this sample we may conclude that during the last years of Shulgi’s reign Geme-Ninlila was entitled to a sadug of thirty sheep a month, that is, one per day. text: 174 PIOTR MICHALOWSKI of Geme-Ninlila. The same official, Kuli, received two oxen for a festival (&lu-lum) of Geme-Ninlila in YOS 4 240, dated only eleven months later (II/S 41). In the first month of 5 43 one ewe was sent “to the kitchen of Geme-Ninlila” (émubaldim geme,-‘nin-Ifl-l4-ka-8é; Limet, RA 49 [1955] 73 no. 12, reading thus with the copy against the transliteration). In the next year, two oxen were transferred to her account for agricultural purposes (Kang Drehem 8, dated IV/5 44). In Legrain TRU 298 (IX/S 48) animals were disbursed to various deities such as Enlil, Ninlil, and Nanna, as well as to Geme-Ninlila. It is noteworthy that the function of maskim was held in this transaction by Arad-mu, who only occurs in this role when persons of high social status are involved. This text may be the last attested reference to Geme-Ninlila. There is a tablet dated to the month $e-kin-KUD of 5 48 which mentions the receipt of three oxen for Geme-Ninlila (BIN 5 20). The text was published as an Umma document, and according to the calendar used in that city this would be the first month of the year. If this text actually comes from Drehem then it would have to be dated to month twelve. The most important new information concerns the cultic activities of Geme-Ninlila. text: 422 children’s literature © 2013 Koninklijke Brill NV ISBN 978-90-04-17642-3 Children’s Literature Children’s literature has existed for a relatively short time, and has played a signiﬁcant role in education only since the 19th century (though examples of children’s literature in Europe have been documented as early as the 17th century, because that is when such literature began to be written, speciﬁcally in Germany). But these were only preliminary attempts to bring this type of literature to the attention of the broader public. It was only during that period that chil- dren began to be perceived as individual human beings with cultural needs of their own (Shavit 1996). Before that time students’ reading mate- rials were based mainly on a selection of Clas- sical sources. The new stress on the importance of a special literature for children was founded on ethical principles and ideals. Children’s literature is, of course, written for an audience consisting of children; it is therefore subject to certain didactic instructions and restrictions. However, because the works are usually chosen according to the tastes of parents and educators, it may also contain ele- ments that address an adult audience, especially allusions to other texts. It is difﬁcult to delimit children’s literature by age; researchers tend to take it to include works intended more-or-less for the entire class of people included in the term ‘children’. Gold- berg (1956) deﬁned children’s literature as a branch of prose and poetry whose contents and style are adapted to the understanding of children between the ages of ﬁve and about thirteen. This deﬁnition extends the concept in the direction of youth literature. Others deﬁne youth literature as works intended for ages twelve to seventeen. Some divide literature for non-adults into literature for small children (for infants and children in kindergarten and lower primary school grades), grade-school-age literature (ages eight to twelve) and adolescent literature (ages thirteen to seventeen or even eighteen). One issue that has been the subject of schol- arly attention is the nature of the difference between children’s and adult literature. Baruch (1985) focuses on two differences. One is age: certainly a two-year-old child’s vocabulary and experience differ from those of an eight-year- old, and a ten-year-old’s differ from both, but they all differ in vocabulary and experience from adults. The second difference is that chil- dren’s literature contains implicit or direct edu- cational elements in keeping with the norms of the period in which the works were composed. Most scholars claim that anyone who writes for children must take their unique experiential world into consideration and that therefore this literature must adapt itself in style and con- tent to children’s conceptual world. Texts for infants usually contain short, rhythmic poems, whose language is simple and minimalistic (for example, the poems of Fanya Bergstein), occa- sionally with onomatopoeic elements and short and simple messages to which a young child can relate. It is an age when children are pre- sented adapted legends and folk tales. The literature for children between the ages of nine and twelve or thirteen consists mostly of stories of youth groups, young detectives, and ‘Dear Diary’. For adolescents writers of children’s literature compose stories that relate to the problems of that age, whose precise age limits, however, are not easy to delineate. Baruch and Fruchtman (1982, as well as Cohen 1988; Regev 1985) note that the values promoted in children’s literature, and, in consequence, also the language, have changed over the years, in step with the changes that have taken place in opinions and style, and in the perception of children and their needs in different periods. According to Goldberg (1956) the unique his- tory of the Jewish people affected the course of Hebrew literature for children. It was only after the education given to Jewish children in the Land of Israel had become Westernized that the literature written locally for Jewish children and adolescents became similar to that of Europe and America, a development with its advantages and disadvantages. Before the advent of Zionism and the revival of Hebrew as an everyday language Jewish children only read the Torah in Hebrew. Literary materials outside holy scripture were only available in primitive form, through oral traditions in the local language. Hebrew children’s literature began with Ze±ev Ya≠veß, whose book תוחיש םדק ינמ »i≤ot mini qedem ‘Tales from the Ori- ent’, written in biblical style, was published in Warsaw in 1887. He was gradually joined by Yehuda Zvi Levin, Yehuda Steinberg, S. Ben- Zion, H. N. Bialik, and a few other writers | True

text: children’s literature 423 © 2013 Koninklijke Brill NV ISBN 978-90-04-17642-3 of their generation who wrote for children. Children’s newspapers in Hebrew also ﬁrst appeared at this time. The style of these pioneering authors was inﬂuenced by the ancient Hebrew sources; this was their strength, and also their weakness. Their language was uniform and normative for the most part (although Levin Kipnis’ early poems, for example, already contain some ele- ments of spoken Hebrew and show a desire to speak to children in their own language). Inter- estingly enough, although H. N. Bialik belongs to the early Modern Hebrew period, when the conventions still dictated that texts for children be formulated in an elevated register, his own works do contain many allusions and (mostly covert) ambiguities that point to additional lev- els in his children’s books, levels not necessarily intended for children (Shamir 1986). Gradually, as the Jewish community in the Land of Israel grew, the ﬁgure of the רבצ ßabar ‘prickly pear; Sabra, a Jew born in the Land of Israel’ became predominant in children’s litera- ture. Until the 1960s in particular ‘mobilized’ poetry was quite common; it stressed the values of work, defense of the homeland, agriculture, the ﬁgure of the Sabra, and the like. The lan- guage in that period was normative for the most part, quite elevated in fact. text: 1, Introduction In his influential book on “the origin and goal of history,” written shortly after World War 2, the German philosopher Karl Jaspers claimed that the period from 800 (o 200 BCE played a particularly crucial role in the intellectwal history of ‘man (Jaspers 1949). Jaspers argued that in the centuries in question, dubbed by him the “axial age,” thinking, for the first time in human history, became the object of itself. Jaspers distinguished China, India, and the eastern Mediterra- nean as the three regions where this dawn of consciousness took place, but de- clared with regard to the last area that it was only with the Hebrew prophets and the Greek philosophers that the axial revolution really began. The earlier em- pires of the region represented a pre-axial state. Up to this day, Jasper's concept of an axial age has retained much of its at- traction. Yet critical discussion of the concept during the past decades by schol ars from different fields has made it increasingly clear that the civilizations of Egypt and Mesopotamia were not as unaffected by “axial thinking" as Jaspers had claimed.’ The present work deals with a group of Mesopotamian texts that display various features of the self-conscious reflection Jaspers characterized as axial: Babylonian and Assyrian commentaries or, to be more precise, text com- mentaries. These commentaries are preserved in cuneiform script on more than 860 clay tablets from different archaeological sites in what is today the republic of Ira. The tablets date to the period from the eighth to the second century BCE, an era that coincides exactly with Jaspers’s axial age.’ The commentaries represent efforts of Babylonian and Assyrian scholars to explain the whole range of Babylonian literary, religious, and scholarly works, from epics and rituals to legal, medical and omen texts. Using a plethora of hermencutical techniques, the commentaries provide unique insights into many aspects of how the Mesopota- mian mind, in its numerous avatars, actually worked. If we regard hermeneutics as a set of intellectual tools that are applied to ar- rive at a better understanding of the world, it would be wrong to claim that the Babylonian and Assyrian text commentaries of the first millennium BCE are the carliest testimonies of “hermeneutical reasoning” in human history. Hermeneu- ics, in this most general sense, can be detected in almost every expression of the human spirit, and Mesopotamia, with its ancient lexical tradition that goes back to the birth of writing in the fourth millennium BCE, and its passion for divina~ tory quests, has lefl us large numbers of documents from much older periods to study it." But if we define hermeneutics more narrowly as pertaining to the in- terpretation of written texts, then Babylonian and Assyrian commentaries can truly be regarded as a “first.” Physically separate from the texts they interpret, these commentaries represent the earliest known corpus of exegetical treatises 2 Fora good overview of the current state of the discussion about axial phenomena in Mesopotamia, see Michalowski 2005 (with comprehensive bibliography). > [will come back to the question of Mesopotamian “axiality” in ch. 12. Introduction that explain cultural texts of canonical or semi-canonical status within a well- defined framework of hermeneutical operations.’ As meta-texts proper, they ing of a tradition of “secondary literature” that features most prominently in the intellectual discourse of almost every major civilization. The significance of the Babylonian and Assyrian commentary tradition is thus threefold. First, the commentaries provide information on myriad aspects of Mesopotamian languages and civilization. It is thanks to a medical commentary from Babylonia, for instance, that we know how to pronounce the name Gilgame’, normally written with a particularly enigmatic sequence of signs.’ Second, they make it possible for us to investigate not only the central texts of ancient Meso- potamia, but also the meaning assigned to these texts by those who read and studied them, a meaning social anthropologists designate with the term “manifest con- tent” (Cryer 1994, 208). And finally, when approached from a comparative per- spective, the commentaries from Mesopotamia emerge as the earliest testimonies to the long and complex history of textual interpretation, an intellectual pursuit prac- ticed all over the world. To one particularly prominent chapter in this history, the exegetical tradition of rabbinic Judaism, they may even be related genetically.* 1.1. History of research The first publications of cuneiform commentaries appeared in the foundational period of Assyriology. As early as 1866, E. Norris provided in 2R, 44 (no. 7) and 47 autographs of two Nineveh commentaries, one astrological, the other commenting on several different texts, However, cuneiform studies were at that Lime still so much in their infancy that Norris, unaware of what the texts actually represented, characterized them simply as bilingual lists. Progress in the analysis, 5 rypt generated some commentary-like works in the second millennium BCE, but since the explanations they give are not separated from the texts commented on, they do not represent real “meta-texts.” See Assmann 199Sb and Rassler-Kébler 1995. © To illustrate this last point, it should suffice to mention here the Aristotelian schol- ars Albertus Magnus (ca. 1200-1280) and Averroes (1126-1198), the Vedanta philos pher Shankara (780-R20), and the Neo-confucian Zhuxi (1120-1200), all essentially commentators of earlier works, but at the same time independent thinkers in their own right, The literature on the hermeneutical traditions of the various world civilizations is of course boundless and cannot be summarized here. A useful introduction to Chinese commentaries is Henderson 1991. while Holdreze 1996 provides an interesting compari- son between Jewish and Indian commentary traditions. For the classical world, see the brief overview by Wilson 1983, for rabbinical hermeneutics, Strack & Stemberger 1996, and for a detailed analysis of modem commentaries on texts from classical antiquity, Gibson & Kraus 2002. The “commentarial” quality of significant portions of the intellec- tual discourse of the West is epitomized in Whitehead’s famous claim that “the safest general characterization of the European philosophical tradition is that it consists of @ series of footnotes to Plato” (Whitehead 1929. 63). 7 CT 41, 43 (BM 54595), obv. 4: “GIS-gim-mas | “gi-il-ga-'mes'. History of research of the genre was slow. But when C. Bezold, between 1889 and 1899, published his catalogue of cuneiform tablets found by the British excavators at Nineveh, he was already able to distinguish in his index a large number of “commentar- ies” from texts that were merely “explanatory lists” (Bezold, Catal., 2098-2100). In an introductory work on Babylonian and Assyrian culture from 1903, Bezold also provided one of the earliest brief general descriptions of the genre.’ Another significant step forward was made when L. W. King, in his book on the Babylo- nian Epic of Creation, presented a full edition of an important text commentary alongside the text to which it referred (King 1902, 157-75). Additional auto- graph copies of commentaries, both from Nineveh and from Babylonian cities, were published in subsequent decades by C. Virolleaud (ACh, 1905-1912), T. Meck (1920), C. J. Gadd (CT 41 (1931), 25-50), and many othei Gadd’s CT volume inspired what remains until now the only monographic treatment of Mesopotamian text commentaries, R. Labat’s Commentaires as- syro-babyloniens sur les présages (Labal 1933), a book that offers editions of altogether twenty-two commentaries as well as an introduction that attempts to define the genre. Labat’s work deserves praise because of its pioneering charac- ter and many valuable insights, but its usefulness is limited by the small number of commentaries considered. Moreaver, some of the author’s conclusions seem unjustified. When Labat claims, for example, that the commentaries “mani- festent trés rarement un effort intelligent d’interprétation” (Labat 1933, 22), his judgement may reflect more of the author's own ability to understand the com- ‘mentaries than their actual exegetical potential. With the exception of J. Krecher’s useful but brief entry on “Kommentare” in RIA 6 (Krecher 1980-83),"° there have been no comprehensive treatments of ‘Mesopotamian commentaries since Labat’s book, but several important studies of individual commentaries and commentary groups have appeared. The number of commentaries available in form of autographs or editions has radically in- creased over the past decades, with the SBTU series authored by H. Hunger and E. von Weiher and a number of publications by U. Koch(-Westenholz) (1999, 2000, 2005) providing the bulk of the new material." Lexical lists are important for a study of Mesopotamian text commentaries for three reasons. First, their tabular form is very similar to that of certain com- mentaries, which, just like the lists, present a word that requires discussion in the left column and its explanation in the right. There is little doubt that the lists provided the model for these commentaries, and it is telling that both commen- taries and bilingual lexical lists were sometimes called sdru, as we shall sce in 4.5.1 and 6.2. Second, lexical lists, by supplying a plethora of examples of how to creatively connect words, sounds, and signs, gave the commentators an idea of how to produce such chains of associations themselves. text: mentary tradition 16 2. Philology and divination: ancestors and correlates of the 2.1.2. Glosses Giosses are notes writen by scribes into the texts copied by them. Inscribed between the lines or on the left edge of the tablet, they can have different purposes. Glosses writen in smaller script indicate the pronunciation of difficult logograms or rarely used syllabic values, or they provide, as in the case of many Sumerian texts copied by students during the Old Babylonian period,” Akkadian translations of individual words and phrases. The gloss hepi ess “new break” indicates that the tablet from which the scribe copied his text was damaged, while fiepi labiru “old break” points to a note about stich a break in an earlier manuscript. Glosses can also be marked, most commonly in the first millennium, by separating cola nor- mally consisting of two diagonal wedges (“Glossenkeile”). Usually, glosses of this type provide alternative readings that had to be noted when a scribe copied from deviating versions of the same text. Outside of Mesopotamia, separating cola would introduce translations of Akkadian terms into local languages, such as Hurrian and Canaanite, or mark foreign words. Philology and divination: ancestors and correlates commentary tradition 2.2. omen texts As stated above, many of the Mesopotamian scholars who wrote and studied commentaries were omen specialists. They dealt with the vast area of divine signs that were believed to be detectable, for those who possessed the necessary knowledge, on the exta of the sacrificial sheep, in the life of plants, the behavior of animals and humans, or in the movement of the heavenly bodies. Interpreting such portents correctly ensured an adequate response to challenges that pre- sented themselves in the present and future.” More than any other ancient civilization, Mesopotamia can be characterized as a “divination culture.” Archival sources, royal inscriptions, and year names teach us that extispicy and other forms of predicting the future were already practiced extensively in the third millennium. But their underlying principles ‘were not yet put into writing at that time, a development that took place only during the Old Babylonian period, from which we have our earliest liver models, omen reports, divination-related prayers and rituals, and, most importantly, compendia that offer long lists of extispical, terrestrial, and astronomical omens.*! The individual entries in these compendia always have a bipartite structure. They begin with an observation, the so-called protasis, and end with a prediction based on the observation, the apodosis, such as: summa manzazu nesi rubti ildnisu izzibiisu “If the Station (a part of the liver) is displaced, the prince will be forsaken by his The compendia were copied, rewritten, and in numerous ways amplified during the following centuries, until, probably towards the end of the second millennium, many of them received their final “canonical” form in large omen series such as Eniima Anu Enlil or Summa alu that we know from the first mil- lennium, with their hundreds tablets and tens of thousands of entries, The omen compendia contain full sentences and not just individual words like the lexical lists, but share with the lists the bipartite structure their entries. Like the lists, the compendia are gigantic collections of equations, based on correspondences of various types. Protascs and apodoses are related to cach other through etymology, etymography, mythological and symbolic association, indigenous conceptions of the laws of nature and culture, and many other prin- ciples that vary in the different branches of Mesopotamian Thus, a gigantic repertoire of analogies permeated the corpus of Babylonian omen ready to inspire the commentators. 9 , 5 f 5° For mantics as a form of hermeneutics that still permeates modem ways of under- standing the world, see Hogrebe 1992. 69 For a detailed overview of the various branches of Mesopotamian divination and their historical development, see Maul 2003. $! Temporal and geographical distribution of the commentaries Before providing a typology of Babylonian and Assyrian commentaries, il may be helpful to offer some reflections on the time span from which cuneiform commentaries are attested and the cities in which they were studied. Because the commentaries a) underwent changes over time and b) were influenced by local traditions of scholarship, an overview of their chronological and geographical range can help delineate the parameters within which analyses can be made. In late Mesopotamian tradition, the origins of commentaries are retrojected to the very beginnings of history. A first millennium text that provides an etiol- ogy of the arts of the diviner claims that the antediluvian king Enmeduranki, @ protégé of the gods Samas and Adad who had received from them the knowl- edge of how to perform oil and liver divination, handed this knowledge down to the citizens of Nippur, Sippar, and Babylon, and also gave them Sa itt’ sai “that with commentary.” The episode is obviously fictitious ~ it is a story invented to ascribe old age to the practices of the diviner, and not a historical account, There is, of course, every reason to assume that scholars and students from very carly on discussed texts in academic environments orally. A line from a Sumerian school satire from the Old Babylonian period alludes to such herme- neutical endeavors when it quotes a father addressing the tcacher of his son with the words: gi-sum-ma ki-dul-dul-a-bi dalla mu-na-an-& “You have clarified for him all the hidden meanings of scripture."*! These libraries will be discussed at greater length in 8.2.4, but it should be stressed already here that the preponderance of Assurbanipal commentaries within our corpus obviously affects this book’s overall picture of the commentary tradi- nn. That our corpus is dominated by exegetical treatises on astrology and ex- tispicy, for example, may be attributed to the fact that Assurbanipal was ex- tremely interested in these divinatory disciplines, which were specifically geared towards kings and rulers. We may conjecture that had we more commentaries from temples and private libraries, commentaries on rituals and medical texts would be better represented. One should note, in this context, that the library of a family of exorcists from Assur (sce 8.2.2.1), which dates to the seventh cen- tury as well, yielded several commentaries on magico-medical rituals, but only one on a divinatory text. Although the Assurbanipal commentaries may thus skew statistics towards texts closely linked to the royal sphere, they are nonetheless extremely impor- tant, not least because many of them seem to belong to or derive from a Babylo- nian tradition that is otherwise difficult to grasp. There are so far no commentar- ies from Babylonian cities that can be dated with any degree of certainty to the period preceding the middle of the sixth century,” and so the Nineveh tablets (including those originally owned by Nabi-zuqup-kému) are the only window we have to take at least an indirect look at the exegetical work in which Babylo- nian scholars of earlier times were engaged. From the middle of the sixth century onwards, Babylonian text commentaries are altested in large numbers. Originating from Babylon, Borsippa, Nippur, Sippar, Uruk, Dilbat, and Ur, they date to the Chaldacan, Achaemenid, early Hellenistic, Seleucid, and Parthian periods. The latest commentaries attested so far were copied at the end of the second century BCE by members of the Egi- batila family (see 8.3.4.3.1). It is interesting to note that colophons on Egibatila tablets mention texts, among them commentaries, that were written on parch- ment scrolls (Frahm 2005). The references to such scrolls allow us to speculate that cuneiform commentaries continued to be copied and studied after 100 BCE, but on a medium so perishable that no traces of this late tradition appear in the archaeological record.*” Our corpus can thus be divided into two large blocks: commentaries from Assyria, almost all dating to the seventh century, on one hand, and, on the other, commentaries from Babylonia from the period between 600 and 100 BCE. A comparison of these two groups reveals a number of significant differences. The Assyrian tradition is characterized by larger commentary tablets and a higher ‘umber of commentaries in a tabular format, while in Babylonia small one-column commentary tablets dominate, with entries structured by separating cola and explanations that seem often more sophisticated, in terms of philological depth, than those found in the Assyrian commentaries. In particular, the Babylonian 8 4 few earlier tablets may surface when the commentaries from the Babylon Collec- tion of the British Museum will be published, but this will not change the overall picture. *7 On the possibility that cuneiform writing and scholarship flourished until the early Sasanian period, see Geller 1997. Geller’s arguments for such a late date for the “death” of cuneiform civilization were questioned by A. Westenholz (2007). 3. Temporal and geographical distribution of the commentaries 27 ‘commentaries include far more often than theit Assyrian predecessors quotations from other literary and religious texts. In addition, the commentaries from Assyria are frequently designated mukallimtu, while their Babylonian counterparts make almost no use of this term. Tis not easy to account for these differences. Are they due to the fact that so. many commentaries from Assyria originate from the library of a politically ac- tive king who may have favored a more “pragmatic” hermeneutical approach, while most of the Babylonian commentaries come from the tablet collections of private scholars operating in an environment that encouraged more contempla- tive and speculative forms of exegetical reasoning? Do the differences reflect a divide between Assyrian and Babylonian scholarly traditions? Or is the chrono- logical gap that separates the two groups the reason for the aforementioned dis- crepancies? While we can speculate that all those factors play a role, we cannot at present answer any of these questions with certainty and have to hope that one day earlier commentaries from Babylonia will be found that may help us tackle them more successfully. A fall history of Mesopotamian text commentaries cannot yet be written. The available material gives the impression, however, despite the Gifferences between the Assurbanipal commentaries and those from Babylonia, that it would be an exaggeration to postulate that a “paradigmatic shift” took place shortly after the fall of the Assyrian empire, from which a completely new tradition of commentary writing emerged." It seems therefore legitimate to present the commentaries from Assyria and Babylonia together in the typologi- cal analysis that follows, pointing out differences wherever necessary. 88 Such a has been postulated by Brown 2000 with regard to the astrological and astronomical sciences of Mesopotamia. According to Brown, during the eighth and sev- ‘nth centuries BCE, a paradigm based on divination was followed, in what amounted to revolution of wisdom, by a paradigm founded on the prediction of celestial phenomena. | False

text: 4. of the commentaries The following typology of Babylonian and Assyrian text commentaries is based on five criteria: medium, relationship to the text commented on, form, types of explanations, and commentarial In the course of the discussion, ! will try to point out to what extent these criteria are related to one another. A basic feature of the commentaries, their essentially atomistic nature, should be mentioned right away. Almost all their explanations concern individual lemmiata, i.c., words or short phrases extracted from the base text. The commentaries virtually never inter- pret a text in its entirety by describing its general ideas,” although short digests of omen texts, such as the so-called rikis gerri to Entima Anu Enlil, existed. Albeit rare and restricted to astrology and extispicy, more theoretical discus- sions of universally applicable rules are occasionally attested in the commentary tradition, contrary to claims that Mesopotamians were incapable of abstract thought. They are, however, normally not strictly text-related. 4.1. Medium From the perspective of the modern scholar, the most important medium used to write cuneiform commentaries is the clay tablet (Akk. fuppuz), the only support on which commentaries have been preserved. Clay tablets bearing commentaries have very different sizes and formats. The largest are multi-column tablets such as BLO, no. 88, a three-column tablet from Assurbanipal’s library inscribed with a mukallimiu-commentary on the fifth chapter of the extispicy series bartiu! This commentary originally contained between 250 and 300 fairly long lines. There is indirect evidence that some commentary tablets may have been even larger. K 1315+ (BLO, no. 42, 1),” a small Assurbanipal tablet in Babylonian script in- scribed with a commentary on the fourth chapter af hdriitu, contains, according to its colophon, an excerpt “from an Assyrian dubgallu (‘big Dubgallu-tablets were large — the subscript of the god list CT 24, 20-46 indicates that they could in- clude more than 1,200 lines.” If this represents what was the standard size of dub- gallu, some commentary tablets must have offered very substantial amounts text. However, such tablets would have been rare exceptions. Berrin 2005, in an attempt to analyze the Pesher-commentaries from Qumran, distinguishes between form, content, method, and motive. The present study will deal with the last three criteria of Berrin’s list in chapters 5, 7, 8.4. and 9. Medium 29 Most of the commentary tablets from Assurbanipal’s library that are well enough preserved to assess their original size have one or two columns only. Sometimes, the content of a large commentary tablet could be distributed over several smaller tablets. Certain /zbu commentary tablets, for example, offer the text of about one column from the so-called “Principal which is attested on a four-column tablet from Assur containing more than 560 (short) entries (see 2). Some Assyrian commentaries owned by private scholars were written on small one-column tablets in the landscape format; one of them, the Eniima Anu Enlil commentary K 872, is labeled as an “wiltu-tablet” (see 7.3.1.5). Most commentaries from Babylonia are written on small one-column tablets as well.”* Colophons often call these tablets im-gid-da (= git, imgiddii, or liginnu).”” Known from the Old Babylonian period onwards, the term im-gid-da is employed for tablets in both landscape and portrait formats, even though it literally means “long tablet.” Im-gid-da tablets were not only used to write commentaries, but also for excerpts, official documents, and other purposes. Colophons providing information on the circumstances of the scribes’ work suggest that most of the commentaries available to us were no spontaneous new creations by students and scribes grappling with a given text, but rather copies of older commentaries.”* This finding is somewhat surprising since we would expect that commentaries were a “living” genre aimed at providing fresh explanations for “canonical” compositions whenever need for this arose. Examples include the Assur and Babylon commentaries on “Marduk’s Address” (see 7.2.2), Late Babylonian commentaries from Nippur and Ur on a collection of incantations and treatments for a woman having difficulties in childbirth (see 7.4.2.1, comm. 1, and 7.4.2.5), as well as LBAT 1530 and TU 17, two Late Babylo- nian commentaries on Eniima Anu Enlil 8 (see 7.3.1.3). They add an additional column to the entries, already in tabular form, of the respective lists. Very rarely, multi-column formats can be found in other com- mentaries as well. Tablet 1 of the extispicy commentary Multabiltu has three columns, the first two of which contain key-terms designating specific phenom- ena referred to in a number of related protases and apodoses, while the third quotes an omen entry in full in order to illustrate the close association between the aforementioned Another three-column commentary is whal may be the second tablet of the serialized astrological commentary Sin ina tamartisu (7.3.1.4). Indentation type commentaries For commentators who wanted to provide longer quotations from the base text and more complex explanations, the tabular list was too restrictive a format. Instead, they would present their exegetical ruminations as a running text, with separate entries indicated by indentation or cola. All the lines containing explanations related to the quotation in question would be indented, making it easy for the reader to identify the begin- ning and the end of an individual commentary In Nineveh, commentar- ies of this type were normally called mukallimtu. text: 40 4. Typology of the commentaries alization of word, as well as its graphemic rendering, were not conventional. The word, whether spoken or written, denoted its object by nature. The concept that not only the content a text, but also its “expressive sub- stance” can be meaningful is not unfamiliar to us. But it is limited in our modern understanding to the aesthetic message, the poem, the work of art. In the scien- tific discourse of today, a belief in the meaningfulness of the expressive sub- stance has no place. Sin Mesopotamia, however, no such distinction was made. As result, we find that Babylonian and Assyrian commentators, as the passage from our Sa-gig commentary demonstrates, would use both the content a text and its phonetic and orthographic “fabric” in their efforts to arrive at a better textual understanding. Ingeniously establishing new meanings through the use of (near) homonyms of words or syllables, as well as through graphemic associa- tion and other forms of analogy, they would produce explanation after explana- tion and regard all of them as equally valid. Hermeneutic techniques used in Babylonian and Assyrian commentaries Early rabbinic scholarship has left us three lists of hermeneutic “rules” for how to interpret the Hebrew Bible: the seven, thirteen, or thirty-two middot ascribed to Hillel, Ishmael, and Eliezer ben Yose, respectively.” They represent differ- cent approaches to an explicit “theory” of hermeneutics. The scholars of Babylo- nia and Assyria did apparently not produce such a theory ~ at least, they never put it into writing. This leaves the task of identifying the basic principles and procedures of cuneiform hermeneutics to the modem scholar, who has to deduce them by means of studying individual commentary entries.” Beginning with the fairly simple and moving towards the more complicated, this chapter will provide an overview and examples of the most important com- mentarial techniques used by Mesopotamian exegetes.””” The fundamental dis- tinction between literal and non-literal modes of interpretation, for which the ancient scholars had their own terminology, has been discussed in 4.2 and is not a factor in the more detailed classification of hermeneutical procedures provided here, Yet it will come as no surprise that to give simple synonyms normally leads to a literal interpretation of a passage, while etymological and etymographical analysis yields itself more to an “allegorical” approach. Hermeneutic techniques used in Babylonian and Assyrian commentaries were more flexible in their interpretation of omens featuring a lugal 80; they could apply them both to the king at home and to the enemy king. Etymology and etymography It has already been pointed out, in 4.4, that Babylonian and Assyrian scholars analyzed not only the content of a text, but also its expressive substance, that is, the sound of its words and the signs with which these words are written. As pointed out in 2.1, Mesopotamian scholars regarded these two languages, in spite of their great differences, as closely re- lated and, unlike other idioms, capable of conveying essential truths. These be- liefs provide the foundation for their strategy to interpret individual elements of Akkadian words (as well as names and logograms) in the light of Sumerian. The technique they used to isolate small word components suitable for such analysis is reminiscent of what is known from later rabbinical tradition as notarikon. A good example of its application is an entry in K 778. a commentary on EAE 15.“ Obv. 3-4 this tablet deal with the Akkadian word bardri (written ba-ra- ri) “at dusk,” which, in the omen commented on, specifies the time of the occur- rence of lunar eclipse. text: 6. Sources of the explanations particularly striking feature of the cuneiform exegetical tradition is its ano- nymity. Subscripts on commentary tablets, while declaring that at least some of their explanations go back to certain “(master-)scholars” (Sa pi umméni), never actually identify these scholars by name.*”* Such anonymity suggests that in Mesopotamia, unlike later rabbinical, Greco-Roman, Islamic, and Chris- tian traditions, it was apparently not only, and perhaps even not primarily, the commentator who provided the commentary with authority. Yet the ies, were frequently copied, evidently did possess authority, and so the question arises where this authority actually came from. One answer seems to be that it derived from various canonical texts — texts that were excerpted and reproduced in the very explanations put forward in the commentaries. For many of these explanations are clearly not just some exe- gete’s ad hoc attempts at understanding. They are, instead, quotations taken textual record that constituted the Mesopotamian “stream of tradi- tion." text: 108 6. Sources of explanations Our overview of commentarial quotations shows an interesting dichotomy. The only texts quoted in commentaries from eighth and seventh century Assyria are lexical lists and explanatory texts, while the later Babylonian commentaries also provide quotations, many of them fairly long, from magico-medical, reli- gious, legal, and literary texts. At first glance, one might be inclined to attribute this difference to an opposition between Assyrian and Babylonian hermeneutics, but this is not a very likely solution since many of the commentaries from As- syria seem to draw on Babylonian traditions. Thus, conceptual changes that cuneiform hermeneutics experienced during the centuries following the downfall of the Assyrian empire may have been a more decisive factor. Of course, one also needs to take into account the nature of the texts com- mented on in commentaries with literary quotations: they include diagnostic and medical treatises, Alu and Izbu, and the lexical series Aa. Commentaries on these texts are primarily attested from Babylonia, while commentaries from Assyria, most of which originate from Assurbanipal’s libraries in Nineveh, cover in their majority astrology and extispicy. There are, for reasons that re- main so far no medical and no Aa commentaries from Assyria at all, there is only one Assyrian commentary on Sa-gig, and most of the Assyrian commentaries on A/u and izbu are tablets in a tabular format and in Babylonian script with fairly elementary explanations only. Yet precisely those texts ~ per- haps because they were more immediately concerned with the condition hu- maine than treatises on the sky or the liver” ~ seem to have been regarded by some of the ancient commentators as being in particular need of an tion that was based on quotations from religious and literary With regard to the form of commentarial quotations, il can be observed that many are marked by opening and closing cola only. Quite a few, however, are introduced more specifically by either /ibbi “as in” or Sa igbii “(this is) what he The term sa igbit has received some attention in recent George (1991, 139) discusses it in connection with the expressions Sti pi and Sa pi ummani from commentary subscripts and remarks: “[Sa igbii] often introduces quotations from the traditional corpus of anonymous literature; but the referent there, small inaccuracies and deviations from the received text when providing quota- tions. Texts commented on and their commentaries: an overview This chapter provides a concise overview of the texts that were commented on in ancient Mesopotamia and of the different commentaries explaining them. It is organized according to the genres represented by the base texts. Due to the large amount of textual material that will be presented here ~ roughly thirty base texts, some consisting of as many as 120 tablets, and more than 860 commentaries — the amount of information given on individual base texts and commentaries is limited. While essential publications, editions, and discussions will be indicated, readers will have to turn to Borger’s HKL and the 4/0 indexes to find more complete information on individual texts and commentaries. The chapter employs a number of specific abbreviations and conventions. C refers to a copy, E to an edition, and D to a scholarly discussion of a commen- tary. AL indicates that a tablet originated in Assurbanipal’s libraries. Commen- taries from Assyria are written in Assyrian characters unless otherwise noted. The form of individual commentaries and the terminology of their subscripts is described in accordance with sections 4.3 and 4.5 of this study: “tab. type” des- ignates a tabular format, “ind. type” a layout that makes use of indentation, and “cola type” the commentary format of a continuous text with entries divided by cola; “mukallimtu 3a” represents the subscript uppi n-kam mukallimtu, etc. The absence of remarks on the subscript or colophon of a commentary tablet” indi- cates that the lower part of the tablet’s reverse, on which these scribal notes might have been written, is lost. They spent comparatively little time on explaining (or, for that matter, on copying) literature, The commentary UET 6/3, 897, which deals with portions of the short mythological tale of the “Cow of Sin,” is not included in this section because its main focus is on the rituals and incantations in which the tale is embedded; it will be discussed in 7.4.2.5. 7.1.1. Eniima elis Also called the “Babylonian epic of creation,” Eniima eli describes in seven tablets how the world came into being and how the god Marduk of Babylon became its ruler after defeating the ancient matriarch Tiamat, a dragon-like creature represent- ing the sca, who was accompanied by a host of terrifying monsters. One of the text’s most important functions was to provide an etiology of the religious and political predominance claimed by the city of Babylon. The text's date of com- Position is much disputed, with suggestions ranging from the reign of Hammurapi to the early first millennium. Some indications point towards the time of Nebuchad- nezzar T (1125-1104 BCE) as the period when the epic was most likely written, Eniima eli was recited on the occasion of important religious festivals, notably the Akitu festival celebrated in Babylon at the beginning of the year, and intensively studied in elementary education in first millennium Babylonia.>” Its reception in Assyria, Babylonia, and beyond will be discussed at greater length in ch. 11.5” Eniima elis is accessible in numerous translations, among them recent ones in English by Foster (2005, 436-86) and Lambert (2008, 35-59). No up-to-date scholarly edition of it is at present available, but a new “pedagogical” edition has recently been provided by Talon (2005); it should be consulted together with the important reviews by Borger (2008) and Oelsner (2009). The “Babylonian Theodicy” Like Ludlul, the “Babylonian Theodicy,” another Babylonian wisdom text (BWL, 63-91, translation: Foster 2005, 914-22), struggles with the problem of divine justice. The “Theodicy” is a dialogue between a sufferer and his who confront each other in stanzas of eleven lines each, all beginning with the same syllable. Read vertically, the syllables of the various stanzas form an acrostic, which points towards a certain (E)sagil-kina-ubbib as the author of the composition. This individual is also attested elsewhere. A Seleucid list of fa- mous scholars (van Dijk 1962, 44-52) identifies him as chief-scholar (ummdnu) of the Isin II rulers Nebuchadnezzar I (1125-1104 BCE) and Adad-apla-iddina (1068-1047 BCE), and the “Catalogue of Texts and Authors” from Nineveh (Lambert 1962, 66-67, K 10802, rev. 1-2) claims that he wrote the under the latter king. Babylonian and Assyrian commentators focused their attention on one specific portion of Udug-bul: a long incantation known as “Marduk Address to the De- mons.” Originally an independent composition, “Marduk’s Address” was at some point integrated into the Udug-bul series, representing its tablets 10 and 11. The extant portions of “Marduk’s Address,” some only known from commentaries, have recently been edited, but without a full overview of the various mamu- scripts, by Geller in his preliminary work on Udug-bul (Geller 2007, XV, 58-63, 150-57, 230-36). An earlier edition of “Marduk’s Address,” now somewhat outdated, is owed to Lambert (1954-56, 1959-60). text: 130 7. Texts commented on and their commentaries: an overview EAE are frequently referred to as Sin (moon), Samaé (sun), Adad (weather), and Jktar (planets). In addition to the “canonical” series, there was a series of tablets with “extraneous” (ati) EAE omens,“* as well as a serialized collection of excerpts called rikis geri." The apodoses of EAE concer the welfare of the king and the state, and the fate of foreign rulers and countries. It therefore comes as no surprise that astro- logical observations and EAE omens are extensively discussed in many of the reports and letters Assyrian and Babylonian scholars sent to the Assyrian kings Esarhaddon (680-669 BCE) and Assurbanipal (669 - ca. 630 BCE). These mes- sages, published in SAA 8 and SAA 10, demonstrate how EAE omens were actually applied to the celestial phenomena observed by the scholars. They occa- sionally refer to or quote from commentaries and are therefore of considerable interest for this study (see 8.2.4.4). The ever increasing significance attributed to astrology in the course of the first millennium may explain why copying and studying EAE did not lose its luster after the overthrow of the “Chaldaean” empire in 539 BCE had eliminated the last independent state of ancient Mesopotamia and with it the royal clients who had been astrology’s main patrons.© Establishing how celestial phenom- ena mirrored and anticipated events on earth remained a central concern for Babylonian scholars. The prestige of EAE was so great that even scholars who specialized in mathematical astronomy continued to call themselves fupéar Eniima Anu Enlil “scribes of EAE."*" Much of what we know about the organization of EAE is owed to contribu- tions by E. Weidner (1941-44, 1954-56, and 1968/69). Unfortunately, only parts of EAE are available in modem editions: tablets 1-6 in Verderame 2002a, tablet 14 in Al-Rawi & George 1991/92, tablets 15-22(23) in Rochberg-Halton 1988 (see also Al-Rawi & George 2006), tablets 23(24)-29(30) in van Soldt 1995 (sce also Gehiken 2000), tablets 42 and 43 in Gehlken 2008, tablets 50-51 in BPO 2, tablet 56 in Largement 1957, tablets 59-62(63) (Venus omens) in BPO 1 and 3, and tablets 63(64)-65 (Jupiter omens) in BPO 4. Unlike astrology, extispicy was a divinatory procedure that aimed at verifica- tion, not at prognostication (Pongratz-Leisten 1999, 128). It answered a specific question asked by someone. The diviners consulted omen compendia that in- cluded very specific apodoses such as “A corpse will be thrown in front of the city gate of the enemy” (BLO, no. 26: but the precise content of such apodoses did not really matter. The only issue of importance was whether the apodosis was auspicious or inauspicious — and it is therefore not surprising that most commentaries on extispicy omens focus on the protases of the relevant texts, Until the first millennium, when its prestige began to be matched, and was eventually surpassed, by that of extispicy had been Mesopotamia’s most esteemed discipline of divination.” Attempts by later tradition to Tetroject its beginnings to the reign of the antediluvian king Enmeduranki of Sippar are obviously unrcliable (Lambert 1998), but there is no question that the practice of making decisions based on an inspection of the internal organs of a sacrificial animal was indeed very old; it is attested in contemporary sources from the 26!" century onwards. Yet the earliest written extispicy compendia date only to the 19" and 18" centuries, the time when other omen traditions began to be put into writing as well.”*” The available evidence shows that extispicy omens were organized in some sort of proto-series in Old Babylonian times, but it appears that these series did hot yet enjoy universal acclaim.”” Extispicy omen texts from the second of the second millennium were found in Babylon, Assur, and the Western and Eastern periphery of Mesopotamia. From this period hail the earliest texts representing the nisirti bariiti tradition (see 7.3.2.2). But il is only from the first millennium that we have a “canonical” collection of omens that was in use all over Mesopotamia and became the subject of numerous commen- taries: the so-called baritu series.””! Texts commented on and their commentaries: an overview Chapter 10: Multabiltu “interpretation” The final chapter of the bardiu series comprises seventeen tablets, whose in- cipits are listed in the catalogue tablets K 1352 and K 3041 (Secrets, no. Unlike the other bariitu sections, Multabiltu is not focused on specific parts of the exta. Instead, it deals with general rules the diviner had to take into account when establishing the outcome of an extispicy. These rules are expressed in abstract terms, but more frequently, they are communicated long lists of protases that serve as illustrations of the system behind central of the diviner’s craft. A passage in the nisirti bariiti text Secrets, no. 58 (lines 57-62) shows the importance Multabiltu held for the ancient scholars, It upon the diviner to take a close look at the various tablets of Muliabiltu when performing an extispicy: “They should be present in your mind (lit., ‘heart’y” (ina libbika libbatkita). Multabiltu quotes and recontextualizes material excerpted from all parts of the bariitu series, as well as from other sources. Even though one can debate whether it is a text commentary in its own right, there can be no question that it shares many features of the mukallimtu-commentaries on bariitu. there is no need for a detailed treatment of the chapter in the present Multabiltu has recently been edited in a comprehensive fashion by U. Koch,*? and it would make little sense to duplicate information that can easily be tracted from this publication. 1 will, however, discuss some of Multabilty’s most characteristic features, and provide data on findspots and scribes of relevant manuscripts. well-known section of Multabiltu is its first tablet (Secrets, no, 2), the extispicy treatise that seeks to explain in systematic terms how bariitu and apodoses relate to one another. The tablet is divided into three columns, homonymity, and symbolic associations govern the analogies drawn. They may be neologisms, based on existing adjectives and verbs, that were specifi- cally created to express the ideas articulated in Multabiltu 1. text: 190 7. Texts commented on and their commentaries: an overview 7.3.2.2. Nisirti bartiti texts More than a hundred manuscripts concerned with extispicy belong to a category of texts that was labeled by the ancient scholars in a number of subscripts as nisirti bariiti “secrets of extispicy.” According to Koch (Secrets, 34), nisirti b4riiti texts, some of which were loosely serialized, “clearly do not belong to any of the chapters of the divination series itself nor are they related to mate- rial such as the famitus, ikribus or ritual descriptions, and they are not commen- taries to any of these genres cither.” Due to this last point, and since all the rele- vant manuscripts have just been edited and (at least preliminarily) analyzed by Koch (Secrets, 34-72, 273-544), they will not be treated again here, even though it should be noted that the texts, with their complicated scholarly deliberations on combined protases, protases in context, small subsections of the liver, and calculations of the “stipulated term” are in many ways part of the same discourse to which the commentaries belong. Unlike those, nisirti bariiti texts are already known from copies that date to the late second millennium and some may have had written forerunners that go back even further the orthography of a few tablets recalls Old Babylonian conventions. Nisirti bartiti texts were found in Nineveh (99 MSS), Assur (4 MSS), Late Babylonian Uruk (4 MSS), and probably in Babylon (1 MS) and Sippar (1 MS). Physiognomic omens (Alamdimmi) Babylonian and Assyrian scholars believed that physiognomy, the observation 1 of physical features of a healthy man or woman, and an analysis of his or her behavior, would yield important clues for establishing the future destiny of that person.” From the Old Babylonian period onwards, they collected pertinent observations in large omen compendia, many of which were eventually united in a “canonical” series compiled by Esagil-kin-apli, an eleventh century scholar who also created the diagnostic compendium Sa-gig (sce 7.4.1). Esagil-kin-apli’s physiognomic omen series, called Alamdimmi “physique, form,” is attested in first millennium copies from Nineveh, Assur, Kalhu, Baby- lon, Sippar, and Uruk. It comprises five sections, or chapters, the first of which; Alamdimmi, gave the whole work its name. This first chapter, the largest and most important of the series, consists of twelve tablets with various | physical features observed on the body of a man. The series’s other chapters are... © { Nigdimdimmi, on the behavior of men (2), Kataduggit, on verbal utterances and what they signify (3), Summa sinnistu gaqgadu rabét, on physical features of as women (4), and Summa liptu, on moles and similar body marks (5). There are. also tablets with “non- omens. A typical “[If the hair of] his (a man’s) is plentiful, he will become rich” (Alam- dimmiéi 2: 63 = Bick 2000b, 76-77). text: 220 7, Texts commented on and their commentaries: an overview commentaries are known almost exclusively from Late Babylonian sources, and are characterized by unusually sophisticated hermeneutics.'”” It seems therefore reasonable to present them together with the therapeutic commentaries in a joint chapter on medical texts. Sa-gig consists of six sub-series, or chapters, cach of which is divided into individual tablets. The total number of these tablets amounts to forty, the sacred number of Ea, patron deity of exorcists, scholars, and scribes. The chapters cover observations the exorcist made on his way to the patient (ch. 1 = tablets 1- 2), specific symptoms listed a capite ad calcem (ch. 2 = tablets 3-14), the rela- tionship between the symptoms, the time when the illness broke out, and its prospective length (ch. 3 = tablets 15-25), different forms of epilepsy (ch. 4 = tablets 26-30), the length of certain fever diseases (ch. 5 = tablets 31-35), and finally pregnancies and illnesses of women (ch. 6 = tablets 36-40). An old edi- tion of the whole series can be found in R. Its findspot is known to have produced many Anu-iksur tablets. 7.4.2. texts Therapeutic medicine was a time-honored discipline in ancient Mesopotamia. Written sources dealing with physicians and medical procedures, among them administrative documents, letters, law codes, and literary texts, are attested from the third millennium No other texts, however, tell us more about the healing strategies Babylonian and Assyrian physicians applied than the nu- merous cuneiform compendia that provide directions on the treatment and care of patients. Dealing with a vast array of diseases, their entries typically comprise three sections: a description, frequently introduced by Summa “if,” of the symp- toms from which the patient suffered, prescriptions for the preparation of drugs and other substances to fight the affliction, and orders on how to apply them. Medication was administered in the form of potions, fumigations, ointments, or More devices such as semi-precious stones put on necklaces played a role as and often, incantations and prayers would accompany the treatment. Babylonian and Assyrian therapeutic texts represent a more complex and less well-explored genre than the diagnostic and prognostic tradition. Subscripts on tablets from first millennium Nineveh and Uruk indicate that efforts were made by the scribes of later periods to serialize the therapeutic corpus. The text was written on large monuments, among them the famous stela from Susa now housed in the Louvre, which is our most valuable source for the text. But it also became one of the central cultural texts of the Mesopotamian “stream of tradi- tion.” While there is little evidence that Hammurapi’s law collection was ever strictly applied in the courts, its importance as a text that was studied in school and handed down from generation to generation of scholars is well documented. The laws provided a lasting model of ideal justice, and the language they were cast in continued to be held in the highest regard. Copies of the laws from both Babylo- nia and Assyria abound, with the last ones dating to the Late Babylonian period. The Laws of Hammurapi are divided into three parts: a prologue outlining Hammurapi’s divine election as a lawgiver, the main section of the text with its almost 300 laws, and an epilogue demanding respect for the laws and inviting those subjected to wrongdoing to consult them. text: 242 7. Texts commented on and their commentaries: an overview Hammurapi’s “code” is the only law collection from Mesopotamia on which ancient scholars commented. Given the great age af the laws, which must have made it difficult for the literati of first millennium Babylonia and Assyria to fully understand them, it is somewhat surprising that only one commentary on them has been discovered so far. The tablet in question, BM 59739 from the “Sippar Collection,” has been published by Lambert (1989b, 96-98, C, E). Un- fortunately, very little of it is preserved. text: 8. The socio-cultural milieu of Mesopotamian commentary studies Assyriology, in many ways a field confronted by significant obstacles ~ lexical and grammatical uncertainties, broken texts, a tradition lost for almost 2000 years — has one significant advantage over a discipline like classics: the original setting of its literary and scholarly texts is, in many cases, well known. A large number of Assyrian and Babylonian clay tablets were discovered in the build- ings where they were studied and stored in antiquity," and many have colo- phons that provide information on their owners and scribes, the whereabouts of the originals from which they were copied, the dates of these copies, and the reasons for producing them. Thanks to such colophons, we can often assess the socio-cultural context even of tablets that originate from undocumented excava- tions or secondary locations. Drawing on the information provided by colophons and archaeological con- text, this chapter will present a short overview of the Assyrian and Babylonian scriptoria and libraries where commentaries were studied and housed, of the ‘owners of commentary tablets, and of the students and scribes who copied them. Of course, remarks on the social background of these individuals will have to be concise, and only limited information can be given on their broader intellectual interests as mirrored by other tablets written and owned by them. Bibliographi- cal references will have to be selective as well.'"” Questions regarding the origins of the commentary tradition and its indebt- edness to processes of canonization and textualization will not be treated here; they will instead be dealt with in ch. 9. 8.1. Mesopotamian library types We can basically distinguish among three types of libraries in Mesopotamia: temple libraries, palace libraries, and the libraries of private individuals." It is, however, not always easy to keep these library types strictly apart. ILis important to note that tablets found in temples are usually not explicitly labeled as property of a sanctuary or a deity; instead, they bear colophons that identify exorcists, lamen- tation-priests, and other scholars as their scribes and owners, According to Clan- cier, the presence, on the temple premises, of tablets written and “owned” by “private” individuals means that we have to distinguish between two types of tablets housed in temples: on one hand, those really belonging to the sanctuary (makkir TN), and, on the other, available in far larger numbers, those belonging to members of professions closely associated with it, such as lamentation priests, (kali) or exorcists (dsipu)."?** ; ; The only palace libraries that have yielded cuneiform commentaries are those of the Assyrian king Assurbanipal at Nineveh (8.2.4). Despite the exceptional char- acter of these libraries,'"” their significance can hardly be overstated. The ma- jority of the commentary tablets presented in this book originate from Assur- banipal’s libraries, and no other single source provides more information on the intellectual milieu in which thrived textual studies in ancient Mesopotamia. Finally, there are the libraries and scriptoria of private individuals, from both. Assyria and Babylonia, that have yielded commentary tablets. The earliest dated commentaries known so far, written in the late eighth century BCE, come from the tablet collection of the Assyrian scholar Nabii-zuqup-kénu (8.2.1.1), while the latest, dating to ca, 100 BCE, belonged to members of the Egibatila family in Babylon (8.3.4.3.1). Of particular interest are the libraries of two families of exorcists from Uruk, from where some of our most sophisticated commentaries originate (8.3.2.2). Among the private owners of commentaries Were prestigious scribes” (see 82.1.1 and 8.2.2.3), exorcists (8.2.2.1, 8.3.2.2), lamentation-priests (83.2.1, 83.23, 8.33, and 8343.1), temple brewers and néfakku-priests (8.3.2.22, 8.3.2.3, 8.3.3), diviners (8.2.4.3, 8.3.4.3.1), and even leather-workers (8.3.4.3.1). All of them were apparently related in some way to the temples of their hometowns, and in some cases to the palace. The scribes who copied the commentary tablets were often advanced students of these specialists and in many cases their sons. The only remains of what may have been a Middle-Assyrian royal library, associated with Tiglath-ileser I, were published by Maul 2003a. It is only through this additional interpretation that Akkulanu manages to justify why he selected the omen about the black lunar horns in the first place. Akkulanu quotes the relevant entries from the commentary out of their origi- nal sequence, and he skips everything that does not apply to the specific case he is writing about. The reference to Saturn standing close to the moon, discussed as yel another possible interpretation of the “black homs” in the Sin ina tamartisu is left out by him because the celestial phenomenon that had occurred did not involve Satu. This method of using commentaries rather freely and without explicit references to specific sources seems to be typical for the way Assyrian and Babylonian scholars of the Late Assyrian period relied on written exegetical treatises. We often do not know whether an explanation provided by a scholar is based on a commentary, a lexical list, or oral lore. It is, for example, difficult to estab- lish the sources of the numerous glosses Nabi-ahhé-eriba and Balasi offer in the reports and letters they wrote between 675(?) and 666 In the letter SAA 10, 58, Balasi quotes a bird omen with the apodosis bitu St igdihw irassi “That house will experience profit (isdiliw),” and then explains: is-di-hu né-me- Ju “Profit (means) ‘gain.”” This equation could be taken from a commentary, for instance the Principal Commentary on Stwmma izbu, where it is attested in line but it could also go back to some unknown lexical tablet or the oral knowledge scholars acquired during their career. Babylon and Borsippa Babylon, ancient metropolis, capital of the Chaldaean empire, and last strong- hold of Babylonian traditions, may have been, together with its sister city Bor- sippa, the most important center of cuneiform learning in first millennium Mesopotamia. Due to the chances of discovery, scholarly tablets from Babylon dating to the early centuries of the first millennium are rare, but large numbers of such tablets have been found that were written between ca, 600 BCE and the beginning of the Common Era. They testify to Babylon’s continuing status as an intellectual hub during the centuries of slow decline that Mesopotamian civiliza- tion experienced after the loss of political independence in 39 BCE. Regretta- bly, most of these tablets come from excavations in the eightcen-seventies and early eighteen-cighties that were very poorly documented. The later, far better documented archacological investigations undertaken between 1899 and 1917 by Robert Koldewey on behalf of the Deutsche Orient-Gesellschaft yielded much smaller numbers of scholarly texts.'“** Yet thanks to recent contributions by Reade (CBT VI, xii-xxxviii), van Driel (1989), and especially Clancier (2005b, 193-335, 2009, 105-213, 409-70), it is nonetheless possible to venture some hypotheses regarding the original setting of the tablets uncarthed by the carlier excavations. 83.4.1. The cultural seting of Mesopotamian hermeneuties 313 8.4, The cultural setting of Mesopotamian hermeneutics The preceding overview of the scribes and owners of cuneiform commentaries, and the libraries where these commentaries were stored, allows a number of conclusions. In the past, many Assyriologists have stressed the didactic aspects of the writing of commentaries. The title of a much-quoted article by Meier, “Kom- mentare aus dem Archiv der Tempelschule in Assur” (Meier 1937-39), epito- mizes this approach. The legacy of Babylonian and Assyrian hermeneutics suggestion.’ Another issue that comes to mind is that a famous founding fij ure of rabbinic exegesis, Hillel the Elder, is said to originate from Babylonii Sukkah 20a reports: “When the Law had fallen into oblivion, it was restored by Ezra of Babylon; when it was a second time forgotten, Hillel the Babylonian came and recovered it.”" Hillel, who lived in Jerusalem during the time of Herod, is credited in rabbinic tradition with having been the first to create a list of rules on how to interpret Scripture,'" and it is somewhat tempting to surmise that he may have instructed Palestinian scholars in hermeneutical techniques that he had drawn from cuneiform traditions. On closer inspection, however, such a scenario becomes rather doubtful. First of all, much of what later sources have to say about Hillel seems fairly unreliable. In fact, the historical connection of Hillel with the seven rules attributed to him cannot be ascertained, Moreover, the rules associated with Hillel reflect far more a Hellenistic than a Babylonian background. They are in many ways reminiscent of the hermeneutical methods applied by the Alexandrinian exegetes of Homer. The name of the second of Hillel’s rules, gezerah Sawah, which refers to an argument from analogy, may actually derive from the Hellenistic rhetorical term synkrisis pros ison. The clos- est resemblances between Babylonian hermeneutical techniques and rules of interpretation listed in rabbinical works can be found, not in Hillel’s catalogue of exegetical tools, but in a later list of thirty-two rules of interpretation ascribed to Rabbi Eliezer." This list includes paronomasia, gematria, and notarikon, hermeneutical techniques whose application is well attested in Babylonian and Assyrian commentaries." But other rules in the list display again a degree of abstraction that seems rather alien to Mesopotamian scholarship. For the time being, it is impossible to give a final answer to the question of whether rabbinic interpretation is based to any extent on Mesopotamian herme- neutics. The parallels pointed out in this chapter suggest, however, that there may well be connections. The question deserves further study, ideally pursued by Assyriologists and scholars in Judaic studies in cooperation. Quite clearly, there are significant differences between the commen- tary traditions of the three aforementioned civilizations. ‘Mesopotamian exegesis deviated in method from the Greek tradition in its reliance on a fixed body of texts, whose authoritative character Was never put into question. Babylonian and Assyrian scholars of the first millennium regarded originality, quite literally, as a return to the origins. They were never haunted by what Harold Bloom (1997) has called the “anxiety of influence.” Greek scholar- ship, in contrast, was characterized by the intellectual concept of “hypolepsis,” the idea that truth was to be pursued through a series of progressive rewritings of earlier studies." ‘An important difference, as already mentioned, between Mesopotamian and Jewish interpretation is that the latter, with its focus on the normative dimen- sions of law and the formative dimensions of history, addresses questions of a far more “existential” character than those dealt with in Mesopotamian herme- neutics, whose main goal was to arrive al a better understanding of omens, medicine, and other learned technical disciplines. The question of why Babylonian and Assyrian commentaries, as well as other scholarly works from Mesopotamia, display so little “progressive” inquisi- tiveness, and why they are largely devoid of discussions of existential concerns such as law and history, is difficult to answer, and any single-cause explanation runs the risk of oversimplification. It would be surprising, however, if the defi- ciencies in question were not in some way linked to the political ideology that predominated in Mesopotamia when the cuneiform commentary tradition emerged. This ideology centered around the concept of a strong king who acted as the only source of authority. No critical questioning and no historical “decon- struction” of the institution of royal rule was in order,"™” and no law was sup- posed to limit the power of the king. In such a climate, “hypolepsis” and a dis- course on legal questions were unlikely to flourish. ‘This brings us back to the beginning of this study, where I have entertained the possibility that the emergence of a commentary tradition in Mesopotamia might be seen as an “axial” phenomenon, related to the dawn of completely new forms of religious and scientific thought that can be observed in other civiliza- tions of the first millennium BCE." In the end, it must be admitted that such a claim cannot be fully held up. The political realities of Mesopotamian civiliza- tion put limits to the “axialization” of cuneiform culture. This statement does not do full justice to the complexities of the scholarly pur- suits in which Babylonian and Egyptian scholars of the late period were en- gaged, and it ignores the more creative dimensions of their work. But nonethe- less, Liverani has a point. Despite all its erudition and, if one may say so, so- phisticated beauty, the latest strata of Babylonian and Egyptian scholarship failed, in the end, to satisfy the intellectual and spiritual needs of an age that witnessed dramatic changes on almost every level. ‘Yet these changes were not necessarily all for the better, even in the areas of scholarship and science. To be sure: the hermeneutical operations of the Baby- lonian commentary tradition appear in many respects quite strange to us today. The associative and accumulative nature of Mesopotamian scholarship stands in sharp contrast to the more modem Greek concept of science, established by Aristotle, which, through the implementation of rigorous epistemological rules, severely limited the freedom to create accepted knowledge.'*? But it must be stressed that the Greek tendency to base theoretical generalizations on insuffi- cient evidence also led to massive errors. An example is the case of the humoral pathology established by Hippocrates, a universal theory seeking to explain the complexities of the human body. It was an clegant doctrine, but one without any ‘empirical foundation. For centuries, people died needlessly because they were treated by doctors who applied therapeutic measures based on Hippocrates’s flawed model. Late Babylonian scholars brought forth some ideas on elements and humors 5} but they never regarded them as doctrine, and Mesopo- tamian medicine, based more on experience than on theory, probably had a far better success rate than Hippocratic healing methods.'*™* We should also bear in mind what some modem philosophers have claimed: that the great problems that have preoccupied Wester scholarship for ages may simply be insoluble. The British logician Colin McGinn has argued that the human mind is innately incapable of comprehending itself entirely, and, in con- sequence, tackles in vain many of the “last questions” Westem philosophy has "831 Liverani 2005, 204. 1832 Even though biological metaphors are always problematic in an investigation of cultural history, the revolution of scholarship that the Greeks brought about when they limited the scientifically acceptable options to gain valid knowledge brings to mind the reduction in the number of brain synapses that characterizes the intellectual development of the small child. '833 sce Scurlock and Al-Rawi 2006. 184 Scurlock (2004a, 30) argues, somewhat polemically, that “Hippocratic physi ‘would have done mankind a great service they had just plagiarized Mesopotami medical treatments, demonic magic and all, leaving to the brilliant minds of the 17” century scientific revolution to sort out the ‘science’ from the ‘magic.”” And in an earlier article (Scurlock 1995/96, 250), she points out that “it has been estimated that the Hippo- cratic iatros had no better than a 50/50 chance of not making the patient worse than he ‘was before he was treated.” 12. The legacy of Babylonian and Assyrian hermeneutics 383 tried to solve ever since the “axial age.” According to McGinn, the strength of the human brain lies instead in creating links, governed by certain principles, between individual clements of various types, a process that McGinn calls “combinatorial atomism.” This term characterizes quite well the hermeneutical operations performed in Babylonian and Assyrian commentaries. In the end, then, the scholars of ancient Mesopotamia may not have been so far off the mark. When they focused their intellectual energies, not on the development of highly abstract ideas, but rather on the innumerable possibilities of combining, jn various ways, elements of language, writing system, culture, and natural envi- ronment, they drew on what the human mind can do best: wielding, as Novalis called it, “the magic wand of analogy” - “den Zauberstab der Analogie ge- brauchen.”"** _ 185 MeGinn 1993. 1836 The quotation is from “Die Christenheit oder Europa,” in: H.
