text: xx Introduction bears the imprint of some Polynesian influence. Tuvaluans, including Nui islanders, speak of the Nui dialect as being a ‘mixture’ (paalutaki) of standard Gilbertese, standard Tuvaluan, and Samoan. A community of about 250 people of Tuvaluan origin is settled on Kioa Island off Vanua Levu in Fiji, which was bought by Vaitupu shortly after the Second World War (see White 1965, Bedford 1967:83–92 and K.-F.Koch 1978 for background history). On Kioa, Tuvaluan is slowly losing ground to Fijian as the traditional ties between Kioa and Vaitupu are loosening. In the first part of the twentieth century, Tuvaluans were regularly employed as contract workers on the phosphate island of Banaba (Ocean Island), and in the second part of the century the Republic of Nauru hosted a community of Tuvaluan contract workers employed by the Nauru Phosphate Company and their families. The latter reached about 500 people in the late 1970s, and included representatives from every island of the group. At the time of writing, because phosphate supplies are almost depleted, Tuvaluan residents of Nauru are in the process of being repatriated. After the separation of Tuvalu and Kiribati in 1975, a few Tuvaluans chose to remain in Tarawa (Kiribati), where they form a small but striving minority. Finally, small but growing migrant communities from Tuvalu are also found in and around Suva (Fiji), Apia (Western Samoa), and Auckland and Wellington (New Zealand). 0.3. TUVALUAN SOCIETY For most intents and purposes, each individual island of Tuvalu forms a separate society with a local island-governing structure, specific institutions, and particular social and cultural practices. Indeed, prior to colonial amalgamation in the late nineteenth century (which probably had little effect on local life until well into the twentieth century), the islands and atolls were independent entities, although they apparently sustained some contacts with one another. However, all island communities also share many traits, and it is on the basis of these commonalities that a sense of national identity has slowly emerged, particularly since independence. Following are some of the social and cultural traits that recur throughout the group: cognatic descent with an agnatic bias; a balance between endogamy and exogamy and between virilocality and uxorilocality with a bias for the former in each case; an avoidance taboo between cousins of different gender which is strongest between first cousins and gradually weakens as genealogical distance increases; pervasive adoption, which does not preclude allegiance to blood relatives; a complex system of land tenure based on corporate ownership by landholding kin-based groups; the importance of exchange in the economic life; and patterns of dual organization that pervade many aspects of social life and culture. All atolls and islands have a chiefly system of one form or the other, whereby a chief is elected by members of a Council of Elders over which he, or more rarely she, presides. However, one also finds everywhere an explicitly articulated ideology of egalitarianism, solidarity, and consensus. Frequent conflicts arise over how these values should be implemented in particular situations, and how they articulate with the authority of chiefs and elders. All chiefly systems have been reinvented in recent times or have undergone major discontinuities during the colonial period. THE TUVALUAN LANGUAGE 0.4.1. Genetic affiliations and sociolinguistic context Native speakers of Tuvaluan refer to it as te ggana Tuuvalu ‘the Tuvaluan language’ or more frequently and less formally as te ggana a taatou ‘our language’ (cf. 2.1.2.1.3). Tuvaluan is one of approximately thirty members of the Polynesian language group. Polynesian in turn is a relatively discrete subgroup of Oceanic (or Eastern Austronesian), one of the two main branches of the Austronesian linguistic family (as summarized in Clark 1987). The lowest-level subgroup of Polynesian to which Tuvaluan is usually attached is the loosely defined Samoic Outlier subgroup (Pawley 1966, 1967), the composition of which is given in Figure 0.1. Arguments have been proposed periodically for subgroupings that either refine further the Samoic-Outlier proposal or provide alternatives to it. For example, Howard (1981) groups Tuvaluan together with several Outlier languages, namely Kapingamarangi, Nukuoro, Takuu, Nukuria, Nukumanu, Luangiua, and Sikaiana, as well as, tentatively, Tokelauan, into a subgroup of either Samoic-Outlier or the higher order Nuclear Polynesian, which comprises all Polynesian languages other than Tongan and Niuean (Pawley 1966). However, these proposals have been based on equivocal evidence, in part because descriptive materials for the relevant languages are still very limited. Indeed, little detailed information is available on the Outlier languages most likely to be most Tuvaluan’s closest relatives. More information is available on Tokelauan, a language spoken on the three atolls of Tokelau, several hundred miles East of Tuvalu (see Map 0.1), and among Tokelauan immigrants in New Zealand. The inhabitants of Tokelau and Tuvalu may have similar origins and have been in sustained contact over the centuries, to the extent that the social organizations, cultures, and languages of both groups exhibit numerous similarities. Whether the resemblance between the two languages is a reflection of a common historical origin or the product of subsequent contact is difficult to gauge. The social, cultural, and linguistic similarities between the two groups have been accentuated by the fact that they have come under the same powerful influence of Samoan missionary- pastors in historical times. Indeed, many borrowings from Samoan found in Tuvaluan are also found in Tokelauan. As a result of these various prehistorical and historical patterns of contact, the two languages are almost mutually intelligible, and descriptions of the Tokelauan language are of particular relevance to this work. text: Introduction xxiii this endeavour should be added useful and more broadly descriptive works by Hooper (1996), Hovdhaugen et al. (1989) and Vonen (1988, 1993). Each of the seven traditionally inhabited islands and atolls of the group where Tuvaluan is spoken natively has its distinct dialect. The seven dialects differ from one another mostly in the phonology (particularly suprasegmental phonology) and lexicon, and, to a lesser extent, through the presence of a few grammatical morphemes in some dialects that are absent or have a different form in other dialects. The seven dialects have essentially the same syntactic structure. Although a comprehensive study of dialectal variations has yet to be published, one can identify a clear division between two dialect areas, one grouping Nanumea, Nanumaga, and Niutao together, and the other Funafuti, Vaitupu, Nukufetau, and Nukulaelae. In the Northern subgroup, Nanumea and Nanumaga probably share more features with one another than with Niutao. No further subgrouping is evident among the Southern dialects. The picture is greatly complicated by patterns of dialect mixing, which may be quite ancient. Frequently, native speakers are at a loss to identify the dialectal affiliation of particular linguistic features because they have been borrowed across dialects. The hegemonic status of the Funafuti and Vaitupu dialects is particularly evident: Funafuti is the seat of the national government and Vaitupu is the location of what was until recently the only secondary school in the group. Many Outer Islanders migrate to Funafuti in particular, where employment opportunities are all located, and everyone in the country listens to Radio Tuvalu which broadcasts from Funafuti. Thus all speakers of Tuvaluan are at least familiar with, and many are bidialectal in, the Funafuti or Vaitupu dialect (the difference between the two is minimal). Tuvaluan has come into contact with and received a strong influence from three languages. The influence of Gilbertese, a Micronesian language, probably goes back the furthest in time. Like many Micronesian and Outlier Polynesian societies, Tuvaluan society borrowed a number of important technologies from Gilbertese society, such as coconut-sap toddy tapping and fishing magic. Along with these technologies, a substantial body of technological vocabulary of Gilbertese origin was incorporated into the Tuvaluan lexicon. During the colonial period (1892–1975), Gilbertese played an important role in the political life of Tuvalu, since the seat of the colonial administration was in the Gilbert Islands. Today, besides being spoken natively on Nui atoll, Gilbertese is the second (and sometimes first) language of many civil servants and other individuals who returned to Tuvalu after the two island groups separated politically in 1975. However, its importance in Tuvaluan daily life is rapidly decreasing. Samoan was introduced to Tuvalu at the time of missionization. It was the ‘vernacular’ for the colonial government’s administration of the Ellice Islands until the 1930s and that of the church before being replaced by Tuvaluan in the 1950s. Until recently, everyone in Tuvalu was proficient in a heavily ‘Tuvaluanized’ form of Samoan, even though many people had very little contact with native speakers of Samoan. Samoan was acquired by reading the Samoan translation of the Scriptures, which also served as the tool for literacy instruction. Today, knowledge of Samoan is rapidly declining, a process which is likely to accelerate since Tuvaluan translations of religious materials have now replaced the Samoan texts. (Religious literature comprises the bulk of reading materials available to most Tuvaluans.) However, Samoan has left a lasting imprint on the vocabulary, morphology, and perhaps syntax of the language. English is the most recent arrival on the Tuvaluan linguistic scene. Early accounts of Tuvaluan life by Westerners (e.g., David 1899) indicate that some sort of pidgin was used in relations with outsiders, the features of which bear close affinities to the plantation pidgins that developed in other parts of the Pacific, if one is to believe the accuracy of quoted dialogues in these sources. Few traces of this variety remain today. Particularly since Tuvalu became a separate political entity in the mid-1970s, competence in English has become increasingly important. Most Tuvaluans speak at least a smattering of English, which is taught as a second language in primary schools. There are many borrowings from English in the Tuvaluan lexicon. But English influence on the structure of Tuvaluan has not reached the magnitude of the Samoan influence. 0.4.2. Typological characteristics Like most other Polynesian languages, Tuvaluan has a basic verb-initial constituent order, although it differs from most other Polynesian languages (other than Outlier languages) in that it allows many constituent-order configurations. It is a prepositional language, in which adjectives follow nouns, relative clauses follow head nouns, and non-pronominal possessors follow possessed expressions. Numerals may precede or follow the noun phrase they modify. The language exhibits a strong bias for clauses consisting of a single noun-phrase constituent. Various discourse and grammatical strategies enable speakers to encode reference to a second nominal participant (if needed) without adding another nominal constituent to the clause. Nominalization is a particularly salient process in terms of its frequency and broad range of meaning and discourse functions. Tuvaluan is a zero-pronominalizing language, and both subjects and direct objects may be zero-pronominalized. Case marking follows an ergative-absolutive pattern. While many syntactic rules refer to subject and direct-object categories, a significant number (e.g., relativization, interrogative-word clefting, and case marking in nominalized clauses) refer to ergative and absolutive categories. The language lacks a passive and an antipassive. Interrogative-words generally remain in situ, although a number of them may also appear in clefted positions. Equi-deletion is typologically unusual in that it may be controlled by and may target both subjects and direct objects. Raising is even more unusual, in that it may target any noun phrase in subordinate clauses and mark it for a broad range of cases in the matrix clause. A rule of advancement-to-possessive, which is also found in other Polynesian languages, can extract noun phrases with a variety of grammatical functions from relative clauses and mark them as possessive modifiers of the head noun of the relative clause. Subject-verb agreement only occurs with some intransitive verbs, and is marked either with infixed reduplication or by suppletion. When an intransitive verb that allows agreement is turned into a transitive causative verb, the causative verb agrees with the derived direct object. A three-number distinction is marked in the pronoun system, while a simple singular-plural contrast is encoded in noun-modifying articles. The first-person inclusive plural pronoun is particularly salient in discourse because it helps emphasize culturally salient values of solidary and consensus. Tuvaluan is crosslinguistically unusual in that dual pronouns, rather than plural pronouns, are used as honorifics. The language has a very large inventory of possessive pronouns, the form of which is fairly predictable. A contrast is made between alienable and inalienable possession. | True

text: Introduction xxv There are relatively few inflectional and derivational morphological processes. The most common morphophonemic process is reduplication, which may be internal or external, and which can have both inflectional and derivational functions. External reduplication may be full or partial, and is a left-to-right process. Tuvaluan has a small phonemic inventory of fifteen or sixteen phonemes, depending on the dialect. Only open syllables are allowed. Gemination is phonemic for both vowels and consonants, and morphophonological patterns of compensatory lengthening are attested. Geminated consonants may appear in any position where ungeminated consonants appear, including word-initially. Primary stress always fall on the penultimate vowel of the word. Intonation varies significantly from one dialect to the other. One typologically unusual characteristic of the intonational system is the fact that interrogative-word questions are uttered on the same intonational contour as yes-no questions. 0.4.3. Previous descriptions The Tuvaluan language was first mentioned in print in 1846 by Horatio Hale, the philologist of the United States Exploring Expedition of 1838–42. In his philological memoir, Hale provides a 120-word list of the Vaitupu dialect of Tuvaluan and the Fakaofo dialect of Tokelauan, adding that ‘it has seemed superfluous to give separate vocabularies for the two clusters, the words obtained at both being for the most part alike’ (H.Hale 1846:357). Several other essays published around the beginning of the twentieth century provided word lists of varying length and various remarks on the language (see Besnier 1981a:xxiii–xliv for a bibliography). There are three more substantial descriptions of the morphology and syntax of Tuvaluan: Kennedy (1945), a phrasebook-style description of the Vaitupu dialect; Ranby (1973), which, despite its title (‘Nanumea syntax’), is an overview of the morphology of the Nanumea dialect; and Besnier (1981b), a pedagogical description of the Southern dialects, with notes on dialectal variations. There are also four attempts at lexical description: Ranby (1980), a brief lexicon of the Nanumea dialect; Besnier (1981a), a preliminary version of a pan-dialectal dictionary currently in progress; Noricks (1982), a lexicon based on the Niutao dialect with information on other dialects; and Jackson (1993), a religiously oriented list mostly inspired by previous publications. More specific aspects of the structure of various dialects which have been the focus of descriptive work are word order and case marking (Wang 1976, Finney 1983, Besnier 1986), zero anaphora (Besnier 1985), raising constructions (Besnier 1988b), reported speech constructions (Besnier 1993b), and colour terms (K.Chambers 1978). Works in anthropological linguistics and socio- linguistics have focused on styles of everyday interactions and their socio-political context and implications (Besnier 1989a, 1989b, 1990a, 1994a, 1994b, 1995b, 1996b) and stylistic variation across spoken and written contexts (Besnier 1988a, 1991, 1995a). 0.4.4. I have chosen to deviate slightly from the organization set by the questionnaire in cases where certain categories could be ordered in one fashion according to formal patterns and another according to function patterns. This grammar is based partly on traditional grammatical elicitation, partly on observations of everyday interactions over many years of field work, and partly on a large database of texts from a wide variety of sources, representing many genres and styles of speaking and writing. Because many examples cited were unelicited, and because my purpose here is to provide as faithful a representation of language structure in use, no effort was made to ‘sanitize’ the examples of sexist overtones or religious references, although the use of such data should be understood as implying no endorsement of any kind on my part. I made restricted use of ‘specialized’ genres, such as proverbs and lyrics of dance songs; examples drawn from such genres are marked accordingly. I also drew as little as possible from translated materials, despite the fact that the bulk of published writing in Tuvaluan consists of translations. However, I have occasionally cited such materials because they illustrate interesting patterns in stylistics or discourse, which are not to be disregarded since they have become part of the linguistic repertoire of the speech community. Translated examples are clearly indicated in the text. While the examples provided herein are all from the Southern dialects (particularly the Funafuti and Nukulaelae dialects), most of the discussion applies to all the dialects of the group, not just because of dialect mixing, but because all seven dialects of the group share essentially the same structure. Dialect differences in the form of particular morphemes are indicated only for the four Southern dialects. 0.4.5. Orthography Tuvaluan does not have a standardized orthography, and efforts to develop such a system have not been successful to date. Most Tuvaluan writers use an orthography loosely based on the Samoan orthography, which does not consistently mark vowel length (phonemic in both Tuvaluan and Samoan) or consonant length (phonemic in Tuvaluan only). Occasionally, vowel length is indicated with a macron or by reduplicating the vowel symbol. Consonant length is sometimes indicated with an apostrophe either preceding or following the consonant symbol, or even by reduplicating the vowel symbol that follows the geminated consonant. Usually, the grapheme g stands for a velar nasal, although older writers sometimes use ng. For a fuller discussion of the various orthographic systems in use and of the politics of standardization, the reader is referred to Besnier (1995a: xiii–xx). The orthography used throughout this book is strictly phonemic. Vowel and consonant gemination is marked with double letters. In the one instance where the gemination of/t/is predictable (cf. 2.1.1.10), it is not indicated. The orthography marks certain allomorphic variations but not others. Briefly, allomorphic variations that consist in phonologically predictable vowel or consonant gemination are not indicated. Allomorphic variations that consist in gemination processes conditioned by factors other than phonology, and allomorphic variations that result in segment alterations (be they conditioned by phonological or other factors) are indicated. Whenever relevant, these orthographic conventions are indicated in the discussion. When examples from other languages are cited, the orthographic conventions follow the system used in the most accessible reference source (e.g., Milner 1966 for Samoan and Churchward 1959 for Tongan). The orthography of Proto-Polynesian reconstructions cited in the text is the more or less standardized system followed by Biggs (1979) and subsequent versions of the Polynesian historical reconstruction project at the University of Auckland (POLLEX), where *q is a glottal stop and all other letters have their approximate IPA value. | True

text: Syntax 1.1. GENERAL FEATURES 1.1.1. Sentence-types 1.1.1.1. Direct speech and quoted speech In Tuvaluan, quoted (or reported) speech is framed with the help of a number of lexical and prosodic devices. These devices mark a particular stretch of discourse as a quote in contrast to the rest of the discourse. Taken out of its discourse context, a quoted string is indistinguishable from a nonquoted string. No lexical marker or prosodic pattern is used exclusively to mark quoted speech. Like many other languages, Tuvaluan has two different quoted-speech styles: one is associated with speech purported to reproduce the exact wording of another utterance (i.e., directly quoted speech); the other is associated with speech purported to reproduce an earlier utterance, but which is structurally modified so that it becomes syntactically part of the structure of the quoting context (i.e., indirectly quoted speech). (a) Transitions between direct speech and quoted speech Both indirectly quoted speech and directly quoted speech are typically introduced by a speech-act verb or nominal expression, usually the polysemic verb fai ‘say, tell’ (in the Nukulaelae dialect, hai) or the nouns muna and pati ‘word, utterance’: (1) Koo fai mai a Palu, “A moolii koo oti ne taamate.” Inc say Dxs Cnt Palu Cnt lamp Prf turn-off ‘Palu said to me, “The lamps have been turned off.”’ (2) Koo fai mai a Palu mo koo oti ne taamate a moolii. Inc say Dxs Cnt Palu Cmp Prf turn-off Cnt lamp ‘Palu told me that the lamps had been turned off.’ (3) Muna a Palu, “A moolii koo oti ne taamate.” word of Palu Cnt lamp Prf turn-off ‘Palu said, “The lamps have been turned off.”’ (4) Muna a Palu mo koo oti ne taamate a moolii. word of Palu Cmp Prf turn-off Cnt lamp ‘Palu said that the lamps had been turned off.’ When the speech-act noun muna or pati is used as a speech-act expression, the speaker or writer to whom the quote is attributed is expressed as a possessive modifier of the speech-act noun, as in examples (3) and (4) above. text: 4 Syntax Quoted turns that are not marked by a speech-act expression are typically short, as illustrated by the above examples. If no speech-act verb or expression appears, pee- adverbs cannot appear. Tense in quoted speech always takes as point of reference the situation in which the quoted string was originally uttered: (17) Ne fai mai mo ko te kau kolaa e olo o pei tili. Pst say Dxs Cmp Foc the group those Nps go Cmp throw fishing-net ‘He told me that it was those guys who were [lit.: are] going net-fishing.’ There is no temporal-agreement system regulating the tense of indirectly quoted speech. Pronominal deixis and demonstrative deixis are sensitive to transitions from and to quoted speech, in that the reference point of the nonquoted discourse may differ from the reference point of the quoted discourse. But since directly and indirectly quoted speech differ in their treatment of these categories, the patterns are described in (b) below. In contrast, the reference point of the deictic adverbs mai ‘hither’ and atu ‘thither’ does not necessarily change in the transition between nonquoted and quoted discourse; further discussion and illustrations are provided in 2.1.3.6.10. (b) Directly and indirectly quoted speech A structural distinction is generally made between direct and indirect quotation. However, in discourse, not all instances of direct quotation exhibit all the features associated with directly quoted discourse; and not all indirectly quoted discourse is marked as such. The characteristics of directly and indirectly quoted speech described in this section are tendencies, rather than absolute distinctions. In informal conversation and narration, directly quoted speech is clearly preferred over indirectly quoted speech. Indirectly quoted speech is primarily used to express a quotation within another quotation, or to quote a communicative act which the reporter did not witness. Furthermore, indirect quotations most commonly consist of one-sentence, one-turn quotes; for quoted discourse that consists of more than one sentence or turn, directly quoted speech is used. A directly quoted string is not linked to the nonquoted discourse environment by any subordinating or coordinating device; it is simply apposed to the non-quoted discourse that precedes it. In contrast, an indirectly quoted string is syntactically incorporated into the nonquoted discourse, and this is often marked morphologically with the help of one of a number of subordinating conjunctions described in 1.1.2.2.3, 1.1.2.2.4, and 1.1.2.2.5, the choice of which is dictated by the type of speech act being quoted: (18) Muna a Tito me e tasi eiloa ttafukeega a telotou word of Tiki Cmp Nps one indeed the+sweep+Nom of their tili, kae ii eiloa kanase i ei. fishing-net and tightly-packed indeed mullet in Anp ‘Tito said that [they] had to open their fishing net only once, and they had it full of mullets.’ (19) E taku mai mo ko au. In indirect quotes, in contrast, the point of reference is the same as that of the nonquoted discourse environment. (c) Quoted thought The strategies described in the previous two sections also apply to quoted thought. The same speech-act verbs are used in the reporting of thoughts as in the reporting of utterances, with the addition of such verbs as maafaufau ‘think’, leaka or leake ‘stuck with the idea’ (cf. 2.1.3.6.10), vvali, with the same meaning, and a metaphorical use of the verb nofo ‘stay’ with approximately the same meaning as leaka and vvali: (25) Au ne vvali loa i te kelo teelaa se Ppaalagi! First, indirect constructions are much more common than direct constructions in thought reporting, while the opposite distribution applies to speech reporting. text: Syntax 7 a rising intonation contour. Intonation is the only factor that distinguishes yes-no questions from their corresponding affirmative sentences. In interrogative-word questions, the interrogative word may remain in situ, may be moved to a preverbal position, may be moved to a clause-initial position, or may take the form of an equational construction. Different interrogative words vary in terms of which of these various choices they allow. 1.1.1.2.1. Yes-no questions 1.1.1.2.1.1. Neutral yes-no questions The syntactic structure of neutral yes-no questions is the same as that of affirmative sentences. The order of the sentential constituents follows the same patterns, and there is no special morphological marking on any element of the clause. For example, the following interrogative and affirmative equivalents have exactly the same morphosyntactic structure: (27) E ola? Nps alive ‘Is [it] alive?’ (28) E ola. Nps alive ‘[It] is alive.’ Neutral yes-no questions are distinguished from affirmative sentences through intonation. The intonational pattern associated with neutral yes-no questions is a steady downward contour that rises sharply on the last stressed syllable: (29) Affirmative sentences are never uttered with such intonational contours (cf. 3.3.4). 1.1.1.2.1.2. Leading yes-no questions Leading or biased yes-no questions are questions in which the questioner expects a particular answer, be it affirmative or negative (Moravcsik 1971). In Tuvaluan, they are commonly marked with the sentence-final tag-question marker inee or nee, whether an affirmative or a negative answer is expected. (According to some native speakers, the two forms may have originally been dialectal variants of one another, but today both forms are used in all dialects.) The tag-question marker is always placed at the end of the sentence. The sentence itself has the intonation of a declarative sentence; the tag-question marker is usually separated from the rest of the sentence by a short pause and uttered on a significantly higher pitch level than the rest of the sentence: (30) (31) ‘It is a good thing that they haven’t surveyed it yet, don’t you think?’ | True

The following dialogue illustrates this usage: (33) T: Se moolii o ttai? a light of the+sea ‘[Is it] a waterproof flashlight?’ S: Mmmm. Itj ‘Hm.’ T: Nee? Tag ‘[Is it] really?’ In addition to tag questions, there are other interrogative constructions that tend to presuppose a particular answer and a particular answer type. For example, there is a tendency for negative questions to be biased toward a negative answer: (34) Ko Sina laa mo ttamaa ne olo seki mmai? Foc Sina then and the+child Pst go Neg come ‘Sina and the child [she] went [with] are not back yet?’ This tendency is widely attested across the world’s languages (Moravcsik 1971, Pope 1973). In addition, when a leading negative question has an obvious answer, it is usually intended to be interpreted as an indirect speech act. For example, the following question, addressed with mild surprise to someone whom the speaker thought had gone to the islets, is meant to be interpreted as a request for a justification, rather than a request for the confirmation of an obvious fact: (35) Koe seki fano ki motu mo te kau? you Neg go to islet with the gang ‘You didn’t go to the islets with those guys?’ [illocutionary force: ‘Why didn’t you go?’] 1.1.1.2.1.3. text: 10 Syntax 1.1.1.2.2. Interrogative-word questions This section covers the following two topics: the range of elements of the sentence that can be questioned (1.1.1.2.2.1); and the behaviour of the questioned element (1.1.1.2.2.2). For a discussion of interrogative-word questions used as exclamations and hedges, see 1.1.1.5(b) and (d) respectively. 1.1.1.2.2.1. Elements of the sentence that can be questioned All constituents of all clause types can be questioned, with two exceptions. First, no interrogative word can function as a transitive verb. (Of course, any element of a transitive sentence other than the verb can be questioned.) Second, topicalized constituents cannot be questioned. The restriction that a topic may not be questioned may be explained functionally: since a topicalized constituent denotes, by definition, given information, and since interrogative-word questions are requests for new information, they are pragmatically incompatible. 1.1.1.2.2.1.1. The analysis of clefted interrogative words as equational clauses with an embedded relative clause is supported by six morphosyntactic parallelisms between equational structures and the clefted interrogative-word construction on the one hand, and between the second half of clefted constructions and relative-clause structures on the other. First, interrogative-word clefted constructions and interrogative-word equational constructions have the same basic morphosyntactic structure. For example, interrogative words take the same form in both constructions, and both constructions are available to the same interrogative words. Second, the ordering of the interrogative word and the rest of the construction is free in clefted constructions (although the interrogative word is commonly clause-initial). This free ordering is also characteristic of equational structures (cf. 1.2.1.1.1(a)). (Because of the tendency for the interrogative word to come first, the other half of these constructions will hereafter be referred to as ‘the second half’ of the construction.) Third, the second half of a clefted construction has the same morphosyntactic structure as a relative clause. Thus the extracted noun is indexed in the rest of the equational construction in the same way as the head noun is indexed in a relative clause (cf. 1.1.2.3.4). Fourth, the extracted noun in the second half of a clefted interrogative-word construction is modified by a relative pronoun (teenei, teenaa, or teelaa, and plural equivalents). That these pronouns are relative pronouns, and not demonstrative pronouns (which are homophonous with relative pronouns), is evidenced by the fact that a second demonstrative may modify the extracted noun. Elsewhere in the language, advancement-to-possessive is confined to relative clause structures (cf. 1.1.2.3.10). text: 24 Syntax On the basis of these six arguments, interrogative-word clefted constructions can be treated as equational constructions in which an interrogative word is equated with a noun phrase consisting of a relative clause modifying an overt or zero head noun. Comparable analyses of interrogative-word questions have been proposed for at least two other Polynesian languages, Niuean (Seiter 1980:106–115) and Maori (Bauer 1991), and, further afield, for Palauan, a Western Austronesian language of Micronesia (Georgopoulos 1991:140–181). The phenomenon is likely to be areally widespread. In Tuvaluan, clefted interrogative-word constructions differ from equational constructions with a relative clause in two ways: the embedded relative clause can have an empty head, and reordering of the equated noun phrases is allowed only if the relative clause is not headless. With ordinary relative clauses, empty heads are generally not allowed (cf. 1.1.1.2.3.6); and there is no syntactic restriction on the reordering of noun phrases in regular equational constructions. Interrogative-word clefting is optional. If the in situ interrogative word is in the absolutive case, there is a clear textual preference for the clefting strategy over the in situ strategy. So the first of the following alternatives is preferred over the second one: (142) Kooi ttino koo uaa mai? Foc+who? the+person Inc noisy Dxs ‘Who is making a noise?’ (143) Koo uaa mai a ai? Inc noisy Dxs Cnt who? ‘Who is making a noise?’ In all other cases, no clear pattern of textual preference is discernible. Echo questions Echo questions are requests for a clarification or verification of a previous utterance. The previous utterance is called the stimulus of the echo construction (McCawley 1987). Various echo-question types occur in Tuvaluan, and they have the same structure as regular questions. For example, yes-no echo questions are indistinguishable from regular echo questions, and both positive and negative yes- no echo questions are encountered: (163) K: Au see fia fano ki te fakaala. (Of course, direct objects can be deleted from imperative clauses by zero pronominalization, independently of imperative formation.) Thus imperative formation targets subjects of intransitive and transitive verbs as a single category, in contrast to direct objects, and provides evidence for the nominative-accusative basis of Tuvaluan syntax. The presence of a subject in postverbal position is less peremptory than its absence. Thus, the first of the following examples is slightly more polite than the second: (193) Vau! come ‘Come [here]!’ (194) Vau koe! come you ‘[Why don’t] you come [here]!’ With certain verbs, there is a strong tendency to change the case marking of the subject of transitive verbs from the ergative nee to the alienable benefactive maa in imperative formation (cf. 2.1.1.2.2(d) for further discussion of conditions under which this change can take place). text: 40 Syntax characteristic of exclamatory sentences is worth describing, as it will be relevant to other structural characteristics of the language. This section covers only some of the more salient conventionalized indirect speech acts, salient in terms of either their overall frequency or their sociocultural prominence. Subordination Crosslinguistically, three types of subordinate clauses are commonly identified: (1) noun clauses (or complements), the clausal equivalent of noun phrases; (2) adverb clauses, which share many grammatical characteristics with adverbial phrases; and (3) relative clauses (or adjective clauses), which are noun modifiers (Thompson and Longacre 1985:172). In Tuvaluan, the structures of noun and adverb clauses share many characteristics. Several general patterns of subordinate constructions can be identified, whose functions resemble the functions of both noun clauses and adverb clauses in other languages. The syntax of these general patterns is described in 1.1.2.1, while their function is overviewed in 1.1.2.2 and 1.1.2.4. In terms of their formal characteristics, relative clauses, discussed in 1.1.2.3, form a clearly defined type of subordinate constructions; in functional terms, relative clauses overlap with adverb clauses, in that certain functions commonly associated with adverb clauses in other languages are associated with relative clauses in Tuvaluan. Advancement-to-possessive, a grammatical process whose domain is the relative clause, is described in 1.1.2.3.10. General markers of subordination Following is a description of the morphosyntactic characteristics of the six major subordination types associated with both noun clauses and adverb clauses. The choices in subordinate construction is determined primarily by the verb of the matrix clause. In cases where matrix verbs can take more than one subordinate-clause type, the different constructions carry different meanings or connotations. The functional characteristics of the subordination types described here are covered in 1.1.2.2 and 1.1.2.4. These sections also cover other types of subordinate clauses, whose functional distribution is less broad than the following six types. No syntactic or morphological feature is shared by all subordinate-clause types. Indeed, the different types are quite disparate in structure. However, it is noteworthy that several subordinate-clause types require that the subordinate clause be verb-initial. 1.1.2.1.1. o-subordination The subordinator o is used in a semantically eclectic range of subordinate constructions, which nevertheless share a number of syntactic properties. However, eligible intransitive verbs of o-subordinate clauses agree in number with their subjects. text: Syntax 63 1.1.2.3. Relative clauses Relative clauses are head-external and always follow the head noun. Relative clauses can be either restrictive or nonrestrictive; both types exhibit essentially the same structural characteristics. Several strategies can be used in the formation of relative clauses. These strategies involve either the deletion of the relativized element or its replacement with a pronoun. There are no correlative clauses (Keenan 1985:163– 168) in this language. 1.1.2.3.1. General markers of relative clauses Relative clauses of all types share a number of structural characteristics. First, relative clauses always follow the head noun that they modify, as illustrated through this discussion. Second, relative clauses follow all other modifiers of the head noun; for example, they follow postnominal possessive phrases: (366) Ne olo o ssala te vaka o pulisimani teelaa [e galo]. Num three Nps come ‘As for the women, [I] don’t know where the three women who are coming are from.’ Third, relative clauses are strictly verb initial; in general, they also maintain the basic word order VS(O)(X), as will be illustrated throughout this section. Fourth, relative clauses are finite, and have the same syntactic and semantic features (e.g., marking for tense, aspect, mood, and transitivity) as their independent-clause equivalents. In particular, subject-verb agreement can apply, even when the element that controls agreement has been relativized: (369) Maatou ne mmai fakatasi mo tama a Alefaio toko lua [e we-3-e Pst come together with children of Alefaio Num two Nps aakkoga i Fiiti]. study+Agr in Fiji ‘We came together with Alefaio’s two children who are studying in Fiji.’ Fifth, a relative clause is always part of a noun-phrase constituent. Also covered here, when relevant, are nonadverbial clauses that express notions typically associated with adverb-clause constructions in other languages. 1.1.2.4.2.1. Adverb clauses denoting time Various constructions can express temporal notions, all of which can denote past, present, or future situations. These constructions fall into three semantic categories, which are discussed in turn: (a) ‘after’ (or sequencing) clauses, which refer to a situation that precedes in time the situation denoted by the superordinate clause (e.g., the italicized clause in ‘After he returned from net-fishing, he washed up’); (b) ‘before’ clauses, which refer to a situation that follows in time the situation denoted by the superordinate clause (e.g., ‘Before she had breakfast, she rolled up the sleeping mats’); and (c) clauses that denote simultaneity (e.g., ‘While she was eating, he smoked his pipe’). text: Syntax 105 Unlike most other conjunctions with similar functions, this conjunction does not appear to be borrowed from Samoan. Neither the Samoan dictionary (Milner 1966) nor the most comprehensive grammar of the language (Mosel and Hovdhaugen 1992) lists a morpheme with comparable form and meaning. Another conjunction with concessive meaning is takua ‘as if, even though not, despite the fact that’, which is not a borrowing either. It is usually modified by the intensifier loa or the downtoner laa, and the time adverb nei ‘now’ (cf. (578) E ita kiaa koe, takua loa nei ne puke nee koe tena gatu. Other adverb-clause types Thompson and Longacre (1985:177–203) provide examples of several adverb-clause types in addition to the above, none of which is attested in Tuvaluan. For example, there is no distinct locative adverb clause. Notions that are expressed with locative adverb clauses in other languages (e.g., ‘I don’t know where he went’) can be expressed with a relative clause with a ‘dummy’ locative head (e.g., koga ‘place’); see 1.1.2.3.6 for an example. Substitutive clauses (e.g., ‘Instead of working, we played’) do not exist either as a separate type. The concept is expressed with two adversatively coordinated sentences: (580) Maatou seki gaallue, kae ne taaffao fua. we-3-e Neg work but Pst play just ‘We didn’t work, we just played.’ Additiveness (‘in addition to’, ‘besides’) is conveyed by discourse conjuncts (cf. 2.1.9). ‘Speech act’ adverb clauses are not syntactic modifiers of the superordinate clause of the sentence, but provide information about the speech act associated with the superordinate clause. Sequence of tenses There is no clear constraint on sequences of tense across superordinate and subordinate clauses comparable to the process which yields the pattern ‘I thought you were/*are a ghost’ in English. In this respect, Tuvaluan offers an interesting contrast to Maori, a language to which it is relatively closely related, where Bauer (1993:74–77) finds exacting constraints on tense in complex sentences. In Tuvaluan, the tense in a subordinate clause always refers to the time of the situation denoted by the subordinate clause itself. Contrast the following three sentences: (586) Koo muna mai [iaa ia ne fano o fai niu i motu]. Inc word Dxs Cmp he Pst go Cmp gather coconut at islet ‘He said to me that he’d gone and gathered coconuts on an islet.’ or: ‘He said that he would go and gather coconuts on an islet.’ (587) Koo muna mai [iaa ia e fano o fai niu i motu]. Inc word Dxs Cmp he Nps go Cmp gather coconut at islet ‘He said that he was going to gather coconuts on an islet.’ (588) Koo muna mai [iaa ia kaa fano o fai niu i motu]. Inc word Dxs Cmp he Fut go Cmp gather coconut at islet ‘He said that he was going to gather coconuts on an islet.’ or: ‘He said that he’d be going to gather coconuts on an islet.’ The complex construction which comes closest to having a constraint on tense sequencing is apposed subordinate clauses with an aspectual verb like oti ‘finished’ or palele ‘depleted’ as superordinate verb, and which denote perfect aspect (cf. 1.1.2.2.2 and 2.1.3.3.1(d)). As discussed further in 2.1.3.3.1, the subordinate clause is always marked for past tense in these constructions. 1.1.2.6. Most commonly, equi-deletion is triggered by verbs that refer to movement, either physical and metaphorical, such as fano ‘go’ (and its plural form olo), vau ‘come’ (and its plural form aummai or mmai), foki ‘return, come back’, eva ‘fly, jump’, sopo ‘board [a vehicle]’, saga ‘turn to, face, to turn one’s attention to’, tuu ‘stand up’, vave ‘[go, do something] quick[ly], fast’: (589) Au ne fano fua [o fakaola taku kaleve]. Textual function of noun-phrase raising Theoretically, if several noun phrases are present in a subordinate clause, raising may target any one of them and may assign to it one of several case markers in the superordinate clause. In the first of the following sentences, any of the three arguments of the subordinate clause are potential targets for raising, as shown in the subsequent three examples: (620) E maasani [o ave nee Sina te tamaliki ki te loomatua]. Nps used-to the child Cmp send Erg Sina to the old-woman (623) E maasani te loomatua [o ave nee Sina te tamaliki ki ei]. Nps used-to the old-woman Cmp send Erg Sina the child to Anp ‘Sina often sends the child to the old woman.’ In such cases, there is a semantic constraint that dictates which noun phrase is to be raised and whether raising should apply at all. To be the target of raising, a noun phrase must be semantically ‘compatible’ with the raising verb, in that it must denote an entity that is responsible for the performance of the action denoted by the entire sentence, or for the inception of the state denoted by the sentence. Contrast, for example, the following sentences: (624) E maasani ia [o faagai saale nee au ki ika ffoou]. Nps used-to she Cmp feed usually Erg I with fish fresh ‘She is used to being given fresh fish to eat by me.’ (625) ? E maasani taku paipu [o faagai saale nee au ki Nps used-to my pipe Cmp feed usually Erg I with puatolo]. cake-tobacco (‘I usually feed my pipe with cake-tobacco.’) These two sentences have the same syntactic structure, in which the direct object of the subordinate clause is raised to the superordinate clause. What makes the second infelicitous is the fact that a pipe has, as an inanimate object, no volitional power, and therefore cannot be instrumental in bringing about the state which the sentence refers to. In contrast, in the previous example, the entity that experiences the usualness is a human referent, and raising can apply. Raising, thus, targets whichever noun phrase denotes the entity with the highest degree of responsibility in the action denoted by the entire sentence, whatever grammatical role may be assigned to that noun phrase. Responsibility differs from animacy and volition, which do not determine whether a noun phrase can be raised (Besnier 1988b). Since raising targets such responsible participants, subjects of deontic verbs are very likely to be targeted by the rule. There is a correlation between the case marking assigned to raised noun phrases in superordinate clauses and the grammatical role that it plays in the subordinate clause from which it was raised: the more oblique the role of the noun phrase in the subordinate clause, the more obliquely it is marked in the superordinate clause. Operational definition for the adjective phrase There are no straightforward arguments for establishing a separate category ‘adjective phrase’. Indeed, like most other morphological categories in the language, adjectival forms are not recognizable as such when disrobed of their syntactic context; in addition, adjectives, particularly attributive adjectives, do not move, and thus external mobility cannot be used as a test for constituency. text: Syntax 143 1.2.3. Adverbial phrases 1.2.3.1. Operational definition for the adverbial phrase There is no clear argument to support establishing a distinct constituent with adverbials as head. As shown in 1.2.1.3.1, adverbials form a very heterogeneous structural category, one which is better defined by default than in terms of the cohesive behaviour of its members. Hence any element which is not a noun, pronoun, verb, adjectival modifier, or a member of a closed class of grammatical morphemes can be considered as an adverbial, and the phrase of which the adverbial is the head can be considered an adverbial phrase. Adverbial phrases rarely undergo movement processes, they are not assigned any marking of any sort which could be taken to be a symptom of adverbial constituency, and the various types of adverbial clauses do not share any characteristic feature. 1.2.3.2. Adverbial modifiers of adverbials Relatively few adverbials can function as modifiers of adverbials. 1.2.3.2.1. Adverbs Adverbs can modify other adverbs, although cases of adverbs which are unequivocally modifiers of another adverb are rare. Indeed, when two adverbs are in the general vicinity of one another, they generally both modify the same head, rather than modify one another. Such is the case of the following: (772) E vau saale eiloa ki temotou fale. Nps come often indeed to our-3-i house ‘[She] often comes to our house.’ Even though the order of the two verb-modifying adverbs is fixed, there is little evidence that one can be interpreted as modifying the other. Rather, the semantics of the clause indicates that saale and eiloa both modify the verb, although no structural argument can be presented to support this interpretation, other than the fact that each adverb can occur without the other. There are instances of adverbs modifying other adverbs. Modified adverbs are clearly verb-derived, faka-prefixed adverbs being most frequent, and modifying adverbs are generally members of the more ‘adverbial’ core of the class, i.e., adverbials whose form does not appear in nonadverbial contexts, and whose meaning is highly ‘grammaticalized’, as is the case, for example, of aspectual and modal adverbs, and intensifiers and downtoners: (773) E teletele fakkaokao saale. Nps run in-manner-of+side often ‘[He] often runs sideways.’ In a context in which the above example describes someone in the habit of running sideways whenever he runs, but not necessarily in the habit of running, the adverb saale can be interpreted as a modifier of fakkaokao ‘sideways’, and not the verb. 1.2.3.2.2. Operational definition for the noun phrase As in many other languages, the noun phrase is the easiest constituent type to define. First, noun phrases other than personal pronouns and proper nouns can be identified by the fact that their first element is almost invariably an article; the only exception is associated with the quantifier soo ‘any’, which precedes the article (cf. 2.1.6.6.4). There are four basic article forms, as discussed in 2.1.1.8.6, one of which is a zero form, namely the definite plural article. They sometimes coalesce with or are replaced by possessive pronouns or quantifiers, as discussed in 2.1.2.4 and 2.1.6.6 respectively. Second, noun phrases, including phrases with a personal pronoun or proper noun as a head, are normally marked for case, although one important case marker, namely the absolutive case marker, appears commonly as a zero form (cf. 2.1.1.2.1.1). NEGATION Both sentence negation and constituent negation are marked with the same set of negative particles, all of which precede the negated element. Negators also precede any bound adverbs and, in sentence negation, clitic pronouns when present. In sentence negation, the negator follows tense-aspect markers, conjunctions, and complementizers. The negator precedes prepositions in the negation of prepositional phrases. As in most Polynesian languages, negators are difficult to assign to any particular part-of-speech category. Historical evidence suggests that Proto-Polynesian negators were verbs, whose subject was the negated sentence (Chung 1970:41–54, Clark 1976b:85–109). text: 186 Syntax 1.4.3. Multiple negatives Most sentences in natural discourse have only one negative element. The possibility of more than one negative element occurring in the same construction is greatly reduced by the fact that this language does not have negative quantifiers and adverbials. When two negators are found in the same sentence, they are usually part of two different clauses, and one is usually a sentence negator and the other a constituent negator. The result is always semantically positive: (995) Seeai se mea e see mafai nee ia o fai. Neg a thing Nps Neg can Erg he Cmp do ‘There is nothing he can’t do.’ No instance was found in natural discourse of three or more negators in the same sentence, and no such example was judged pragmatically acceptable or even processable. 1.4.4. Negation of coordinated elements The scope of negators cannot reach beyond the boundaries of a clause. When more than one clause in a coordinate construction is negated, each clause must be negated separately: (996) [See tii koukou] kae [see tii fano ki te aakoga]. Neg often bathe and Neg often go to the school ‘[He] never washes and never goes to school.’ Coordinated constituents can be negated with a single negator if constituent coordination is used (cf. 1.3.1.3): (997) E see ko Ioopu mo Pule ne olo o pei tili. Nps Neg Foc Ioopu and Pule Pst go Cmp cast fishing-net ‘It’s not Ioopu and Pule that went net-fishing.’ If only one coordinate is negated, clause coordination must be used (cf. 1.3.1.1): (998) E see ko Ioopu ne fano o pei tili, kae ko Pule. Nps Neg Foc Ioopu Pst go Cmp cast fishing-net but Foc Pule ‘It’s not Ioopu, but Pule, that went net-fishing.’ In no case do the negator and the coordinator combine into a single form. 1.4.5. Negation in subordinate clauses Negation is marked in exactly the same fashion in independent, superordinate, and subordinate clauses. In all cases, the negator must mark the negated element directly. In complex sentences, the subordinate clause cannot be negated by a negator in the superordinate clause. The negation of a subordinate clause and the negation of a superordinate clause yield different results: (999) E maasani o see ppusi. Subordinators with inherently negative meaning Several subordinators have inherently negative meanings or implicatures. These include the precautionary-mood marker maa and the precautionary conjunction moo aa ‘lest’, and the conjunction manuu ‘while’. COMPARISON There are two principal means of expressing comparison, which are discussed in 1.8.1 to 1.8.5. Correlative comparison can also be expressed in two ways, and these are described in 1.8.6. 1.8.7 treats various means of expressing superlative comparison. text: Syntax 219 Sentential standards of comparison must be first nominalized and then can be marked like nominal standards of comparison: (1162) Te tulamu e loa atu i te lauefa o te sefe. the drum Nps long Dxs at the wide of the larder ‘The drum is taller than the larder is wide.’ (1163) Te tulamu e loa atu i tena lauefa. the drum Nps long Dxs at its wide ‘The drum is taller than it is wide.’ Constructions with sentential standards of comparison are very rare in discourse. These constructions are more idiomatically expressed with the alternative comparative construction described in (b) below. Taken out of a discourse context, many comparative structures are semantically ambiguous. Indeed, in most cases, the deictic adverb can potentially be given a noncomparative deictic interpretation, and the locatively marked object can be given one of the many other meanings that locatively marked prepositional phrases can carry. For example, note the two possible interpretations of the following sentence: (1164) Koo sua aka eiloa ttai i aso kolaa. Inc full Dxs indeed the+tide at day those ‘In those days the high tide was very high.’ or: ‘In those days the high tide was higher [than these days].’ Comparative constructions can be disambiguated by using one of the complex forms of the comparative use of the locative preposition, namely i loo i, i loo o, or i loo. The morpheme loo can only be followed by a noun phrase referring to a standard of comparison (cf. 2.1.1.2.6), and it thus disambiguates the entire construction. However, it does not disambiguate between different possible comparative interpretations of the same sentence, as discussed in 2.1.1.2.6. Of course, in most discourse contexts, ambiguities between a comparative interpretation and other interpretations rarely arise. Another way of disambiguating comparative interpretations from other interpretations is to use as the sentence verb a lexeme with the general meaning of ‘large’ or ‘small’, e.g., lasi ‘large’, maaluga ‘high’, or fooliki ‘small’, or the Samoan borrowings sili and silia ‘exceed’ (the two forms have the same meaning in Tuvaluan). The entity being compared, the parameter of comparison, and the standard of comparison can be expressed in one of two ways. In one, the subject of the verb refers to the entity being compared, the parameter of comparison is expressed as a locatively marked nominalized clause, and the standard of comparison is provided in another locatively marked modifier: (1165) Koo maaluga atu koe i tou taina i te aava ki ei. Inc high Dxs you at your sibling at the respect to Anp ‘You respect him more than your brother [does].’ In the other construction, the parameter of comparison is nominalized and functions as the subject of the verb, the entity being compared is encoded as the subject of the nominalized clause referring to the parameter of comparison, and the standard of comparison is expressed as a locative phrase: (1166) Koo maaluga atu te aava o koe ki ei i tou taina. (b) Coordinated comparative clauses Alternatively, comparison can be expressed by coordinating two clauses, the verbs of which are antonyms or otherwise contrastive in meaning. The first clause contains a noun phrase that refers to the entity being compared, and the second clause contains a noun phrase that refers to the standard of comparison. The two noun phrases usually have the same syntactic and semantic role in their respective clauses, and the standard of comparison is commonly marked for contrastiveness or focus or both: (1167) Ne poa maalosi telotou vaka, a ko temotou vaka seki Pst catch-fish strongly their-3 canoe but Foc our-3-e canoe Neg poa maalosi. catch-fish strongly ‘Their canoe caught more fish than ours.’ [lit.: ‘Their canoe was very lucky, but our canoe was not very lucky.’] Either additive coordination by apposition (cf. 1.3.1.1.1) or additive-adversative coordination with kae or one of its allomorphs (cf. 1.3.1.1.2) can be used in these constructions. This strategy works well when the parameter of comparison can be expressed with an antonymic pair or otherwise contrasted lexically (e.g., poa ‘catch fish’ v. its negation, matua ‘old’ v. maalosi ‘healthy’). It is particularly appropriate when the entity being compared and the object of comparison are sentential elements, rather than noun phrases. For example, compare (1162) above with the following equivalent sentence, which is pragmatically better formed: (1168) E loa te tulamu, kae lauliki te sefe. Nps long the drum but narrow the larder ‘The drum is taller than the larder is wide.’ [lit.: ‘The drum is tall, the larder is narrow.’] These constructions have all the syntactic and semantic characteristics of coordinated clauses. They are always ambiguous between a simple contrastive and non- comparative interpretation and a comparative interpretation. Generally speaking, the more structural and semantic parallelism there is between the two clauses, the more likely they are to be interpreted as a comparative construction. For example, the structural and semantic differences between the two clauses are reduced to a minimum in the following sentence, and as a result the sentence is normally interpreted as a comparative construction, unless the context indicates otherwise: (1169) Koo maattua tino konei, a koo foolliki tino kolaa. Inc old person these but Inc young person those ‘These people are older than those people.’ 1.8.2–4. Omission under identity in comparative constructions Most constructions in which comparison is expressed with a deictic adverb and the standard of comparison is expressed with a locative preposition (cf. 1.8.1(a)) are monoclausal constructions. They can only be biclausal when the standard of comparison is a nominalized clause, which occurs rarely. When it does, as in examples (1162) and (1163), there is no evidence of any systematic process of omission of elements under identity with the superordinate clause. Rather, the nominalized clause consists of the constituents most essential to its interpretation | True

text: Syntax 221 as a standard of comparison. Indeed, the longer the nominalized clause, the less idiomatic it is. However, no grammatical statement can be produced to predict what must be deleted or what must not. Coordinated comparative clauses of the type described in 1.8.1(b) usually consist entirely of constituents that are not coreferential. Any ‘peripheral’ materials, i.e., constituents that are not essential to the comparison such as a prepositional phrase, can be deleted. However, peripheral materials are infrequent because these constructions generally consist only of the most essential constituents. This bare- bone tendency helps to highlight the comparative contrast and thus to minimize the possibility that the construction will be interpreted as something other than a comparison. 1.8.5. Differences between comparative structures The difference between the two comparative structures is principally a matter of style (the former being more formal than the latter), as well as potential ambiguity, in that deictic adverbs and prepositional standards of comparison are less ambiguously comparative than coordinated comparative clauses. There is no clear contrast between the expression of comparison with a comparative particle plus reduced comparative clause and the expression of comparison with a preposition plus standard of comparison. 1.8.6. Correlative comparison Correlative comparison can be expressed in one of two ways. One consists of a conditional-temporal construction marked with the conditional conjunctions kaafai or maafai or their allomorphs (cf. 1.1.2.4.2.1 and 1.1.2.4.2.5), which can always be interpreted as either a correlative comparative construction or a regular conditional or temporal clause: (1170) Kaa uke taimi e fakattolo ei koe, kae oola maalosi a Fut many time Nps play-drafts Anp you and alive healthy Cnt mataa pulaka. head-of swamp-taro ‘The more you play drafts, the healthier the swamp taro will be.’ or: ‘When you play drafts a lot, the swamp taro are healthy.’ The ambiguity between the two possible readings of such constructions can be diminished (but not completely done away with) by marking the verb of either the superordinate clause or the conditional clause or both with a deictic adverb: (1171) E gali atu te fekei mana uke atu kaleve. Superlative comparison Superlative comparison (e.g., She is the best mat-weaver of all women of this island) can be expressed in several ways, some of which are inherently ambiguous while others are not. (a) Unmarked constructions Superlative comparison is most simply, but also most ambiguously, expressed with no marking whatsoever. Whenever an entity is singled out among other entities as being associated with a gradable characteristic, the resulting construction can be interpreted as a superlative construction if this interpretation is appropriate to the context: (1174) Mataua ko te tino teenei o ttou kaaiga koo matua. Mataua Foc the person this of our-3-i family Inc old ‘Mataua is the oldest person in our family.’ or: ‘Mataua is the one person of our family who’s got old.’ While these constructions are always inherently ambiguous for obvious reasons, several grammatical strategies can ‘help’ the interpretation of these constructions as superlative constructions. One is the strategic use of aspect marking; in the above clause, for example, the verb is marked with the perfect aspect koo, which frequently carries affective and evidential connotations, as illustrated in 2.1.3.3.1(a). The other is the specification of a standard of comparison, expressed with the help of a locatively marked preposition, as in regular comparative clauses: (1175) Au e matua ia maatou. Constructions with tafasili are identical to constructions with sili(a) ‘exceed’ described in 1.8.1(a): (1184) Te tino tafasili loo te mmalu i loto i te fale, ko te the person superior indeed the honour at centre at the house Foc the maaloo teelaa e oko mai. guest that Nps reach Dxs ‘The most honourable person inside the house is the guest who’s [just] arrived.’ 1.9. EQUATIVES Equatives can be expressed in one of two ways. The first makes use of demonstrative forms that function either as an adverbial modifier of the verb or as the main verb of the clause. The second employs one of several verbs that denote similarity or identity between the referents of nominal constituents. 1.9.1. Means of expressing equatives (a) Demonstrative verbs and adverbs Equatives may be expressed with the help of demonstrative forms in pee-, namely peenei ‘thus’ (near speaker), peenaa ‘thus’ (near the interlocutor), peelaa ‘thus’ (away from speaker and interlocutor), which are also used in adverbial clauses of manner (cf. 1.1.2.4.2.2). The meaning and form of these demonstratives are discussed in 2.1.2.5(c). Demonstratives in pee- can take two types of object that differ in meaning, grammatical structure, and overt marking. Objects marked with the comitative preposition mo denote the standard of realis equation; objects marked with the complementizer me (or its phonologically-conditioned allomorphs ma and mo) are predicates, and they denote the standard of irrealis equation. A demonstrative in pee- can serve as the main verb of the clause, in which case it takes as a subject the noun phrase referring to the entity being equated and as an optional object the standard of equation: (1185) Koo peelaa mo koo taumafai o ofa nee ia te vaa llei o Inc thus Cmp Inc try Cmp break Erg he the gap good of taaua. we-2-i ‘It’s as if he were trying to break the good rapport that you and I have.’ | True

Omission under identity in equative constructions The only biclausal constructions with equative meaning are constructions with predicative objects. Generally speaking, noun phrases that are identical in the main clause and in the clausal object of comparison are deleted. text: Syntax 263 1.16.5. Preposition and case marker Both case markers and prepositions form closed classes (cf. 2.1.1 and 2.1.5.1), but the boundary between them is difficult to determine precisely because a number of forms function as both prepositions and case markers (and ambiguously so in certain contexts), and because they occupy the same positions in the phrase, where they are in complementary distribution (with one minor exception discussed in 2.2.6.1.1). The two basic case markers, the ergative and pseudoergative nee and the optional contrastive-absolutive a, are the least ambiguous: they clearly differ from other grammatical morphemes in that they function solely as markers of case relations. The three basic prepositions, locative i, directional ki, and source mai, take a prefix -(a)a when their object falls in certain categories, as discussed in 2.1.5.2 and 2.1.5.3, and this morphological peculiarity places them in a class of their own. However, they take the same suffix when they are used as case markers, and thus suffixation is not a good discriminating criterion. The same three prepositions can also take another, more archaic, suffix -te under the same conditions, but three other grammatical morphemes may also take this suffix, albeit more rarely: the alienable possessive a, the inalienable possessive o, and the comitative mo. Finally, both case marking and prepositional uses of i, ki, and mai can be the basis for the formation of complex prepositions (cf. 2.2.6.1.2). 1.16.6. Numeral, quantifier, and interrogative word Numerals do not form a separate word class. Rather, they function like verbal adjectives (cf. 2.1.6.1 to 2.1.6.5). Quantifiers do not form a separate word class either, nor do they behave in a homogeneous fashion: one finds in their ranks adverbs, verbs, affixes, and articles. For further discussion, see 2.1.6.6. The same can be said of interrogative words, some of which behave like nouns, and others like verbs or adverbs; their morphological classification is discussed in 2.1.2.6. | True

text: Chapter 2 Morphology 2.1. INFLECTION Like other Polynesian languages, Tuvaluan tends to encode syntactic and semantic information onto isolated morphological categories, rather than onto bound affixes, morphophonemic alternations, clitics, or derivational processes. For example, the syntactic and semantic functions of noun phrases are generally expressed with the help of prepositional morphemes. Apart from number agreement in some verbs and adjectives, very few processes modify the form of lexemes, be they nouns or members of other word classes. The consequence of this tendency is that there are very few form-internal criteria whereby members of various word classes can be distinguished (cf. 1.16). 2.1.1. Noun inflection 2.1.1.1. Means of marking syntactic and semantic functions As noted above, information on the syntactic and semantic functions of noun phrases is primarily encoded by prepositions and particles that function like prepositions. In addition, word order plays a minor role in marking syntactic and semantic functions (cf. 1.2.1.2.6). Indeed, certain prepositions are lost when their objects occur in certain syntactic positions, but their syntactic and semantic function is retrievable from their position in the sentence. However, the marking of syntactic and semantic functions is not the primary role of word order, but rather an incidental function. First and foremost, word order marks information structure (cf. 1.12.1). A summary of prepositions and preposition-like markers that encode the syntactic and semantic functions of noun phrases, along with cross-references to their various uses, is provided in 2.1.5.1. 2.1.1.2. Syntactic functions Attention is drawn to processes discussed elsewhere in this grammar that affect the morphological marking of syntactic functions as well as, in some cases, these syntactic functions themselves. These include: advancement-to-possessive (cf. 1.1.2.3.10); noun-phrase raising (cf. 1.1.2.7); nominalisations (cf. 2.1.1.3.4); and ‘double’ additive coordinated constructions (cf. 1.3.1.6). In the following discussion, I refer to tests for transitivity, which are summarized in 2.1.3.1. 2.1.1.2.1. Agentive subject of intransitive verb All agentive subjects of intransitive verbs (with the exception of the third-person singular pronoun in certain positions, as discussed below) can be marked with a zero case marker, no matter where in the clause the noun phrase occurs, and whether the noun phrase is a full noun phrase or a pronoun (cf. 2.1.2.1.1.3 for illustrations of the latter case): (1376) Koi tele ø tena gafa. still run his genealogy ‘He still has descendants.’ (1377) ø te gaaluega teelaa e see ttogi. the work that Nps Neg pay ‘That work doesn’t pay [anything].’ The one exception to this pattern is the nonzero form of the third-person pronoun (cf. 2.1.2.1.1.1–2) and in situ interrogative words that function as subjects of intransitive verbs (cf. 2.1.2.6). Definite agentive subjects of intransitive verbs can be marked with the preposed case marker a, glossed throughout this description as an ‘contrastive-absolutive’ marker. For example, the following are roughly equivalent in meaning to sentences (1376) and (1377) respectively: (1378) Koi tele a tena gafa. still run Cnt his genealogy ‘He still has descendants.’ (1379) A te gaaluega teelaa e see ttogi. In many cases, it has a contrastive function, as illustrated in 1.11.2.1.7. Even though it is uniformly glossed as a contrastive marker for convenience in this description, a does not always mark information structure and, in many instances, it has a very low functional load. Indeed, it tends to appear as a ‘filler’ whenever a definite noun phrase lacks an overt article and a case marker or preposition. Since both the plural definite article and the absolutive case marker are zero forms, a noun phrase appears with no article or case marker when it is definite, plural, and in the absolutive case, or when it occurs in preverbal position, where noun phrases are not marked for case (cf. 1.2.1.2.6 and 1.12.1): (1380) Kae kesekkese a tala. but different Cnt story ‘But there are different [versions of] the story.’ (1381) A pou o te fale e tofu loo mo tino. With these verbs, the noun phrase that receives absolutive-case marking is often the patient, while the agent is marked for the oblique case with the comitative preposition mo. Of course, in all these cases, which noun phrase functions as the syntactic subject of the verb is an empirical question, which is addressed in the following. text: 280 Morphology 2.1.1.2.2. Subject of transitive verb Several case-marking strategies are associated with subjects of transitive verbs. The most basic is the ergative case, which does not distinguish between agentive and nonagentive subjects, but upon which certain semantic restrictions are imposed. Its morphology is covered in (a) and its affective value is described in (b). The subject of a transitive verb is frequently expressed as the possessive modifier of the direct object, as discussed in (c), and, in certain constructions described in (d), as a benefactive phrase. The discussion in (e) delineates the implications of the previous subsections for an understanding of ergativity as a morphological and syntactic category in Tuvaluan. Other sections of relevance to the topics covered here are the discussions of clitic pronouns (cf. 2.1.2.1.1.5(a)), of restrictions on the agentive argument of causative verbs (cf. 2.1.3.1.3(a)), and of the transitivizing suffix (cf. 2.1.3.1.3(c)). (a) Ergative case marking Subjects of transitive verbs are commonly marked with the ergative case marker nee, which is obligatory when the noun phrase is postverbal: (1465) Toko uke tino ne ave nee vaka kaisoa. Num many person Pst send Erg ship steal ‘Many people were stolen by slave ships.’ (1466) E see iloa foki nee tino taumua o tauloto fakallei. Nps Neg know also Erg person former Cmp study properly ‘People in the olden days also did not know how to study properly.’ The marker is optionally reduced in form to ne when the following word consists of more than two morae. This predictable alternation is not indicated in the orthography used here. The marker can be followed by any article, noun, or preposed noun modifier, with the exception of the plural indefinite article ne, with which it is nearly homophonous: (1467) * Ne sau mai nee ne tino. Pst carry Dxs Erg some person (‘Some people carried [her] here.’) When the subject of a transitive verb is indefinite and plural, its article is simply dropped, and the noun phrase then becomes homophonous with its definite plural counterpart, since the plural definite article is a zero form: (1468) Ne sau mai nee tino. Pst carry Dxs Erg person ‘Some people carried [her] here.’ No restriction applies to the sequencing of nee with the singular indefinite article se, the plural definite article (a zero form), or the coalesced form of the indefinite plural article niisi ‘some, other’. Thus the above restriction clearly has a phonological motivation. The ergative case marker nee is an irregular reflex of the Proto-Polynesian case marker *e; the regular reflex e is found in the three Northern dialects and is occasionally heard in the Southern dialects, particularly in religious discourse. When the subject of a transitive verb occurs in preverbal position, it is left unmarked for case, or it is marked with the absolutive-contrastive case marker a (cf. 1.2.1.2.6). (b) Affective value of the ergative case Although no morphological distinction is made between agentive and nonagentive subjects of transitive verbs, ergative case marking is constrained by a number of semantic restrictions. While the morphological category ‘ergative’ is strongly associated with the syntactic category ‘subject of transitive verb’, the ergative case may mark categories other than subjects of transitive verbs and some subjects of transitive verbs are not marked ergatively. In the majority of cases, the ergative case marks a personal pronoun, whether it functions as the index of a moved noun phrase or a full pronoun. When it marks full noun phrases, these are typically definite and specific. However, indefinite and nonspecific noun phrases are not grammatically excluded from ergatively- marked argument slots: (1471) Fakanofonofoga kolaa e faigataa o fakassee nee se tino. resolution those Nps difficult Cmp Cst+wrong Erg a person ‘It is difficult for someone to dispute these resolutions.’ The propensity for personal pronouns and definite noun phrases to be marked ergatively is symptomatic of the fact that the ergative case has strong affective connotations. An ergatively marked noun phrase commonly refers to an entity that is centrally involved in bringing about the situation denoted by the clause. It is thus not surprising that pronouns, i.e., animate entities which are high in topicality, should be so commonly marked with the ergative case, and that definite noun phrases should be much more common than indefinite noun phrases in ergative slots. (e) Ergativity as a morphological and syntactic phenomenon When faced with an ergative-absolutive system, the grammarian must ascertain the extent to which the morphological categories ‘absolutive’ and ‘ergative’ reflect syntactically significant categories, i.e., whether ergativity is a morphological phenomenon superposed on a syntactic structure based on a nominative-accusative pattern, or whether the categories of ergative and absolutive are also recognized as syntactic categories in the structure of the language (Dixon 1994:143–181). Several processes provide evidence that Tuvaluan syntax is based on a nominative-accusative system.
