Thus subjects of middle verbs may be marked for the absolutive case, as in finite middle clauses: (1588) Te alofa te loomatua ki tena mokopuna! the feel-empathy the old-woman to her grandchild ‘The old woman feels so sorry for her grandchild!’ They may alternatively be marked for possession, according to the same patterns as intransitive verbs: (1589) Te alofa o te loomatua ki tena mokopuna! the feel-empathy of the old-woman to her grandchild If pronominal, a middle subject may be expressed with a possessive pronoun of the inalienable class: (1590) Tena alofa ki tena mokopuna! her feel-empathy to her grandchild ‘She feels so sorry for her grandchild!’ 2.1.1.3.4.3. Subject of nominalized transitive verb Subjects of transitive nominalized verbs are most commonly marked for the ergative case, and thus nominalization does not affect their case marking. If they are pronominal and under certain conditions, they may also be expressed with a possessive pronoun of the alienable class. Each of these two possibilities is reviewed here in turn. Postverbal subjects of transitive nominalized verbs cannot be possessively marked, whether or not they be pronominal, whether or not a direct object is present in the nominalized clause, and whatever case marking is assigned to the direct object: (1591) * te ssalaaga a/o toku taina (o/i) tena aavaga i te vao the search+Nom of/of my sibling of/at his spouse in the bush (‘my brother’s search for his spouse in the bush’) The case marking of subjects of nominalized transitive verbs is sensitive to the case marking of the direct object under certain circumstances. A summary of grammatical and ungrammatical case-marking patterns in transitive clauses is provided in 2.1.1.3.4.4(e). (a) Finite case marking Subjects of transitive nominalized verbs may be marked for the ergative case with nee: (1592) Te kalagaaga nee koe au seki lagona nee au. the hear+Nom Erg you I Neg hear Erg I ‘I didn’t hear [you] when you called me.’ This strategy is allowed whether the nominalized clause has an overt direct object (as in the above examples) or not: (1593) Te kalagaaga nee koe seki lagona nee au. the hear+Nom Erg you Neg hear Erg I ‘I didn’t hear [you] when you called [him].’ When the direct object of the nominalized verb is marked for the absolutive case (cf. 2.1.1.3.4.4(a)), the linear order of the two noun phrases follows the same patterns as in finite clauses (cf. 1.2.1.2.5). Direct object of nominalized verb Four case-marking patterns are associated with direct objects of nominalized verbs, many of which are sensitive to the case marking of the subject of the clause. This section closes with a summary of case-marking possibilities for subjects and direct objects in transitive nominalized clauses (cf. (e) below). (a) Finite case marking Direct objects of nominalized verbs may be case-marked in the same fashion as they are case-marked in finite clauses, i.e., for the absolutive case. Illustrations are provided in 2.1.1.3.4.3(a) and in example (1594). This strategy is possible no matter how the subject of the transitive nominalized verb is marked, and whether a subject is present or not in the clause. It is unidiomatic but not ungrammatical if the subject is expressed with a possessive pronoun (cf. 2.1.1.3.4.3(b)). (b) Inalienable possessive pronoun The pronominal direct object of a nominalized verb may be expressed as a possessive pronoun of the inalienable class preposed to the nominalized verb: (1600) Toku kalagaaga nee koe seki lagona nee au. my hear+Nom Erg you Neg hear Erg I ‘I didn’t hear [you] when you called me.’ This strategy is possible only if the possessive-pronoun slot is not already occupied by a possessive pronoun referring to the subject of the clause (cf. 2.1.1.3.4.2(b)). (c) Inalienable possessive noun phrase The direct object of a nominalized verb may alternatively be marked for inalienable possession with the preposition o: (1601) Koo ffati ana lima i te ttaa ssoko o gatu o ana tama nee Inc broken her hand in the wash often of clothing of her child Erg ia she ‘Her hands are broken from constantly washing her children’s clothes.’ (1602) Te kalagaaga o au nee koe seki lagona nee au. the hear+Nom of I Erg you Neg hear Erg I ‘I didn’t hear [you] when you called me.’ This strategy is grammatical either if the subject is overt and marked for the ergative case, as in the above examples, or if the subject is non-overt: (1603) Koo ffati ana lima i te ttaa ssoko o gatu o ana tama. Inc broken her hand in the wash often of clothing of her child Direct objects of nominalized verbs are never marked for alienable possession. If both a subject and a possessively marked direct-object noun phrase are present in the same clause, there is a preference for the possessively marked direct object to precede the ergatively marked subject. This preference is probably related to the fact that ‘true’ possessive modifiers tend to precede other postposed modifiers of a noun. It is only a tendency, and examples that violate it are attested: (1604) A ko au seki lavea nee au a mea konaa ki te fakamoeega and Foc I Neg see Erg I Cnt thing those to the Cst+sleep+Nom nee ia o tamaliki. Erg he of child ‘And I never saw him hypnotize children.’ | True

text: Morphology 309 This strategy is also grammatical, but less than fully idiomatic, if the subject is expressed as a possessive pronoun, as illustrated in (1596). (d) Middle-object marking Finally, if the subject of a transitive nominalized verb is expressed as a possessive pronoun, the direct object may be marked with the middle-object marker i (but not the alternative middle-object marker ki). This pattern, which is preferred when the conditions for its use are met, is illustrated in (1595) and in the following example: (1605) A laatou koo lasi telotou iloa i te nofoga o te Cnt they-3 Inc large their-3 know at the stay+Nom of the fenua mai mua. island-community from back ‘They know a lot about how the island community was run in the olden days.’ This pattern is not possible under any other circumstances; for example, the direct object cannot be marked with i if the subject is ergatively marked, as in (1606), or if it is non-overt, as in (1607): (1606) * Te kalagaaga nee koe i au seki lagona nee au. the hear+Nom Erg you at I Neg hear Erg I (‘I didn’t hear [you] when you called me.’) (1607) * Te kalagaaga i au seki lagona nee au. the hear+Nom at I Neg hear Erg I The unusual distribution of this case-marking pattern and its preferred status suggests that a grammatical filter blocks certain case-marking patterns. Indeed, middle-object marking is a preferred alternative to the cooccurrence in the same clause of, on the one hand, a possessive pronoun (the subject) and an absolutively- marked modifier (the direct object), and, on the other hand, a possessive pronoun (the subject) and a possessive noun-phrase modifier (the direct object). Neither of these alternative configurations is ungrammatical, although they are both perceived as lacking in idiomaticity and elegance. The cooccurrence of two possessive modifiers in the latter configuration is unique, because in all other circumstances only one possessive modifier is allowed (cf. 2.1.1.4.6 and 2.1.2.4.5–6). That the former configuration is less than idiomatic undoubtedly results from the fact that it expresses the subject with a less referential strategy than the direct object, a state of affairs which is universally marked (Hopper and Thompson 1980). I have assumed here that the marker i is indeed the middle-object marker i. However, this preposition also marks many other syntactic and semantic functions (cf. 2.1.5.1 for a complete list). Whether or not the preposition i in nominalized clauses is truly a middle-object marker cannot be ascertained, because middle objects are not syntactically distinguishable from obliques (cf. 2.1.1.2.8(a)), and Seiter (1980:120–122) is perhaps wise to call the equivalent construction in Niuean ‘fake accusative marking’ (in reference to the fact that middle objects in Niuean have direct-object properties). Nevertheless, it is noteworthy that middle objecthood is marked with both the case markers ki (homophonous with the directional preposition) and i, whereas only i can appear as a direct-object marker in nominalized clauses. This distribution suggests that the two categories are not exactly the same (despite the expedient terminology I have adopted here), a point whose significance is discussed in 2.1.1.2.8(a). | True

text: 310 Morphology (e) Summary of case marking with nominalized transitive verb Table 2.1 summarizes case-marking possibilities in nominalized transitive clauses. Only two strategies are available in marking overt subjects, only one of which is available for nonpronominal noun phrases. The direct object may be case-marked in one of four ways, or may be non-overt. In this table ‘A-class’ and ‘O-class’ refer to alienable and inalienable possessive marking respectively (cf. 2.1.1.4.6.1).16 2.1.1.3.4.6. Other objects and modifiers of nominalized verbs As noted in 2.1.1.2.8(a), the marking of middle objects is not affected by nominalization. Thus middle objects that are marked with ki in finite clauses are also marked with ki in nominalized contexts, and the same applies to middle-object marking with i: (1608) Toku alofa ki toku taina! my feel-empathy to my sibling ‘I feel so sorry for my brother!’ 16 It is interesting to compare the Tuvaluan case-marking system in nominalized clauses with descriptions of the same phenomenon in other Polynesian languages, the most informative being Chung (1976) and Clark (1981). Chung (1976:667) identifies three marking systems among the Polynesian languages she surveys: a syntactic system, in which arguments are assigned to possessive classes on the basis of their grammatical function; a neutralizing system, in which all arguments are assigned to the same possessive class; and a semantic system, in which arguments are assigned to possessive classes on the basis of their semantic role (i.e., to the A-class if dominant, O-class if subordinate). In the last system, direct objects are always assigned O-class possession, while subject marking can follow two different patterns: in languages like Samoan, subjects of both intransitive and transitive verbs are assigned either A- or O-class possession depending on their semantic role; in languages like Pukapukan, subjects of transitive verbs are invariably assigned A-class possession, while subjects of intransitive verbs are assigned either A- or O-class possession depending on their semantic role. The Tuvaluan system appears to fall into the same category as Pukapukan, although the terms in which the typology is established do not describe the Tuvaluan system well. First, it does not capture the complex patterns of interdependence between the marking of subjects and direct objects within the same clause, and the fact that case marking is sensitive to whether the arguments of the verb are pronouns or full noun phrases. Second, while possessive class assignment in intransitive clauses is related to semantic criteria, it is ultimately dictated idiosyncratically by the verb (cf. 2.1.1.3.4.1). Nonlocal semantic functions Each of the following sections comprises three subsections. The first describes adverbial modifiers in normal clauses; the second, attributive elements of noun phrases; and the third, complements of copular constructions, which are predicative constructions in this language. In many cases, the same construction is used for the first two syntactic positions. The third position is the most ‘deficient’, in that many semantic functions cannot be expressed with a predicative construction. Negative functions (e.g., negative instrumental, negative quality) can always be and often are expressed paraphrastically. For example, the coordinated clause in (1611) denotes negative circumstance and qualifies the referent of the first clause in the sentence; in (1612), the relative clause denotes negative circumstance: (1611) Ffoki mai ttoko luaa kae see aumai nofoga. return Dxs the+Num two but Neg bring chair ‘Those two came back without the chairs.’ [lit.: ‘Those two came back, but didn’t bring the chairs.’] (1612) Maatou e iinu ki tii seki palu ki suka. we-3-e Nps drink to tea Neg mix to sugar ‘We drink tea without sugar.’ [lit.: ‘We drink tea that has not been mixed with sugar.’] The following discussion does not cover such cases of paraphrase. Benefactive (a) Adverbial element in a clause Benefactive noun phrases are marked with the benefactive prepositions maa and moo when they function as adverbial elements in a clause. The first form can be roughly characterized as an alienable benefactive marker and the second as an inalienable benefactive marker, according to the criteria described in 2.1.1.4.6.1. Thus when the referent of the benefactive phrase is the recipient of an entity, and when the ensuing possessive relationship would be marked for alienable possession in a possessive phrase or clause, the alienable benefactive preposition is used: (1614) Koo maua nee koe o lafo mai ne tusi maa maatou. Inc can Sbj you Cmp send Dxs some letter Ben we-3-e ‘You can [afford to] send letters to us.’ In contrast, the inalienable benefactive preposition is used when the benefactive process may result in a possessive relationship of the inalienable type. For example, when the referent of the benefactive phrase is the recipient of a canoe, inalienable benefactive marking is obligatory because vaka ‘canoe’ is an inalienably possessed word: (1615) Te vaka teenei e taa moo toku mokopuna. the canoe this Nps build Ben my grandchild ‘I am building this canoe for my grandchild.’ The first-person singular pronoun coalesces with the benefactive prepositions maa and moo, as shown in 2.1.2.1.20. To be noted here is the formal resemblance between the alienable possessive and benefactive markers on the one hand (a and maa respectively) and between the inalienable possessive and benefactive markers on the other (o and moo respectively). However, the marking of alienability and inalienability in benefactive phrases is much less strict than in possessive phrases. In particular, when the benefactive relationship does not result in a possessive relationship, the inalienable marker moo is often used across the board: (1616) E manako ko te looia o tino kee tuu moo ia. Nps wish Foc the lawyer of person Sbj stand Ben he ‘He wants the people’s lawyer to defend him.’ (1617) E seeai se tino ia taatou e ola moo ia eiloo. Nps Neg a person among we-3-i Nps live Ben he indeed ‘No one among us lives only for himself.’ Even when the benefactive relationship does result in a possessive relationship, the inalienable marker is often used even if the resulting possessive relationship is of the alienable type: (1618) Konei laa tala moo taatou i ttaimi nei. these then news Ben we-3-i at the+time this ‘This is the news (for our benefit) for the time being.’ (1619) E iloa nee laatou i te gaaluega nei e aogaa moo te Nps know Erg they Cmp the work this Nps useful Ben the fenua. island-community ‘They know that this work is of use to the island community.’ | True

In other Polynesian languages (e.g., Tongan), the contrast between alienable and inalienable benefactives is not as loose as in Tuvaluan, which suggests that the contrast is in the process of disappearing in the latter. However, the form of the alienable preposition is not disappearing because it has functions other than the marking of benefactive functions (for cross-references, see 2.1.5.1). Source (a) Adverbial element in a clause Source as a nonlocal semantic function is not distinguished formally from source as a local function (‘motion from’). The least marked way of denoting source is with the general locative preposition i: (1626) Te fuaa taki teenei ne maua i te taki a saa Iokapeta. the egg+of duck this Pst get at the duck of group Iokapeta ‘[I] got this duck’s egg from Iokapeta’s family’s duck.’ Alternatively, source can be denoted by the preposition mai, which can be used instead of i or in addition to it (yielding the complex preposition mai i). In many cases, the difference in meaning between i and mai or mai i is of an affective nature, and in most cases either preposition can be used without there being a difference in grammaticality: (1627) Koo ola manuia mai tena masaki. text: 316 Morphology Instruments marked with this preposition must denote entities that are centrally involved in the situation denoted by the clause. Thus ki cannot be used to mean ‘with the help of’ (this notion is expressed paraphrastically with the verb fakaaogaa ‘make use of’). This also means that ki can be used to connote that a situation could not take place without the referent of the object of the preposition. Two transitive verbs, kiki ‘eat as accompaniment to protein food’ and ppeke ‘eat with a sauce, dunk’ (cf. 5.1.4.2), take both a direct object and an instrumental modifier. text: 322 Morphology Kinship terms and related words fall into possessive classes predictably in light of the characterization of the two possessive classes emerging from the above discussion. The distribution reads as follows for nonborrowed basic kinship terms (for precise glosses of the terms, see 5.1.1): alienable tama ‘(classificatory) child’ inalienable tamana ‘(classificatory) father’ maatua ‘(classificatory) mother, (classificatory) parent’ taina ‘(classificatory) sibling of same gender’ tuagaane ‘(classificatory) sibling of opposite gender’ tupuna ‘(classificatory) grandparent’ mokopuna ‘(classificatory) grandchild’ maa ‘(classificatory) sibling-in-law of same gender’ fugaona ‘in-law’ (archaic) The term aavaga ‘spouse’ is usually alienably possessed, but can also be marked for inalienable possession, in which case it acquires connotations of greater respect. The terms faanau ‘children (as a whole)’, a borrowing from Samoan, toekimuli ‘last- born child’, toekimua and uluaki ‘first-born child’, and the Samoan borrowing ulumatua, synonymous with toekimua and uluaki, are marked for alienable possession if the possessor is the referent’s parent, and for inalienable possession if the possessor is the referent’s sibling, sibling set, or kin group. However, toe ‘child’ (with affectionate connotation) receives inalienable possession marking. Terms for kin- group categories to which one belongs, from which one descends, and of which one is the ancestor are all inalienably possessed: kaaiga ‘family’, mata kaaiga or pui kaaiga ‘clan’, tupuga ‘ancestry’, gafa ‘genealogy, descent, ancestry’, fakatelega and fakasologa ‘descent’. The noun fanauga ‘children issued from the same parents, sibling set’ is alienably possessed if the possessor is a parent, and inalienably possessed if the possessor is a member of the sibling set. It should be clear from the above description that possessive classes are not gender categories or Bantu-style noun classes. Rather, possessive classes are best analysed as characteristics of possessive relationships, even though all nouns that can be marked for possession have an unmarked association with either alienable or inalienable possession. The best generalization of the assignment of possessive classes to particular possessive relationships is identical to that described insightfully by Wilson (1976) for Hawaiian: when the possessor controls the initiation of the possessive relationship, the relationship will be marked for alienability; otherwise, the relationship will be marked for inalienability. The structure of local semantic functions in other positions is easily derived from adverbial positions. First, the category traditionally referred to in Polynesian linguistics as ‘local nouns’ (cf. Bauer 1993:262–263) forms a closed class of lexemes referring to ‘generic’ locations and directions. The most important are mua ‘front’, tua ‘back’, luga ‘top’, lalo ‘bottom’, loto ‘centre’, fafo (or fofo) ‘outside’, and tafa ‘side’, as well as fale ‘settlement’, gaaloto ‘home’, namo or tai or gaatai ‘lagoon(wards)’, and uta or gaauta ‘land(wards)’ (cf. 2.1.1.5(c) and (d)). These nouns appear without an overt article when used as generic locations and directions, a feature which can be simply explained as a consequence of their plural number, since plurality is marked with a zero article (cf. 2.1.1.8.6). That they are plural nouns is attested by the following: when they are marked with a possessive pronoun, the plural form of the pronoun is obligatory. On the other hand, one finds borrowings whose phonological shape is not adapted to the phonological structure of the language, which are not standardized as fully-fledged members of the lexicon of the language, and whose use depends on the speaker’s knowledge of the donor language. Classes and genders There are no classes or gender categories in the language. As shown in 2.1.1.4.6.1, the alienable-inalienable contrast identified in possessive structures should not be analysed as a gender-like phenomenon, because it has a clear semantic basis, because the categories it defines are not mutually exclusive, and because it is only relevant to one specific type of structure. Unlike certain other Oceanic languages (e.g., Palauan, Kilivila), Polynesian languages do not have classifier systems, and Tuvaluan is no exception. Certain inflectional and derivational morphemes resemble classifiers, such as the collective morphemes described in 2.1.1.8.5, some of the specialized numeral forms identified in 2.1.6.3, the numeral modifiers described in 2.1.6.5.2, and some of the quantifiers discussed in 2.1.6.6.3. Obligatoriness of indefiniteness marking Indefinite articles appear in one of two contexts: as markers of nonreferential indefiniteness and in a number of grammatical constructions that are conventionally associated with indefinitely-marked noun phrases. The former case is discussed in 2.1.1.12. The following discussion focuses on the latter case. Indefinite noun phrases appear most frequently as the subject of positive and negative existential verbs (cf. 1.2.1.1.1(b) and 1.4(d) respectively), including existential verbs that denote possession (cf. 1.10.1.1), and as an element of equational constructions (cf. 1.2.1.1.1(a)), including interrogative equational constructions (cf. 1.1.1.2.2.2(b)). The reason why these grammatical functions are associated with indefiniteness is simple, given the definition of indefiniteness as an information category used when the speaker-writer assumes that his or her interlocutor is not able to identify the referent of the noun phrase (Chafe 1976). Since both existential and equational constructions commonly serve to identify and qualify new nominal referents, they are canonical contexts for indefiniteness. Note that indefinitely marked noun phrases in such contexts can refer to either specific or nonspecific entities. Furthermore, in some grammatically conditioned contexts, the indefinitely marked noun phrase may alternatively be marked with a definite article. Such is the case, for example, of existential constructions that function as possessive clauses, where the alternation between indefiniteness and definiteness results in subtle differences in information structure (cf. 1.10.1.1). However, indefiniteness is more frequent than definiteness in these contexts. In addition, indefiniteness is preferred when the noun phrase appears with certain quantifiers, in particular isi ‘other’, suaa- ‘other’, soo ‘any’ (cf. 2.1.6.6), and when it is the object of the irrealis equative construction peenei me, peenaa me, peelaa me (cf. 1.9.1(a)). When their final vowel is geminated, the connotation is that the nonreferential referent contrasts with another entity mentioned in the same stretch of discourse, or that it is located at or associated with a generically distant point in space or time, from which it has little or no relevance or influence on the situation at hand: (1921) Peelaa mo koo tai kkese te tala a ttinoo, tai thus Cmp Inc quite different the story of the+person+Nrf quite kkese ttala a ttinoo. different the+story of the+person+Nrf ‘Like, one person says one thing, another person says something else.’ (1922) Me seei se tuu peelaa kee vau se tino o fenuaa, kae because Neg a custom thus Sbj come a person of island+Nrf and nofo i te nofoaga teelaa. stay at the chair that ‘Because it’s not part of custom for someone from another island to come along, and [begin] occupying that position.’ Words ending in a high vowel do not undergo nonreferential final-vowel gemination. Thus the noun taimi ‘time’, which one would expect to be a member of the closed class of nouns described above, is never found with a geminated final vowel. | True

text: 372 Morphology Final-vowel gemination has functions other than the marking of nonreferentiality. First, certain ‘local nouns’ optionally undergo final-vowel gemination in contexts where they are used as independent fixed framework locative expressions (cf. 2.1.1.5(d)), that is, not as part of complex prepositions (cf. 2.1.1.5(c)). The following local nouns can undergo this process: tua ‘back part of the village’, mua ‘front part of the village’, namo ‘lagoon(ward)’, uta ‘land(ward)’, and fale ‘towards the settlement’. Other terms are excluded either because of their phonological structure (e.g., tai ‘lagoon(ward)’, the antonym of uta, ends in a high vowel), or because of the unproductive nature of the process. The difference in meaning between regular and geminated forms of local nouns is rather insignificant. Geminated forms tend to connote greater distance, either physical or metaphorical, between the point of reference of the discourse and the referent of the local noun. Regular and geminated forms do not differ from one another in terms of referentiality in the usual sense of the term, although it is noteworthy that local nouns denote very general locations and directions, and thus are inherently less than fully referential. Second, proper names that are marked with the preposed collective morpheme saa (or haa in the Nukulaelae dialect) optionally undergo final- vowel gemination, as discussed in 2.1.1.8.4–5, unless they already end in a geminate vowel. These cases differ from final-vowel gemination with dummy and local nouns, as proper names ending in a high vowel can undergo final- vowel gemination (e.g., saa Peetelii ‘Peteli and her group’, saa Mauu ‘Mau and his group’). Similarly, noun phrases with tama ‘what’s-his-name, what’s-her- name’ and toko lua ‘those two’ as head, which have other unusual characteristics, can also undergo final-vowel gemination, and in certain cases must do so (cf. 2.1.1.8.4–5, 2.1.6.5.1(a)). Final-vowel gemination carries no identifiable meaning in these cases, and there is no semantic or pragmatic difference between nongeminated and geminated equivalents when both are possible. It clearly does not mark nonreferentiality, since these expressions always refer to specific individuals or groups of individuals. Final-vowel gemination is not a productive process, and an integrated characterization of its various uses should not be sought. In a significant number of cases, it denotes both nonreferentiality and distance or lack of relevance to the discourse context. In other cases, it does not have an identifiable function. 2.1.1.12.2. Obligatoriness of referentiality marking The marking of nonreferentiality is obligatory in equational and existential constructions, since only referential noun phrases can appear in these contexts. Similarly, the marking of nonreferentiality is obligatory in other indefinite noun phrases insofar that these are always nonreferential. The marking of nonreferentiality with final-vowel gemination is never obligatory. 2.1.1.12.3–4. Referentiality and nominal categories Both plural and mass nouns are marked for referentiality in the same general fashion as singular nouns, although with different morphemes, as shown above. 2.1.1.13. Genericness Genericness is a significant category insofar as generic noun phrases can only be marked with definite articles. | True

text: Morphology 373 2.1.1.13.1. Means of marking genericness Definite articles, principally the singular form, are used to mark generic noun phrases of all types: (1923) Te atu e gali ki te ota. the bonito Nps nice to the eat-raw ‘Bonito is nice raw.’ (1924) Teenaa te kesekkeseega o te tagata mo te fafine. that the different+Nom of the man and the woman ‘That’s how men and women differ from one another.’ Alternatively, but less commonly, generic noun phrases can be marked with the plural definite article (i.e., with a zero form): (1925) E tai mmafa ki luga i taagata a te masaki teelaa ko te Nps quite heavy to top at men Cnt the illness that Foc the faatauemu. mock ‘That sickness, namely [being in the habit of] mocking, is more a man’s [habit].’ Mass nouns and nouns that denote inherently plural or collective entities are marked for genericness in the same manner. 2.1.1.13.2. Obligatoriness of genericness marking Indefinite articles cannot be used to mark genericness, and thus the category can be considered to be obligatory. 2.1.1.14. Obviation Obviation, the marking of the relative importance of actors in discourse, is not marked. Relative importance is marked on a clause-by-clause basis with the same strategies as those used for ordinary pragmatic salience (cf. 1.11 and 1.12). 2.1.2. Pronouns Tuvaluan has clearly identifiable classes of personal pronouns, possessive pronouns, demonstrative pronouns, and relative pronouns. There are no separate forms of reflexive or reciprocal pronouns. Also covered in this section are nonpronominal demonstrative forms (2.1.2.5), which share semantic characteristics with demonstrative pronouns, and interrogative words, most of which are not pronominal (2.1.2.6). Overt personal and possessive pronouns (i.e., forms other than zero pronouns) generally refer to human entities or, marginally, nonhuman animate entities. This tendency does not apply to pronominal traces associated with movement processes and other coindexing phenomena, such as topicalization and relativization. Following are examples of such traces referring to nonhuman or inanimate entities: (1926) Te Tautai ne liakina nee ia Funaafuti i te aso nei. the Tautai Pst leave Erg she Funafuti in the day this ‘The M.V.Te Tautai left Funafuti today.’ | True

Optionality of free pronouns First- and second-person personal pronouns of all numbers are normally expressed overtly. Indeed, the zero form is the basic form of the third-person singular pronoun, and it is less marked than the overt form ia. Several arguments support this analysis. First, ia is obligatorily case-marked except in a few contexts, and hence is morphosyntactically less ‘free’ than the zero pronouns. Second, the zero form is pragmatically less marked than ia, and as a result it is statistically more frequent in natural discourse. The following discussion elaborates on these two arguments in turn. The pronoun ia must be overtly case-marked, except in one instance. When it functions as the subject of an intransitive verb or a direct object, it may appear with the zero form of the absolutive case marker (cf. 2.1.1.2.1) as long as it immediately follows the verb and its postverbal modifiers. Personal pronouns in unemphatic and emphatic contexts Emphasis does not affect the segmental and suprasegmental form of pronouns. 2.1.2.1.1.5. Reduced pronouns Reduced forms of personal pronouns are used in three restricted contexts: as subject clitics of verbs suffixed with the transitivizing suffix - gina; as subject clitics following the complementizer moo; and, in the second-person dual and plural only, in imperative clauses. text: 380 Morphology 2.1.2.1.2. Person distinctions in pronouns Distinct forms exist for all number categories in the first, second, and third persons. Following is an illustration of the three-way contrast in the singular: (1964) Au e fano maataeao. I Nps go tomorrow ‘I’m leaving tomorrow.’ (1965) Koe e fano maataeao. you Nps go tomorrow ‘You’re leaving tomorrow.’ (1966) ø e fano maataeao. he Nps go tomorrow ‘[He]’s leaving tomorrow.’ 2.1.2.1.3. Inclusion v. exclusion The distinction between inclusion and exclusion is morphologically encoded in the pronoun paradigm for both nonsingular numbers in the first person only. The first- person inclusive pronouns taaua (dual) and taatou (plural) refer to ‘you and I’ and ‘you, I, and at least another referent’ respectively, while the first-person exclusive pronouns maaua (dual) and maatou (plural) refer to ‘I and a referent other than you’ and ‘I and at least two referents other than you’ respectively. In the first person, there is no pronoun form with ‘general’ reference, i.e., unspecified with respect to inclusion or exclusion, and the choice between an inclusive or exclusive form is obligatory. The first-person plural inclusive pronoun taatou and all first-person plural inclusive possessive pronouns have important affective connotations. Inclusive pronominal reference is frequently used to refer to such entities as the speaker’s family, to her or his home island and its inhabitants, or to Tuvalu, its inhabitants, and its attributes: (1967) Te Niivaga e vau nei, Niulakita, ki taatou eiloo. the Nivaga Nps come now Niulakita to we-3-i indeed ‘The M.V.Nivaga is coming this way, [first to] Niulakita, [and then] straight to us [to Nukulaelae].’ (1968) [The speaker castigates her interlocutor for relying on kinship ties in a business setting] Fai te mea ttonu, saa fai te mea faka-taatou! do the thing straight Neg do the thing in-manner-of+we-3-i ‘Go about it in a straight, above-board manner, don’t go about it in the Tuvaluan way!’ The stylistically and affectively least marked way of referring to Tuvalu as a nation is with the pronoun taatou. ‘Tuvaluan’ is te ggana a taatou ‘our language’ or (te ggana) faka-taatou literally ‘(the language) in our manner’. What is viewed as characteristic of an often reified ‘Tuvaluan culture’ becomes tuu mo aganuu a taatou ‘our customs and traditions’ or tuu mo aganuu faka-taatou ‘customs and traditions in our manner’, and so on: (1969) A te tusi teenaa kaa ffuli ki te ggana a taatou. Cnt the book that Pst translate to the language of we-3-i ‘That book is going to be translated into Tuvaluan.’ | True

Nps thus also we-3-i men in inside in Tuvalu this ‘This also applies to us men in Tuvalu.’ First-person inclusive plural pronouns are preferred to more ‘referential’ noun phrases even in cases where the interlocutor is not a member of the community being referred to. Thus a speaker of Tuvaluan will use taatou when addressing a foreigner or an islander from another island, even though, strictly speaking, the interlocutor is not included in the reference of the pronoun. Witness also the following utterance, addressed to a Nukulaelae Islander who has just returned from Funafuti to Nukulaelae, and who has just told the speaker about the weather on Funafuti during the previous week: (1972) Ppau eiloo mo taatou! same indeed with we-3-i ‘It was just the same here!’ Clearly, the pronoun cannot be given its literal meaning in this utterance, since it refers to a situation in which the interlocutor could not have taken part. First-person inclusive possessive pronouns may have the same affective connotations as the corresponding personal pronoun: (1975) Au e fia ssili mua ki te failautusi kee taku mai aka te I Nps want ask please to the secretary Sbj tell Dxs please the aofaki o te kaitaalafu a tettou taina. amount of the loan of our-3-i sibling ‘I would like to ask the secretary to please tell us how much the money that our brother has borrowed amounts to.’ | True

text: 382 Morphology However, when the affective connotations of first-person inclusiveness are centralized, the possessively-marked personal pronoun taatou is generally preferred to an equivalent possessive pronoun. Thus there is an affective contrast between the expression pati a taatou ‘utterances in Tuvaluan’ (lit.: ‘utterances of us’), which has the positively affective connotation of inclusion, and ttou pati ‘our utterances’, which is affectively neutral. The idiomatic uses of the first-person inclusive plural pronoun are indexical of the explicit emphasis on consensus, inclusion, and togetherness that permeates many aspects of Tuvaluan social life (Besnier 1995a:145–147, 1996a), which are relevant to other aspects of the use of pronouns (cf. 2.1.2.1.4.3–4). 2.1.2.1.4. Number A three-way distinction between singular, dual, and plural referents is encoded obligatorily in the morphology of both personal and possessive pronouns. This is a more elaborate distinction than the singular-plural distinction marked on ordinary noun phrases (cf. 2.1.1.8). 2.1.2.1.4.1. Number distinction in pronouns Personal and possessive pronouns of all persons are marked for one of three number categories: singular, dual, or plural. In the first person, both inclusive and exclusive forms exist in the dual and plural. Following is an example of the number contrast in the second person: (1976) Koe/koulua/koutou e fano maataeao. you you-2 you-3 Nps go tomorrow ‘You/you (two)/you (three) are leaving tomorrow.’ 2.1.2.1.4.2. Obligatoriness of number The number distinction is obligatory for all persons and for both inclusive and exclusive reference. 2.1.2.1.4.3–4. Overlaps between number categories There are no overlaps between number distinctions, other than in the honorific use of the dual number (cf. 2.1.2.1.12). In socially-unmarked usage, the dual number is always used to refer to two entities, and two entities can only be referred to pronominally with dual pronouns. Similarly, the plural number always refers to three or more entities. In natural discourse, care is always taken to choose pronoun forms that refer to the most inclusive and broadest range of referents. For example, if an individual performs a task in the presence of other individuals, the activity is described as having been performed by everyone present, even when the witnessing parties play no active role in the performance of the activity, and plural pronouns are used. Thus if three people go angling in a canoe with fishing gear for only one person, they will describe the activity as follows: (1977) Maatou ne olo o maattau i tua. we-3-e Pst go Cmp angle at outside ‘We (three) went angling outside the reef.’ A fuller description of the expedition might then detail the division of labour, but the overall activity will be considered, through pronoun choice and otherwise, to have been performed by every adult present, including inactive parties. Again, these patterns are consistent with the concern prevalent throughout Tuvaluan society (and many other Polynesian societies) with sharing, partaking, and including (cf. 2.1.2.1.3). From a Tuvaluan perspective, the act of ratified witnessing (taapuaki) is qualitatively on a par with the actual performance of a task in terms of its importance. | True

Its affective meaning and stylistic specialization are obviously related. The most prototypical context in which the honorific dual is used is in formal oratory. The most common is mmalu ‘respect, honour’, which may be used, along with proper or common modifiers, as an alternative to second- or third-person pronouns with the meaning of ‘honourable, excellency, exalted’. It may function as a verb, in which case the specifier is encoded as a subject. Alternatively, it may function as a noun modified by a possessive noun phrase or pronoun of the inalienable class or a locative prepositional phrase. As a noun, it can also be apposed with a descriptive noun phrase. Contrast, for example, the restricted inventory described here with the elaborate honorific codes found in Samoan (Duranti 1992, Milner 1961) and Tongan (Philips 1991). The comparable paucity of honorific forms and usages must be understood in the context of the meaning of hierarchy in Tuvaluan society. At the same time that the socio-political organization of the islands of Tuvalu is stratified, and this stratification is deemed desirable by the inhabitants, much emphasis is placed on egalitarianism, particularly at the ideological level (Besnier 1996a). Indeed, the convergence of these different propensities makes Tuvalu one of the least stratified societies in Polynesia, along with other atoll societies. The dearth of honorific terms (and the foreign origin of many of the terms that do exist) can thus be seen as a reflection of the ideology of equality that permeates the speech community. In fact, the few honorific forms that are found in the language are better understood as indexes of genre and situation, rather than as honorifics in the more usual sense of the term. 2.1.2.1.13. Semantic categories associated with demonstratives For each demonstrative category, several semantic parameters distinguish the meaning of the different forms: location in space, location in time, textual reference, and affective distance, as well as combinations of these. These parameters concern principally the semantic differences among the bound morphemes nei, naa, and laa, which constitute the second element of most demonstrative forms. The following discussion applies to canonical demonstrative pronouns, locative nouns, demonstrative adjectives, relative pronouns, demonstrative adverbs, demonstrative verbs, and demonstrative discourse conjuncts. There are a few exceptions and qualifications to the general patterns described presently, the result of certain forms having acquired specialized meanings; these are discussed in the previous section. Demonstrative forms are rich in indexicality, in that they may invoke different types of meaning in different contexts, and particular instances of their use are often ambiguous between various readings. (a) Location in space Location in space is the most basic semantic parameter that distinguishes semantically among nei, naa, and laa forms. It is based on a contrast among locations in the general vicinity of the speaker (nei forms), the general vicinity of the interlocutor (naa forms), and away from both the speaker and the interlocutor (laa forms): (2111) te pausi teenei/teenaa/teelaa the suitcase this that that ‘this/that suitcase [near me]/[near you]/[away from both you and me]’ It is on the basis of these basic semantic values that I refer to forms in nei as ‘first person’, forms in naa as ‘second person’, and forms in laa as ‘third person’. No distinction in relative distance (e.g., contact v. closeness), relative location (e.g., inside v. outside), or visibility (e.g., visible v. invisible) is relevant. If a location can be equally characterized as being in the vicinity of the speaker and of the interlocutor, first-person forms are used, unless parameters other than location in space (e.g., possession, see below) apply: (2112) te fale teenei e nnofo ei taaua the house this Nps stay Anp we-2-i ‘this house in which we both are located’ Similarly, if the location is in the vicinity of both the speaker and a third party, first- person forms are used: (2113) Maaua nei seki iloa tonu me e olo me see olo. we-2-e this Neg know right whether Nps go or Neg go ‘We two here, we still don’t know whether we’re going or not.’ If the location can be equally described as being near the interlocutor and a third party, second-person forms are used: | True

Cnt the council ruler that Inc in centre ‘The Island Council is in there.’ (2146) A te fono pule konaa koo i loto. However, not all nouns denoting groups behave this way; for example, in contrast to kau malaga ‘travelling party’, malaga, which has essentially the same meaning, can only take singular demonstratives. Generally speaking, compounds that are made up of a noun denoting a type of group (e.g., fono ‘council’, tau ‘pair of [kin categories]’, kau ‘group’) and of a qualifier tend to offer a choice, while lexically simple terms do not. In other cases, only plural demonstrative forms can appear. When nouns are modified by numerals or numeral expressions greater than one or by quantifiers with plural meaning (e.g., avaa- ‘both’ and its alternative forms; cf. 2.1.6.6 for an exhaustive listing), plural demonstratives must be used, even when singular articles appear: (2149) Konei mea e lua ne faippati taatou ki ei. these thing Nps two Pst speak we-3-i to Anp ‘These are the two things we talked about.’ (2150) Konaa tau luafulu lima taalaa. these your twenty five dollar ‘Here are your twenty-five dollars.’ Similar patterns obtain with the group marker saa (cf. 2.1.1.8.4–5). Demonstratives are therefore more sensitive to semantic number than articles. The above discussion should be contrasted with patterns of number agreement with the verb, which differ from the above in some respects (cf. 2.1.3.6.5(a) and 2.1.3.6.5(b)). 2.1.2.5.5. text: Morphology 421 2.1.2.5.6. Case marking of demonstratives Demonstratives other than locative pronouns are never marked for case. If a particular syntactic context calls for a demonstrative form to appear in a case-marked or prepositionally marked phrase, a ‘dummy’ noun (e.g., tino ‘person’, koga ‘place’, mea ‘thing’, feituu ‘aspect’) is used as the head of the phrase, which can then be modified by a demonstrative adjective: (2151) Au see faipati ki te feituu teenaa. I Neg speak to the aspect that ‘I am not talking about that (aspect).’ The locative pronouns konei, konaa, kolaa, and koo are always marked with a preposition (cf. 2.1.2.5(b)). These forms optionally coalesce with the directional preposition ki to yield the forms kkonei, kkonaa, kkolaa, and kkoo: (2152) Aku muna nei ma kaa vau au kkonei, koo llei. my word this Cmp Fut come I to+here Inc good ‘I thought that when I got here, [it]’d improve.’ (2153) Moo mea atu kkoo. little thing Dxs to+there ‘[Make a little room by] moving down that way.’ 2.1.2.5.7. Other grammatical categories marked in demonstratives No other grammatical category is marked in the form of demonstratives. 2.1.2.5.8. Adjectival uses of demonstratives Adjectival forms of demonstratives are described in 2.1.2.5(c). 2.1.2.6. Interrogative words There are only four interrogative-word roots, each of which can be attached to a variety of prefixes and case markers to form morphologically-complex interrogative words. In the following discussion, simple and derived forms are treated together under the base form. Two morphologically complex interrogative words are derived through a productive derivational process, namely faka-prefixation; the derivational morphology utilized in deriving other complex interrogative words is unproductive. Interrogative words do not form a special morphological class. Instead, they behave like other preforms of different morphological categories. Some are anaphors for nominal entities, in the sense that their morphosyntactic behaviour is the same as that of a noun (e.g., they receive case marking and take articles); others are proverbs, in that they are marked and behave like verbs (e.g., they are marked for tense, aspect, and mood, and they may be modified by adverbs); still others are adverbials and adjectives. Generally speaking, interrogative words are not readily distinguishable in terms of their syntactic behaviour from members of the morphological categories of which they are anaphors. Table 2.10 summarizes the range of morphological categories associated with each interrogative word, simple and complex (the English glosses provided in this table are approximative). More detailed discussion and examples can be found under each individual interrogative word in the rest of this section. | True

text: 422 Morphology This section provides information on the following characteristics of interrogative words: their range of meaning; their allomorphic variants, if any; their morphological class affiliation; and the range of grammatical morphemes that can mark them. For a discussion of the types of syntactic structure associated with each interrogative word, the range of syntactic positions that each interrogative word can occupy, and the anaphoric marking left behind by moved interrogative words, see 1.1.1.2.2.2. For a discussion of the use of interrogative-word questions in various indirect speech acts, see 1.1.1.5. 2.1.2.6.1. ai The interrogative word ai and its allomorphs ei and oi, as well as the compound kooi, are primarily used to form questions about the identity of human entities or about choices between human entities: (2154) A Luta e ia ai ttamaliki? Cnt Luta Nps belong-to who? the+child ‘Luta is whose daughter?’ (2155) A kkoulua mo oi e olo ki motu? and Foc+you-2 with who? Nps go to islet ‘And who is going with you to the islets?’ (2156) Te moolii ne taamate nee ei? the lamp Pst turn-off Erg who? ‘Who turned the lamp off?’ (2157) Kooi ia laaua ne mua mai? Foc+who? at they-2 Pst come-first Dxs ‘Which of the two came here first?’ The same interrogative word is also used in questions about names of places of regional or political import. Islets, islands and atolls, island groups, countries, and continents fall in this category: (2158) Kooi tou fenua? Foc+who? your island ‘What’s your home island?’ or: ‘What’s your native country?’ Table 2.10 Morphological status of interrogative words | True

text: Morphology 423 (2159) A Niu Kaletonia e puke nee ei? Cnt New-Caledonia Nps hold Erg who? ‘Which country does New Caledonia belong to?’ However, when the name of an island or country is used adjectivally to denote a nationality, the interrogative word aa is used (cf. 2.1.2.6.2). Finally, ai and its allomorphs are used in questions about months: (2160) Kooi te maasina e fano ei koe? Foc+who? the month Nps go Anp you ‘What month are you leaving in?’ (2161) Ko te maasina o oi e fano ei koe? Foc the month of who? Nps go Anp you ‘What month are you leaving in?’ A question with ai calls for an answer that consists of a personal name, the name of a location, or the name of a month. Occasionally, ai is used in questions seeking a characterization of an individual in terms of his or her kin relations: (2162) Kooi laa Taukiei? Foc+who? then Taukiei ‘Who is Taukiei?’ [i.e., ‘What is he to other people?’] If the answer being sought is of a different type, e.g., a description, ai cannot be used, and the question must be worded instead as follows: (2163) Se tino peefea e faipati koe ki ei? a person how? Nps talk you to Anp ‘Who are you talking about?’ [lit.: ‘What kind of a person are you talking about?’] The basic form of the interrogative word is ai (from Proto-Polynesian *hai). The form oi is used if the interrogative word is preceded by a grammatical morpheme whose final vowel is /o/ (e.g., o ‘of’, mo ‘with, and’). When the interrogative word is marked with the focus marker ko, the two morphemes coalesce. The result is written as one word in the orthography used in this grammar, and in the orthographic system used by most native writers. The allomorphic change to oi is obligatory in informal spoken discourse. Occasionally, in oratorical contexts, the forms mo ai, o ai, ko ai, etc. are heard, particularly in religious discourse. These are Northern Tuvaluan forms, and are connotatively marked in the Southern dialects. (Their appearance in religious discourse may be caused by the fact that they resemble the Samoan form ai, which is invariant.) The form ei is used following grammatical morphemes whose final segment is /e/ (principally the ergative case marker nee). It is only characteristic of conversational discourse. In contrast to allomorphic variation between ai and oi, the form ei is optional. Morphologically speaking, ai is a proper noun. It is not modified by articles, but receives case marking. Prepositions that take on the suffix -a(a) when marking proper nouns (cf. 2.1.5.2) treat ai as a proper noun: (2164) Koe naa koo kaitaua kia ai? you that Inc angry to who? ‘Who are you angry at?’ There are two peculiarities in the way ai is marked for case. text: 428 Morphology 2.1.2.6.3. fea The base form of the interrogative word fea ‘where?, which?’ is discussed in (a). The complex forms teefea and kofea ‘where?’ are discussed under (b), peefea ‘how?’ under (c), and the temporal anafea, maafea, and aafea under (d). (a) Base form The interrogative word fea (in the Nukulaelae dialect, hee) has two meanings. Used as a noun, it refers to locations: (2196) Koe e fano ki fea? you Nps go to where? ‘Where are you going?’ (2197) Mai fea tou fou? from where? your flower-crown ‘Where did you get your flower crown?’ (2198) Au uu ne puke i fea? your coconut-crab Pst grab in where? ‘Where did you get these coconut crabs?’ Location may be a metaphorical notion, as in the following: (2199) Koe e tuu i fea i te paalota? you Nps stand at where? in the election ‘Where do you stand as far as the elections are concerned?’ Used as an adjective, fea indicates that the question concerns a choice, like English ‘which’: (2200) Kae ne gatu laa foki fea e manako koe ki ei? and some clothes then also which? Nps wish you to Anp ‘And which types of clothes do you want now?’ (2201) Te aso lima fea e fai ei te paalota? the day five which? Nps do Anp the election ‘Which Friday is the election going to be held on?’ The interrogative word can therefore function as either a noun or an adjective. As a noun, it behaves like a locative noun, i.e., it is marked as a plural definite noun with a zero article. It may be marked by prepositions. Because of its meaning, fea as a noun is most commonly marked with the locative preposition i, the directional preposition ki, or the source preposition mai. Used as a sentence fragment, fea must be marked by a preposition: (2202) I fea? at where? ‘Where?’ For a discussion of the demonstrative short forms nei and naa, which are closely related in function to some of the uses of fea, see 2.1.2.5(c) and 2.1.2.5(d). (b) teefea, kofea Like fea, teefea and kofea are used in questions about locations or choices. Unlike the base form of the interrogative word, they function as nominal predicates; teefea (in the Nukulaelae dialect, teehee) is the singular form, kofea (in the Nukulaelae dialect, kohee) the plural form: | True

(d) anafea, maafea, aafea These three interrogative words (in the Nukulaelae dialect, the first two are anahee and maahee respectively) are all used in questions about time. They differ from one another as follows: anafea is used for past events; maafea for future events; and aafea for both: (2211) Koutou ne oko mai anafea? you-3 Pst reach Dxs when? ‘When did you get here?’ (2212) E fakaoti maafea te maasina? text: Morphology 431 2.1.2.6.4. fia This numeral interrogative word comes in two forms, a base form fia, discussed in (a), and a form prefixed with faka-, described in (b). (a) Base form The interrogative word fia is used in • questions about numbers: (2218) E fia katoa masi keke i loto i te sefe? Nps how-many? all cracker cake in inside in the safe ‘How many biscuits are there in the safe?’ • quantities of a particular unit: (2219) E fia gafa kolokolo e manako koe ki ei? Nps how-much? fathom sennit Nps wish you to Anp ‘How many fathoms of sennit do you want?’ (2220) E fia laa te ttogi o futi? Nps how-much? then the price of banana ‘How much are the bananas?’ • the time of the day: (2221) Koo taa nei te fia? Inc strike now the how-many? ‘What time is it?’ (2222) Ko te fia e fai ei te fakaala? Foc the how-many? Nps do Anp the feast ‘At what time is the feast?’ [lit.: ‘It is the how-many that the feast is held at?’] • days of the week or days of the month: (2223) Koe e fano i te aso fia? you Nps go in the day how-many? ‘What day of the week are you leaving on?’ This interrogative word behaves like a numeral. This state of affairs is common in all languages, and is clearly related to the fact that transitivity must be understood not as a binary opposition, but as a set of nondiscrete parameters involving not just verb morphology but many other features of the clause, including tense and aspect, the obligatory or optional presence of arguments of the verb and their number, the dynamics of the situation denoted by the clause, and the pragmatic function of the clause in the discourse context in which it appears (Hopper and Thompson 1980). Thus a particular construction, and a particular instance of this construction, may behave as a transitive clause according to certain parameters but not others, and discrepant results across transitivity tests can be expected to be the norm rather than the exception. Because Tuvaluan has ergative-absolutive morphology, many transitivity tests are also useful as tests for the category ‘subject’. The existence and importance of this category is always potentially problematic in ergative-absolutive languages, in that subjects of transitive and intransitive verbs receive different morphological marking, which raises the question as to whether they are different syntactic categories or not. Elsewhere in this work, I make use of transitivity tests to address this question (see in particular 2.1.1.2.1 and 2.1.1.2.2). The following can be listed as transitivity tests that refer to the entire clause or to the arguments of the clause and their morphosyntactic behaviour (this is not a complete list): case marking in relative clauses and interrogative-word questions in which the interrogative word does not appear in situ (cf. 1.1.2.3.4 and 1.1.1.2.2.2 respectively); case marking and general behaviour when the verb is prefixed with faka- (cf. 2.1.3.1.3(a)); the possible appearance of a clitic pronoun when the clause is moo-subordinated, which only intransitive clauses allow (cf. 2.1.2.1.1.5); and the ability of the clause to undergo -gina suffixation, which is passed by all transitives but only some intransitives (cf. 2.1.3.1.3). Transitivity tests that refer specifically to the subject of the clause, and thus help distinguish subjects from nonsubjects, include: advancement-to-possessive in clauses where the only argument is marked for the absolutive case, which indicates that the clause is intransitive (cf. 1.1.2.3.10); whether the noun phrase can control object equi-deletion (cf. 1.1.2.6); whether the subject can trigger verb agreement, which indicates that the clause is intransitive (cf. 2.1.3.6.1); and the formation of imperatives (cf. 1.1.1.3 and 2.1.3.4.3). Transitivity tests that refer specifically to the direct object of the clause, and thus help distinguish direct objects from other categories, include: the ability to undergo incorporation (cf. 2.1.3.6.1); the ability to undergo causative inversion (2.1.3.1.3(a)); and the ability to be targeted by equi- deletion (cf. 1.1.2.6). 2.1.3.1.1. Valency-decreasing processes The valency of a verb can be affected in a number of ways. This section reviews verb forms that may occur in constructions with different valency. Valency can be affected by the presence or absence of a subject (cf. (a) below), the presence or absence of a direct object (cf. (b)), different case-marking patterns (cf. (c)), and the ability of certain verbs to take on an inherently reciprocal meaning (cf. (d)). Another morphological process that decreases valency is described in 2.1.3.1.4. The grammatical features described in this section are properties of verbs as lexemes. Verbs do not fall into classes that are easily identifiable in terms of their internal structure or their semantics. In certain cases, it is not clear whether forms with different valency should be considered different manifestations of the same lexeme or homophonous lexemes. For example, the verb kai ‘eat’ can appear in transitive, intransitive, and middle constructions. In each case, it takes on a slightly different meaning, as shown presently. Is it the same lexical item throughout, or should its various manifestations be considered to be separate words? One characteristic of this verb supports the first analysis: when the direct object of the transitive verb kai is incorporated into the verb (cf. 2.1.3.6.12), the verb agrees in number with its subject, a property of intransitive and middle manifestations of kai. Hence there is a structural link between intransitive, middle, and transitive forms. Furthermore, in the case of certain verbs, it is not clear whether the least marked form is its transitive or intransitive manifestation. For example, the verb uku ‘dive (for recreation or food-gathering)’ is a verb of type (b) below; in natural discourse, it is most frequent as an intransitive verb, but it may take on transitive morphosyntax and take as direct object a noun that refers to any edible marine species that one commonly gathers by diving (e.g., in the Funafuti dialect, kalea ‘spider shell’). (f) Suffix -(C)ia The unproductive morpheme -(C)ia can be suffixed to verb roots and affect their valency in a complex manner. Cognates of the suffix are found in most, perhaps all Polynesian languages, where their form and meaning have been the subject of an extensive literature. The meaning of this suffix differs from one language to another in the Polynesian family, and many of these differences are still poorly understood. Before characterizing the form and meaning of the suffix, it is important to note that many Samoan words with cognates of this suffix have been borrowed into the Tuvaluan lexicon (e.g., aafaaina ‘(not) matter’, afaatia ‘caught in a storm’, amuia ‘blessed’, fakataasia ‘assembled’, inosia ‘ostracized’, lausia ‘counted’, maafatia ‘worried’, maalaia ‘doomed’, maataulia ‘recognizable’, motusia ‘of a relationship, broken’, puapuagaatia ‘distressed’, taagisia ‘mourned’, taulia ‘prized’, tiigaaina ‘in pain’, vaaoia ‘rejected’). These forms were borrowed as unitary lexical items, and did not undergo suffixation after borrowing. They must be carefully distinguished from manifestations of the suffix in autochthonous words, as they differ in form and function from Tuvaluan suffixed forms, as discussed presently. The situation is further complicated by the fact that, corresponding to many suffixed forms borrowed from Samoan, one also finds unsuffixed forms of Samoan origin (e.g., inoino ‘abhor’ v. inosia, puapuagaa ‘distressful’ v. puapuagaatia) as well as unsuffixed Tuvaluan cognates of borrowed Samoan suffixed forms (e.g., tagi ‘cry’ v. tagisia, vvao ‘prevent’ v. vaoia). To add to the potential confusion, many suffixed borrowings have been so thoroughly incorporated into the lexicon in everyday usage that many speakers of Tuvaluan do not recognise these forms as borrowings. text: 456 Morphology The following illustrates the derivation of a causative from a transitive verb: (2330) Tevasa ne inu nee ia taku kao. Tevasa Pst drink Erg he my sour-toddy ‘Tevasa drank my sour toddy.’ (2331) Tevasa ne fakainu nee maatou ki taku kao. Tevasa Pst Cst+drink Erg we-3-e to my sour-toddy ‘We made Tevasa drink my sour toddy.’ Not all verbs can be prefixed with faka-. The process is most productive with intransitive verbs including middle verbs, although many common intransitive verbs like fano ‘go’ and vau ‘come’ cannot be faka-prefixed. The number of transitive verbs that can be prefixed is more restricted. A handful of transitive verbs, like kai ‘eat’, have suppletive causative forms (faagai ‘make (something) eat, feed’);28 others can be made causative with the verb fai ‘make’ (cf. (b) below). In a handful of cases, the prefix can be attached to a string made up of the negative verb see (cf. 1.4(a)) and the verb being negated; thus one finds faka-see-aogaa ‘treat as useless, render useless’ (cf. aogaa ‘useful’), faka-see-talitonu ‘dismiss’ (cf. talitonu ‘believe’), and faka- see-aamanaia ‘depreciate’ (cf. aamanaia ‘treasure, esteem’). For some unknown reason, all such cases fall into the same semantic field of devaluing activities. The prefix can be attached to borrowings; for example, from puapuagaatia ‘distressed’, a borrowing from Samoan, can be derived fakapuapuagaatia ‘distress (someone)’, and the suffixation of leevolo ‘level’, a borrowing from English, yields the form fakaleevolo ‘level (something)’. The prefix faka- has two allomorphs. When it is prefixed to a verb with k as an initial segment, the prefix is reduced to fak-, as in fakkoukou ‘make (someone) take a bath, bathe (someone)’, from koukou ‘wash up, bathe’. The other allomorph, faa-, is found in causative forms borrowed from Samoan (e.g., faauu ‘nurse’, faaina ‘illuminate’, faaopoopo ‘add’). Some borrowed forms have retained their causative meaning, while others have not. Members of the first category do not differ in behaviour from causative forms of autochthonous origin. The prefix faka- cannot be attached to a word already affixed with faka- even when the latter has a non- causative meaning. However, it may be attached to Samoan borrowings in faa-that do not have causative meaning (e.g., fakafaanoanoa ‘sadden’ from faanoanoa ‘sad’). Even after noncausative uses of faka- are set aside, not all forms prefixed with faka- are causative in the strict sense of the word. Many faka-prefixed forms resemble causatives but diverge from canonical causatives in their semantic and morphosyntactic behaviour. Some are relexicalized causative forms; for example, the verb matala ‘open’ can be causativized as fakamatala ‘open (something)’. But there is another form, homophonous with the causative fakamatala, which bears the metaphorically related meaning of ‘explain, clarify’. However, the latter form cannot be considered to be derived from matala ‘open’ because the unprefixed verb cannot be used with the meaning of ‘explained, clarified’, and should be analysed as having undergone relexicalization. The form fakamatala ‘explain’ is thus a word which is separate from and homophonous with fakamatala ‘open’, even though it may have originally been a metaphorical extension of the latter. text: 460 Morphology Ditransitive verbs do not undergo faka-causative formation. Causative verbs differ from other transitive verbs in one significant respect, namely the fact that many can undergo number agreement, which no noncausative transitive verb does. Agreement with causative verbs is sometimes controlled by the direct object, sometimes by the subject; for further details, see 2.1.3.6.1–6 and 2.1.3.6.12(a). It is noteworthy that faka-causative formation treats the subject of intransitive and transitive verbs as the same category, in that both become the direct object of the causative verb. The above patterns also verify Comrie’s (1978) hypothesis to the effect that causees occupy the highest position on the Noun Phrase Accessibility Hierarchy (cf. 1.1.2.3.7) not already occupied by another argument of the verb. Causative verbs derived from transitive verbs can undergo an unusual process whereby the causee is demoted to the oblique position occupied by the former direct object of the noncausative sentence, which then comes to occupy the position left empty by the demotion, i.e., that of the direct object. No other changes take place in the clause. This process is optional, and it derives sentence (2358) from sentence (2357), which is in turn derived from the noncausative sentence (2356): (2356) Ne masaua nee au au pati. Pst remember Erg I your word ‘I remembered what you told me.’ (2357) Au ne fakamasaua nee Teika ki au pati. The awkward English translations of the above sentences are an attempt to render the informational structure of the resulting construction with the passive voice. text: 464 Morphology suffixes are easily distinguished from one another in that one has alternative forms -gina and -ga while the other does not. The three forms of the transitivizing suffix, -gina, -gia, and -ga, originate from three different dialect areas: -gina is a Northern Tuvaluan form, -gia was probably the original form in the Funafuti and Vaitupu dialects, and -ga that of the suffix in the Nukufetau and Nukulaelae dialects. Today, all three forms are in current use throughout Southern Tuvalu. The form -ga has retained its marked dialectal characteristics, but not -gina and -gia; in fact, -gina is more common today than -gia, which is mostly characteristic of language use by older individuals. In the following discussion, -gina will be assumed to be the base form. Reflexive and reciprocal verb forms There are no special reflexive forms of verbs. Reciprocal forms of many verbs can be derived by attaching to the root a circumfix fe-/-(C)aki, whose morphology is described in 2.1.3.6.9. The circumfix may be attached to verbs of all valencies. The tense-aspect-mood marker which most frequently undergoes ‘discourse governed’ deletion is the universal and nonpast marker e (cf. 2.1.3.2.1(a), (b), and (d) below). Second, certain grammatical environments are particularly favourable to deletion of the tense-aspect-mood marker. These include the presence of a negator (cf. 1.4) or of certain aspectual adverbs like the inceptive faatoaa ‘just’ (cf. 2.1.3.3.2.1(e)). Deletion cannot take place under certain circumstances, such as when a clitic pronoun is present (cf. 2.1.2.1.1.5(a)). The deletion of the universal tense- aspect-mood marker is conditioned by specific factors when it appears in certain numeral expressions or quantifiers (cf. 2.1.6.2.2, 2.1.6.2.3, and 2.1.6.6.1). As briefly discussed in 1.1.1.1(a) and 1.1.1.1(b), tense in reported speech does not differ from the patterns described below. As illustrated in 1.1.2.5, there are no sequence-of-tense constraints across superordinate and subordinate clauses. The absence of formal tense marking in equational structures is discussed in 1.2.1.1. 2.1.3.2.1. Tense distinctions Relatively few tense distinctions are made. There is a basic contrast between the past tense on the one hand, marked with the tense marker ne, and the nonpast and universal tense, marked with e. Aspect As in all languages, aspect can be denoted in a number of ways, some more grammaticalized than others. At the most grammaticalized end of the spectrum, one finds tense-aspect-mood markers comparable to the markers described in 2.1.3.2, whose sole or primary function is to mark aspect (or tense or mood depending on the case). Second, aspect can be marked with verbs whose primary function is to denote aspect. Typically, these verbs function as the superordinate verb in a complex construction, to which the rest of the sentence is subordinated. Finally, the least grammaticalized end of the spectrum is occupied by aspectual adverbs. text: Morphology 495 (j) Simultaneous aspect Simultaneity is not marked as a special aspectual category. For a description of constructions associated with temporal simultaneity, see 1.1.2.4.2.1(c). (k) Telic aspect There is no formal marking of telic aspect. However, many syntactic and morphological processes produce structural variants which differ from one another in terms of telic aspect. For example, some transitive verbs may be detransitivized by not mentioning the direct object (cf. 2.1.3.1.2(b)), and the detransitivized version is always less telic (i.e., less likely to denote telic situations) than the transitive version. Similarly, verb forms that can govern either transitive or middle-case marking (cf. 2.1.3.1.2(c)) are more telic in their transitive manifestations. The stativizing prefix ma-, discussed in 2.1.3.1.2(e), and the prefix ma- that denotes potentiality (cf. 2.1.3.4.7) both decrease the telic value of the situation denoted by the verb to which they are affixed. 2.1.3.3.2.2. Possible combinations of categories There are both semantic and morphological constraints on the combination of aspectual values. Semantic constraints forbid the combination of inceptive, terminative, and semelfactive aspect markers on the one hand with, on the other hand, continuous, iterative, progressive, and habitual aspect markers. The perfect-aspect markers also cannot cooccur with the continuous and progressive marker koi. Several other restrictions are noted in the foregoing discussion. No other cooccurrence patterns are disallowed, as long as morphological constraints do not apply. Morphological constraints forbid the occurrence in the same clause of more than one tense-aspect-mood marker, and forbid the occurrence of tense-aspect-mood markers in nonfinite clauses (cf. 2.1.3.5). Tense, aspect, and mood categories that are not constrained by morphological factors can freely cooccur with one another. 2.1.3.4. Mood Attention is drawn to the remarks made in the introduction to sections on tense and aspect (2.1.3.2 and 2.1.3.3 respectively), some of which are relevant to the following discussion. 2.1.3.4.1. Indicative There is no formal marking of the indicative mood. The indicative mood is denoted, by default, by the absence of nonindicative mood marking. 2.1.3.4.2. Conditional The conditional mood may be marked overtly in one of two mutually exclusive ways: with mood markers identical in form and behaviour to tense and aspect markers described in the previous sections; or with conditional conjunctions morphologically related to the conditional-mood markers. As discussed further in 1.1.2.4.2.5, the choice between these two strategies is governed by two factors: whether the ‘if clause (i.e., the protasis) is preposed or postposed to the ‘then’ clause (i.e., the apodosis); and whether conditionality is imaginary or nonimaginary. I use the term ‘nonimaginary’ as in 1.1.2.4.2.5(b-c), to denote situations that may have taken place, may be taking place, or might take place, be they hypothetical or counterfactual, and the term ‘imaginary’ to denote the opposite. | True

text: 496 Morphology (a) Preposed nonimaginary conditionals A preposed nonimaginary ‘if’ clause can be marked either with the mood marker kaa, which is identical to the future-tense marker (cf. 2.1.3.2.1(d)), or with the conjunction kaafai (in the Nukulaelae dialect, kaahai) compounded from the marker kaa and the verb fai ‘do, make’ (in the Nukulaelae dialect, hai): (2559) Kaa(fai koo) foki mai koe, koo olo taaua o taaffao ki motu. if Inc return Dxs you Inc go we-2-i Cmp play to islet ‘If you come back, we’ll go and have fun at the islets.’ Kaafai may introduce a clause marked for any tense, aspect, or mood category other than the optative mood. In particular, it can be followed by the future marker kaa: (2560) Kaafai kaa oko mai te vaka, koo sopo ei au. if Inc reach Dxs the ship Inc board Anp I ‘If the ship comes, I’ll get on it.’ (b) Postposed nonimaginary conditionals A postposed nonimaginary ‘if’ clause can be marked either with the mood marker maa or one of its allomorphs, which is identical to the precautionary-mood marker (cf. 2.1.3.4.11), or by introducing the clause with maafai or manafai, or, more rarely, manefai or manifai (the Nukulaelae forms are maahai, manahai, manehai, or manihai). The latter forms are compounded from the precautionary-mood marker and the verb fai ‘do, make’ (in the Nukulaelae dialect, hai): (2561) Koo olo taaua o taaffao ki motu maa(fai e) foki mai koe. Inc go we-2-i Cmp play to islet if Nps return Dxs you ‘We’ll go and have fun at the islets, if you come back.’ Postposed conditional clauses cannot be marked with kaa and kaafai, which are reserved for preposed conditional clauses. (c) Imaginary conditionals Imaginary conditionals (cf. 1.1.2.4.2.5) are marked either with the optative-mood marker moi (cf. 2.1.3.4.4), the compounds moifai or, more rarely, moinefai or moinifai, which are compounded from moi, the past-tense marker ne or ni, and the verb fai, as in (a) and (b) above. text: 508 Morphology The adverb fia has a secondary function. Preposed to words denoting social categories, it conveys the affectively charged meaning of ‘pretend (to be), act as, imagine oneself (to be)’, usually in a derogatory manner: (2616) Koi fooliki fua, a koo fia tamataene! still small just and Inc want young-man ‘[He]’s just a kid, and he’s trying to act like a young man!’ Compounds thus formed are noun-derived verbs (cf. 1.16.1), which can be nominalized in turn. The two functions of fia are closely related and potentially ambiguous. Given the strongly behaviouristic manner in which intentionality, motivation, and personhood are defined in Tuvaluan society (Besnier 1989b, 1990a, 1991), I am tempted to see the polysemy of fia as a translation phenomenon, and to consider it to have a unified meaning from an emic perspective. A similar analysis may be applicable to the notions of ‘hunger’, ‘thirst’, and ‘sleepiness’, which can only be translated as the compounds fia kai ‘want to eat, hungry’, fia ota ‘want to eat raw food, hungry for raw food’, fia inu ‘want to drink, thirsty’, and fia moe ‘want to sleep, sleepy’. According to the proposed analysis, fia kai does not have two meanings, ‘hungry’ and ‘want to eat’, but rather a single meaning, because hunger would be defined locally as the desire to eat. The desiderative adverb is never modified by other adverbs, it never functions as an independent lexeme, it can modify verbs of all valencies, and it does not govern case marking or alter the valency of the sentence. Thus it has no verbal properties. However, it is associated with interesting patterns of preference with regard to the choice in ‘desirer’ among the various noun phrases in the clause. When it modifies an intransitive verb, the ‘desirer’ must be the subject of the clause. This is the case of (2615) and (2616). text: 510 Morphology 2.1.3.5. Finite and nonfinite forms The only clear category of nonfinite verbs in the language are nominalized verbs. Virtually all verbs in the language can undergo nominalization (see 1.15.1 for an exception), including existential verbs (cf. 1.2.1.1.1(b)), negative existential verbs (cf. 1.4(d)), predicative prepositional phrases (cf. 1.2.1.1.1(c)), and, with some qualifications, predicated possessive phrases (cf. 1.10.1.2). Nominalized verbs are very frequent in natural discourse, and a broad range of constructions and processes either require or favour nominalized verb forms. Nominalized verbs come in two types, which are described in turn below: a ‘bare’ form, which is identical to that of the finite form of the verb; and a suffixed form, which is derived by attaching the nominalizing suffix -Vga to the verb (which may then undergo minor structural modifications). In both cases, the verb loses its tense-aspect-mood markers, but it may keep any adverbial modifier, including those with temporal, aspectual, and modal meaning, as well as negators: (2627) Au e ofo i te fui vau o te vaka. I Nps surprised at the slow-to come of the ship ‘I am amazed by how late the ship is.’ (2628) Te see lava te maalamalama i aso kolaa, nee? the Neg enough the enlightenment in day those Tag ‘There was so little understanding in those days, right?’ Both types of nominalized verbs resemble nouns in their basic external morphology. For example, they take articles, although they tend to occur mostly with the singular definite article (cf. 2.1.1.8). The syntactic characteristics of nominalization are described in 1.1.2.2.6 and 1.1.2.4.3, and its clausal morphology in 2.1.1.3.4. Subject-verb number agreement in nominalized clauses is discussed in 2.1.3.6.6.
