However, bare nominalized forms of verbs must be distinguished from cognate nouns for several reasons. First, the meaning of bare nominalized forms can be derived predictably from that of the verb, while the meaning of cognate nouns is often idiosyncratically related to that of the verb. Second, bare nominalized forms refer to situations, while cognate nouns generally refer to objects or abstract entities. Third, cognate nouns are frequently more specific in meaning than nominalized verbs. Fourth, bare nominalized forms and cognate nouns often take different possessive modifiers; for example, the arguments of the nominalized forms of asu ‘scoop, bail’ and tau ‘harvest’ are marked for inalienable possession, following patterns regularly associated with nominalization (cf. 2.1.1.3.4), but the corresponding cognate nouns can only be possessed alienably (cf. 2.1.1.4.6). Nominalized forms must also be distinguished from words that function as nouns in their basic form but that can sometimes be used as verbs (cf. 1.16.1). For example, pati ‘word’, kkano ‘flesh’, and ala ‘road’ can sometimes appear as verbs, with the meaning of ‘say’, ‘related’, and ‘motivate’ respectively. As discussed in 1.16.1, several criteria can be applied to such cases to show that the nominal use of these words is unmarked and their verbal use marked. Clearly, no nominalization process is at play here. Bare nominalized forms refer to situations that are viewed as temporally unbounded. With singular verb forms, the noun phrases tend to be seen as collective entities; when they control plural agreement, they take on a more distributive meaning. In Tuvaluan, independent occurrences of this affix are attested in a few words whose meaning generally evoke plurality, such as fepaki ‘collide’ (also feipaki, perhaps related to paa ‘burst’), fekiki and fetolo ‘struggle, wrestle’ (cf. tolo ‘crawl’), fenuminumi ‘all tangled up’ (cf. numi ‘tangled’), and perhaps fekai ‘ferocious’ (cf. kai ‘eat’). The prefix is unproductive, and the meaning of prefixed forms usually cannot be derived simply from that of the root forms.31 The suffix -(C)aki is a little more frequent across the lexicon, but it is also unproductive. Reflecting a Proto-Polynesian morpheme *-(C)aki, which appears to have given an instrumental focus to the verb, this suffix does not have a generalizable function in contemporary Tuvaluan. In some forms, shades of its former function as an instrumental marker remain; for example, taapuaki ‘worship’ (from tapu ‘sacred’), tuulaki ‘(of birds, etc.) use as a stand’ (from tuu ‘stand’), and pikitaki ‘stuck with objects’ (from piki ‘stick’). However, the meaning of many suffixed forms is derived from that of the root in arbitrary fashion. Witness alafaki ‘keep wake’ (cf. ala ‘(a)wake’), alofaki ‘beckon’ (cf. aalo ‘row’), akasaki ‘strive’ (perhaps from aka ‘kick’), and fatuaki ‘begin weaving’ (from fatu ‘compose’). Occasionally, the suffixed and root forms (or a derived form) have essentially the same meaning; for example, moeaki and fakamoemoe ‘hope’, fakatuanaki and fakatuatua ‘have faith’. Some suffixed forms are nouns: such is the case of aofaki ‘total’ (from ao ‘collect’), tuiaki ‘fish bait consisting of a strip of fish meat and used for pelagic fish’ (probably from tui ‘insert [a thin object]’), tumuaki ‘crown (of the head)’ (probably from tumu ‘tree stump’, cf. Proto-Polynesian *tumu ‘summit’), and uluaki ‘first-born child’ (cf. ulu ‘head’). Finally, some forms have undergone idiosyncratic phonological changes in either the root or the affix; witness tuugaki ‘bonfire lit as a beacon’ (probably from tutu ‘set fire’), tiaki ‘leave’ (cf. tii ‘drop’), polopolooki ‘give advice, admonish’ (also polopoloaki, cf. poloaki ‘advice’), and the two forms palutaki and pulutaki ‘mixed up’ (cf. palu ‘mix’). The most productive form of fe-/-(C)aki is fe-/-aki, which is found in the majority of reciprocal forms, e.g., fetapaaki ‘kick one another’, fetagiaki ‘cry for one another’, femusuaki ‘murmur to one another’, fefusuaki ‘punch one another’, fetuliaki ‘chase one another’, and femaasaloaki ‘jealous of one another’.32 Verbs that take other forms of the circumfix tend to have acquired nonreciprocal meanings; for example, fetuulaki ‘(of a large group of individuals) stand in a defined area’ (cf. tuu ‘stand’), feuufaki ‘tête-bèche’ (cf. uu ‘shelter’). This is not to say that all fe-/-aki forms have reciprocal meanings; as illustrated in 2.1.3.1.4, the circumfix has other meanings that are related but not identical to the marking of reciprocality. Furthermore, many verbs denoting situations that lend themselves to reciprocality do not allow circumfixation (e.g., ita ‘angry, displeased’, which does not have a form *feitaaki), and no semantic or structural criteria can be isolated to predict which do or do not. However, one pattern is clear: compounded or morphologically complex verb forms (e.g., fakkoukou ‘make (someone) wash oneself’, faipati ‘talk’) never take the circumfix. Verbs that do not have reflexive forms can be marked for reciprocality with the verb fakatau ‘compete’ (cf. 1.7.1.5). 2.1.3.6.10. Verbal deixis Deixis is marked on the verb primarily with the help of a small set of adverbs, cognates of which are found in all Polynesian languages, the semantics of which has puzzled many scholars (e.g., Platt 1986 on Samoan). In Tuvaluan, two basic binary semantic oppositions underlie the system, opposing on the one hand the forms mai ‘towards the point of reference of the discourse’ (henceforth ‘hither’) and atu ‘away from the point of reference of the discourse’ (henceforth ‘thither’); and on the other hand aka ‘up’ and ifo ‘down’. As will be discussed in this section, the translations provided here are expedient oversimplifications. The deictic aka occupies a special place in this paradigm, in that it also functions as a polite downtoner and thus can cooccur, in this function, with other deictics. (It can also mean ‘other’, as discussed in 2.1.6.6.2(c).) In all other instances, only one deictic per verb is allowed: (2688) Koo ttolo mai te fonu! Inc crawl Dxs the turtle ‘A turtle is crawling up [to land]!’ (2689) Kee faitau atu nee au te ueta i te ggana Ppaalagi. Sbj read Dxs Erg I the weather-report in the language Westerner ‘Let me read out to you the weather report in English.’ Deictic adverbs are primarily associated with verbs of motion, verbs of sending and receiving, verbs denoting sensory and perceptual categories, verbs denoting evolutions in time, as well as communication verbs denoting speech acts, acts of writing, acts of calling out, and so on (cf. 1.1.1.1(a) for examples). However, they can also modify many other types of verbs, as will be illustrated presently. The four deictic adverbs exhibit a number of formal and distributional idiosyncrasies. First, the deictic aka, an irregular reflex of Proto-Polynesian *(h,s)ake, has an alternative, slightly archaic form ake (the regular reflex of the protoform), used occasionally instead of aka (it is also the regular form of the deictic in the Northern dialects).33 Second, one verb of motion, vau ‘come’ is never modified by a deictic adverb, presumably because the action it denotes is already inherently oriented in space. Yet vau follows the same semantic principles as mai, and its meaning can be thought of as incorporating the meaning of mai (it contrasts with fanatu ‘go thither’). The optional suppletive plural forms of vau, namely mmai, aummai, and ommai (cf. 2.1.3.6.2), are historically related to mai (although they are not synchronically derivable from it), and are also distributionally incompatible with mai. In contrast, both aka and ifo can modify verbs to which they are etymologically related, namely ake ‘reach land, beach oneself’, sake ‘slant, raise one’s foot into an elevated area, (of a school of fish) beach oneself’, ifo ‘prostrate oneself, humble oneself’, and ssifo ‘slant down, lean down’: 33 With one verb, ati ‘build’, which when modified with the deictic takes on the meaning of ‘develop, progress’, the form ake appears more frequently than aka, although both are acceptable. | True

Third, the deictics coalesce with certain verb forms. The verb fano ‘go’, when modified by the deictic atu, takes on the form fanatu; with aka (or ake) it becomes fanaka or fanake (both forms are equally common); and with ifo it becomes fanaifo. (In the Nukulaelae dialect, all coalesced forms with fano have a /h/ in initial position instead of a /f/.) Similarly, ave ‘send, give’, when modified by the deictic atu, becomes avatu; with aka it becomes avaka (or less, commonly, avake); and with ifo it becomes avaifo. While kilo ‘look’ coalesces with atu to yield kilotu, and with ake to yield either kiloke or kiloko (there is no form *kiloka). None of these coalescing processes is obligatory, although coalesced forms are distributionally unmarked. Coalescence with aka or ake can take place even when the adverb is a polite downtoner, rather than a deictic. Furthermore, mai is recognizable in the verb form aumai ‘bring, give hither’, which probably results form the diachronic coalescence of the deictic with the verb ave ‘send, give’. Similarly, atu and aka appear in the adverbial forms faatu and faaka, both adverbial intensifiers which are not analysable synchronically but probably result from the coalescence of fai ‘do, make’ and the deictics. Finally, aka and ake are recognizable in the speech act verbs leaka and leake ‘think erroneously, stuck with the idea’ (cf. 1.1.1.1(c)), although the morpheme to which they are coalesced, probably a reflex of Proto-Polynesian *lea ‘speak’, is not attested as a lexical item in contemporary Tuvaluan. None of the coalesced forms, be they synchronically derivable or not, can be further modified with a free deictic other than the polite downtoner aka. Whenever a deictic notion can be expressed with one of the four deictic adverbs, the adverb is preferred over a prepositional phrase with equivalent meaning. Furthermore, a deictic adverb is present whenever a situation is deictically oriented (according to the multifaceted definition of ‘deixis’ described presently), even when its orientation is obvious from the linguistic or extralinguistic context. As a result, deictic adverbs are very frequent in discourse. The following discussion first treats the meaning of mai and atu, which are semantically more complex, before turning to aka and ifo. For a discussion of the use of these deictics in comparative structures, see 1.8.1(a). (a) Deictics mai ‘hither’ and atu ‘thither’ When they modify verbs of motion and related notions, mai and atu denote respectively motion towards and away from the speaker or writer. In their most unmarked usage, they take as point of reference the general area in which the speaker or writer is located, particularly in opposition to the location of the interlocutor. However, in some cases, the deictics appear to violate this generalization. For example, in the first of the following, mai ‘hither’ modifies a verb denoting a speech act that is clearly oriented towards the interlocutor, and not the speaker; in the second example, atu ‘thither’ cooccurs with the prepositional phrase ki au ‘to me’ (i.e., ‘hither’): (2695) E fakasii mai kee fanatu koe. Nps utter-interjection+Itj Dxs Sbj go you ‘[He] is whistling (hither) [to you] for you to come over.’ (2696) Fakamuli kee fanatu ei koe ki au. later Sbj go+Dxs Anp you to I ‘Later on, come and [see] me.’ These examples demonstrate that the deictic frame of reference can shift from the speaker or writer onto the interlocutor. This shift is generally governed by non- syntactic factors except in one context: when the speaker refers to motion by the interlocutor towards the speaker, the frame of reference must be the interlocutor’s; thus motion towards the speaker must be marked with atu rather than mai (and with fano ‘go’ rather than vau ‘come’). This shift is obligatory in nonquoted and directly quoted speech, and does not take place in indirectly quoted speech: (2697) Fai aka kia Semo kee tele mai mo te ulo lasi! tell please to Semo Sbj run Dxs with the pot large ‘Tell Semo to bring (hither) the large cooking pot in a hurry!’ (2698) Fai aka kia Semo, “Tele atu koe mo te ulo lasi!” tell please to Semo run Dxs you with the pot large ‘Tell Semo [the following], “take (thither) the large cooking pot in a hurry!”’ The deictic adverbs frequently appear in discourse in which neither first-person nor second-person entities are participants. In such cases, the speaker chooses the participant with whom he or she identifies most closely as the deictic frame of reference. The following example appears as the conclusion of a story about a man who began delivering a church sermon, but then forgot what he was going to say: (2699) Koo kkata atu ei a tino, koo fano. In cases where mai and atu modify verbs that denote situations which are not oriented towards any human participant in the context, several factors may dictate the choice in deictic frame of reference. Evolution in time treats the absolute or relative present time as the frame of reference, so that situations oriented towards this reference point are marked with mai, and situations oriented away from the present with atu: (2700) mai te tausaga teenaa kee oko mai ki te tausaga teenei from the year that Sbj reach Dxs to the year this ‘from that year until this year’ Changes from sleeping to waking, from childhood to adulthood, from nonbeing or death to life, from darkness to light, from poor to good health, and from less to more desirable states are marked with mai: (2701) [in answer to a query about the speaker’s health] Fakafetai me teenei koo feoloolo mai. thank because this Inc middling Dxs ‘Thank you, I’m feeling better.’ Atu modifies verbs denoting changes in the opposite direction: (2702) A te tusi teenaa ne ffuli nee Alovaka Maui, teelaa koo oti ne Cnt the book that Pst translate Erg Alovaka Maui that Prf galo atu. disappear Dxs ‘That book was translated by Alovaka Maui, who has now passed away.’ Two additional minor uses of the deictics are worth mentioning. Mai may appear when the situation denoted by the verb has reached a conclusion, in which case it often implies that the participants have returned from the venue of the situation: (2703) Laatou koo pei tili mai. they-3 Inc cast fishing-net Dxs ‘They have returned from net-fishing.’ In contrast, atu may appear when the situation denoted by the verb is continuous or recurring: (2704) Au e takatokato atu fua. text: 538 Morphology 2.1.3.7. Serial verbs The existence of verb serialization, or verb chains, is well attested among Oceanic languages other than members of the Polynesian family (e.g., Foley and Olson 1985, Harrison 1984a). In contrast, no Polynesian language has so far been described as having structures of this type, although Hooper (1993:239) suggests that they exist in Tokelauan. No Tuvaluan structure can be unequivocally identified as verb chains, but certain strings of verbs resemble verb chains. Such is the case, for example, of the verbs fakasiga ‘[make oneself] fall’ and tagi ‘cry’ in the following: (2781) Ne fakasiga tagi ki vae o tena maatua kee fakamaagalo ia. Pst Cst+fall cry to foot of his mother Sbj forgive he ‘[He] fell cry[ing] to his mother’s feet [for her] to forgive him.’ I have not encountered series consisting of more than two verbs, and, if indeed these structures are examples of verb serialization, they are considerably more modest in scope than verb series in languages that make productive use of them. Paired verbs that resemble verb series are ordered according to a general principle, to the effect that the most dynamic verb comes first, while the second verb generally denotes a more backgrounded, atelic, and continuous situation. Many strings have the status of more or less set idioms. In this category fall such series as mind mmae ‘urinate painfully’ (mimi ‘urinate’, mmae ‘hurt’), moe ssogo ‘wet one’s bed’ (moe ‘sleep’, ssogo ‘smell of urine’), tagi too ‘(of a fowl) to cluck after laying an egg’ (tagi ‘cry’, too ‘lay [an egg]’), and fakalogo ssee ‘mishear’ (fakalogo ‘listen’, ssee ‘wrong’). In a few cases, the first verb only occurs in serial constructions: fakamagii does not have any meaning other than in the series fakamagii tagi ‘whine, cry softly’ (from tagi ‘cry’). The verb fakamisi ‘think longingly’ appears in series with specialized meanings: fakamisi kata ‘smile’, fakamisi alofa ‘harbour unexpressed feelings of empathy’ (from alofa ‘feel empathy’), and fakamisi tagi, synonymous with fakamagii tagi. Verbs in series cannot be separated by anything, and share the same tense-aspect- mood marker. However, they need not share the same argument structure and need not agree in valency. For example, tanu ‘bury’ and ola ‘alive’, kai ‘eat’ and maluu ‘soft’, and fai ‘do’ and sao ‘get away’ in each of the following have both different valencies and different subjects: (2782) Laatou ne tanu ola nee au. they-3 Pst bury alive Erg I ‘I buried them alive.’ (2783) Te loomatua e kai maluu ana masi. the old-woman Nps eat soft her cabin-biscuits ‘The old woman dunks her cabin biscuits.’ (2784) Maatou ne ssoko te fai ssao. we-3-e Pst constant the do get-away+Agr ‘We had [a lot of fish] get away.’ In general, the argument structure of the entire clause follows the pattern associated with the first verb in the series. However, some postverbal adverbs and prepositional modifiers are clearly associated with the second verb: (2785) Au koo nofo masausau atu kiaa koe. I Inc stay reminisce Dxs to you ‘I constantly think longingly about you.’ | True

text: Morphology 539 When serialized verbs are agreeing verbs (cf. 2.1.3.6.1), several possibilities obtain. If both verbs are agreeing verbs and the grammatical subject of the series refers to the agent of both verbs, both verbs agree with it: (2786) E kkata vaallea. Nps laugh+Agr stupid+Agr ‘[They] laugh stupidly.’ When both verbs are agreeing verbs but the subject does not refer to the agent of both verbs, the first verb generally agrees with the subject, while agreement patterns associated with the second verb are idiosyncratic. For example, in the same idiolect, the verb maluu ‘soft’ does not agree with the subject in (2787) but does so obligatorily in (2788) (the latter is to be compared with (2783)): (2787) A atu koo fai ssoko te kkai ma*(al)luu. Cnt bonito Inc do constant the eat+Agr soft*(+Agr) ‘The bonitos keep nibbling [at the lure].’ (2788) Loomaattua e kkai ma*(al)luu olotou masi. old-women Nps eat soft*(+Agr) their-3 cabin-biscuit ‘The old women dunk their cabin biscuits.’ In no case do verbs in series agree with different arguments in the clause. Agreement patterns vary across clauses, as well as across idiolects. In some situations, agreement is optional within the same idiolect: (2789) Koo laku ta(at)tela nee ia ana gatu ki lalo! Inc throw scattered(+Agr) Erg he his clothes to down ‘He is throwing his clothes all over the place!’ These constructions can be analysed in at least two alternative ways. First, they can be considered to be compound verbs, and the formation of concatenated structures can be considered to be part of derivational morphology. However, the productivity of verb concatenation, and the fact that concatenated verbs behave autonomously of one another with respect to agreement, suggest that the phenomenon differs from other lexical compounding processes. Second, the second serialized element could be understood to be an adverbial modifier of the first element. The fact that the argument structure of the clause generally conforms to the syntax and semantics of the first element supports this analysis. However, no adverb in the language agrees with subjects, and the fact that both serialized elements can undergo agreement militates against this analysis. 2.1.4. Adjectives As discussed in 1.16.4, there are three classes of adjective: a productive category of verbal adjectives; a less productive category of nominal adjectives; and a restricted residual category of preposed adjectives. The following discussion concentrates on the first two categories. None of the processes and categories overviewed in this section apply to preposed adjectives, which can only function attributively, do not undergo agreement, and cannot be marked for comparison or degrees of quality. In addition to the three main adjective categories, one also finds verbal noun- adjective compounds (cf. 2.2.6.3.3). They are a subcategory of verbal adjectives, in that they resemble ordinary verbal adjectives in most respects. They differ from other verbal adjectives with respect to agreement, and these differences are described below. | True

text: 540 Morphology 2.1.4.1. Predicative and attributive adjectives Both predicative and attributive adjectives are attested. From the perspective of the category ‘adjective’, the attributive function is unmarked, since it is shared by all words that have adjectival properties. Not all adjective categories can function as predicates, and the ability to do so is one of the principal motivations for identifying two main categories of adjectives. All and only verbal adjectives can function as predicates, although some forms are predicated more commonly than others. Following are a few contrastive predicative-attributive pairs: (2790) Koo mmafa tena fesili. Inc heavy her question ‘Her question is a difficult one.’ (2791) tena fesili mmafa her question heavy ‘her difficult question’ (2792) Koo taaua te aso nei i maafaufau o tino. Inc important the day this at mind of person ‘This is an important day in people’s thinking.’ (2793) se aso taaua i maafaufau o tino a day important at mind of person ‘an important day in people’s thinking’ (2794) Konei omotou manu e tausi nee maatou. these our-3-e animal Nps keep Erg we-3-e ‘These are the animals we keep.’ (2795) omotou manu tausi konei our-3-e animal keep these ‘these domestic animals of ours’ The internal morphology of verbal adjectives is the same whether they are used predicatively or attributively. Members of the subcategory of verbal noun-adjective compounds can also appear in either predicative or attributive contexts without undergoing any formal changes: (2796) Ttamaliki teenaa ko ia loo koo pati matua. the+child that Foc he indeed Inc word old ‘That child is verbally very mature.’ (2797) ttamaliki pati matua the+child word old ‘a verbally mature child’ (2798) Ttoeaina teenaa koi mata taulekaleka faeloa. the+old-man that still face handsome constantly ‘That old man still has a handsome face.’ (2799) ttoeaina mata taulekaleka faeloa the+old-man face handsome constantly ‘the old man with a handsome face’ When verbal adjectives (including verbal noun-adjective compounds) are used predicatively, they are indistinguishable from regular verbs. | True

text: Morphology 541 In contrast, nominal adjectives can only function as attributes. For example, the nominal adjective modifier in (2800) cannot appear as a predicate: (2800) te fale kaapa the house corrugated-iron ‘a corrugated iron house’ (2801) *E kaapa te fale. Nps corrugated-iron the house (‘The house is made of corrugated iron.’) Predicates corresponding to noun phrases with noun-derived attributive adjectives must be constructed with a full verb (e.g., faaite ‘make’), which takes a nominal form of the adjective as an argument or modifier: (2802) Te fale e faaite ki kaapa. the house Nps make with corrugated-iron ‘The house is made of corrugated iron.’ The structure of the resulting sentence is not predictable. 2.1.4.2. Absolute and contingent states No distinction is made between absolute (permanent, normal) and contingent (temporary, abnormal) states. 2.1.4.3. Noun-adjective agreement 2.1.4.3.1. Number agreement Whenever an adjective agrees with a noun, the category upon which agreement is based is number; adjectives take on a plural form formally identical to the form of plural verbs (cf. 2.1.3.6.1). Adjective classes behave differently with regards to agreement. The following discussion identifies three distinct patterns: one associated with nominal adjectives; another with verbal adjectives; and a last pattern relevant to the noun-adjective compound subclass of verbal adjectives, whose behaviour with respect to agreement is complex enough to deserve separate treatment. (a) Nominal adjectives Nominal adjectives never agree with any feature of the noun they modify. Thus the form of the nominal adjectives in the following is invariant regardless of whether the modified noun is singular or plural: (2803) te tifa fatu the plate stone ‘a porcelain plate’ (2804) tifa fatu plate stone ‘the porcelain plates’ This feature of nominal adjectives is particularly important in identifying the derivation of adjectives from forms that can function as either nouns or verbs. text: 542 Morphology indicates that it is derived from the etymologically related and homophonous verb alofa ‘have empathy’: (2805) ko tusi alofa Foc letter empathy ‘personal letters’ (2806) ko taagata aallofa Foc men feel-empathy+Agr ‘empathetic men’ There is one exception to the above pattern. The two nominal adjectives tagata ‘male’ and fafine ‘female’ have obligatory agreement forms taaggata and faaffine. The nouns to which these adjectives are related, tagata ‘man’ and fafine ‘woman’, are among the very few nouns that have a plural form. Significantly, their plural forms differ from the plural forms of the adjectives (taagata v. taaggata, faafine v. faaffine), suggesting that the adjectives may be derived from verbs formed from the nouns, even though they are never used predicatively. For further discussion, see 2.1.1.8.3. (b) Verbal adjectives When they function as predicates, verbal adjectives are not distinguishable from regular intransitive verbs (cf. 1.16.4.1). Thus all agreement patterns described in 2.1.3.6.1 also apply to predicative adjectives, insofar as it makes sense to identify such a class. An attributive adjective derived from an intransitive verb that has an agreement form (cf. 2.1.3.6) agrees in number with the noun it modifies if that noun functions as the subject of the adjective when the latter is predicative. (For a discussion of another peculiarity of verb-derived colour adjectives in such compounds, see 5.1.2.) text: Morphology 543 agree with nouns that do not correspond to their subject. Compare (2811), in which the adjective tale ‘cough[ing]’ fails to agree with its head noun because it is not its subject in corresponding predicative constructions, with (2814), where agreement takes place because the head noun is the subject of corresponding predicative constructions: (2811) ne vai tale some water cough ‘cough medicine’ (2812) ne tamaliki ttale some child cough+Agr ‘coughing children’ Other verbal adjectives sometimes undergo agreement with their head noun even when the latter does not correspond to the subject of predicative manifestations of the adjective: (2813) taka taaffao sandal play+Agr ‘sports shoes’ (2814) ne faoao aakkoga some exercise-book learn+Agr ‘school exercise books’ The behaviour of verbal adjectives in attributive position with head nouns that do not correspond to their subject in predicative constructions is lexically determined, and varies from speaker to speaker, and perhaps from context to context. If the adjective derives from a verb that agrees with its direct object, i.e., a canonical causative verb (cf. 2.1.3.6.1), and if the noun it modifies corresponds to its direct object in a predicative context, number agreement between the noun and the adjective is optional, as it is between the direct object and the verb in predicative contexts. Compare the optionality of agreement in the noun phrase in (2815) with the parallel pattern in the clause in (2816): (2815) ne tino faka(i)ita some person Cst+angry(+Agr) ‘people made angry’ (2816) Tino kolaa ne faka(i)ita nee olotou tama. person those Pst Cst+angry(+Agr) Erg their-3 children ‘Those people were made angry by their children.’ When the adjective modifies a noun that does not function as its direct object in predicative contexts, patterns of idiosyncratic variation similar to those described above emerge. For example, fakaita ‘cause to be angry’ does not undergo agreement when it modifies a noun that corresponds to an oblique participant in a predicative clause, but fakamatakutaku ‘scare’ does so optionally:36 (2817) * pati fakaiita word Cst+angry+Agr (‘angering words’) 36 However, if the adjective includes an incorporated direct object (cf. 2.1.3.6.12), agreement does take place with the head noun, as in pati fakaiita tino ‘words which make people angry’. | True

text: 544 Morphology (2818) faifaiga fakamataku(t)taku action Cst+afraid(+Agr) ‘actions that make [one] afraid’ Relexicalized causative forms (cf. 2.1.3.1.3(a)) behave like regular adjectives derived from intransitive verbs. For example, the intransitive form fakamataku ‘dangerous’ must undergo agreement when it modifies a noun that can function as its subject in predicative contexts: (2819) aamioga fakamaattaku behaviour dangerous+Agr ‘dangerous behaviour’ Adjectives that are derived from verbs without an agreement form do not agree with their head noun. To summarize, number agreement between the noun and its verbal adjective takes place whenever it does in the corresponding predicative context. In addition, number agreement takes place in certain idiosyncratically defined situations whose corresponding predicative sentences do not undergo agreement. (c) Verbal noun-adjective compounds Noun-adjective compounds that have been ‘recycled’ as adjectives form a subclass of verbal adjectives (cf. 2.2.6.3.3), since they can all function as predicates. With respect to agreement, several patterns can be distinguished, which apply to both predicative uses of noun-adjective compounds and their attributive uses with head nouns corresponding to the subject of predicative structures. Whether a particular noun-adjective compound follows one or the other pattern is determined lexically. According to one pattern, agreement is controlled ‘internally’, in the sense that the adjective of the compound agrees with the noun within the compound. Such compounds generally are always either singular or plural. For example, aso llasi ‘spend end-of-year holidays’ is always plural, and hence the adjective element in the compound is always a plural form: (2820) se fakaala aso llasi a feast day big+Agr ‘an end-of-year feast’ [lit.: ‘a big-days feast’] (2821) Au e aso llasi ki Nukufetau i te tausaga nei. I Pst day big+Agr to Nukufetau at the year this ‘I’ll spend the end-of-year holidays at Nukufetau this year.’ [lit.: ‘I’ll big-days to Nukufetau this year.’] According to the second pattern, agreement is ‘externally’ controlled. The adjective element of the compound agrees with the subject of the predicate or the head noun. Such is the case of compounds like pati matua ‘verbally precocious’ (literally ‘old worded’): (2822) ne tamaliki pati maattua some child word old+Agr ‘verbally mature children’ (2823) Tamaliki konei e pati maattua. child these Nps word old+Agr ‘These children are verbally precocious.’ | True

text: Morphology 545 In a third pattern, agreement is sensitive to both internal and external factors. Compounds like mata kivi ‘blind’ (literally ‘blind eyed’) may be pluralized when they refer to a single individual with two blind eyes, or when they refer to several individuals with one blind eye each. Compare the various possibilities: (2824) Te loomatua teenaa e mata kivi/kkivi. the old-woman that Nps eye blind/blind+Agr ‘That old woman is blind [in one eye]/[completely] blind.’ (2825) * Loomaattua konaa e mata kivi. old-women those Nps eye blind (‘Those old women are blind [in one eye each].’) (2826) Loomaattua konaa e mata kkivi. old-women those Nps eye blind+Agr ‘Those old women are [all completely] blind.’ or: ‘Those old women are blind [in one eye each].’ Equivalent attributive uses of the noun-adjective compound exhibit identical patterns. Compounds like vae tteka ‘fast walking’ (literally ‘rolling legged’), which refer to a pair of body parts, are only attested, in most idiolects, with the plural form of the adjective teka. Of course, noun-adjective compounds in which the noun refers to such ‘loci’ as the face, the heart, or the stomach, can be analysed as belonging to either the second or the third category, with the same results, since subjects never have more than one of these ‘loci’ each (except in fictional worlds into which native speakers of Tuvaluan rarely venture anyway). Thus, with compounds like ulu tula ‘bald’ (literally ‘bald headed’) and loto maasei ‘resentful’ (literally ‘bad hearted’), agreement can be understood as being controlled either externally by the agreement-controlling category or by the internal semantics of the compound: (2827) E ulu tula. Nps head bald ‘[He] is bald.’ (2828) Laaua e ulu tula. they-2 Nps head bald ‘They are bald.’ Noun-adjective compounds do not occur readily in attributive position with head nouns that correspond to elements other than the subject in corresponding predicative structures. As with regular verbal adjectives, noun-adjective compounds that appear in terms referring to biological (mostly zoological) species do not undergo agreement under any circumstances; for example, the last word in muu gutu loa ‘fish sp.’ (Gnathodentex aerolincatus, literally ‘long-mouthed muu’) never takes the agreement form lloa associated with regular uses of loa ‘long’. 2.1.4.3.2. Factors affecting agreement As shown above, agreement is affected by the category in which the adjective falls. The relative position of the noun and the adjective and whether or not the noun is overtly expressed are not relevant factors, because the relative position of nouns and attributive adjectives is fixed, barring a few marginal exceptions, and attributive adjectives can only modify overt nouns. | True

text: 546 Morphology 2.1.4.3.3. Agreement and noun categories Conflict between grammatical and semantic categories are resolved with both predicative and attributive adjectives in a manner which is identical to that used to resolve such conflicts with verb agreement; see 2.1.3.6.5 for discussion of the latter. 2.1.4.4. Comparison Since nominal adjectives never denote gradable notions, comparison is only relevant to verbal adjectives. Predicative verbal adjectives function exactly like regular verbs, and the discussion of comparative structures in 1.8, of equative structures in 1.9, and of superlatives in 1.8.7 apply to predicative verbal adjectives as much as to regular verbs. (The latter category is not distinguished from the former in this section, which include illustrations of regular verbs.) The most natural way of expressing comparisons with attributive adjectives is to turn them into predicative adjectives and then mark them for comparison. This can be achieved least disruptively by turning the adjective into a relative clause. For example, the attributive adjective in (2830) is marked with the universal tense- aspect-mood marked e and turned into a relative clause before being marked for superlative comparison as an ordinary verb: (2829) te loomatua mata alofa the old-woman face feel-empathy ‘a kind-looking old woman’ (2830) te loomatua [e mata alofa atu i loomaattua katoa i the old-woman Nps face feel-empathy Dxs at old-women all at konei] here ‘the most kind-looking old woman of all old women here’ Adjectives can also be marked for comparison in attributive positions. However, the resulting constructions are less idiomatic than the predicated constructions described above. Adjectives in attributive position can be marked for equative comparison by modifying the noun with an object of equation (cf. 2.1.1.2.7). The entire noun phrase must be marked for equative comparison, and the comparison cannot be marked on the adjective itself. The resulting noun phrase has exactly the same structure as any other noun phrase marked for equative comparison (cf. 1.9.1(a)). Following are examples of attributive adjectives marked for realis and irrealis equative comparison respectively: (2831) ne pati taaua peelaa mo pati i loto i se tusi some word important thus with word at centre at a book ‘words as important as words in a book’ or: ‘important words like words in a book’ (2832) te tagata loto lailai peelaa me se manu the man heart dirty thus Cmp a animal ‘a man as dirty-minded as an animal’ or: ‘a dirty-minded man like an animal’ Adjectives can also be marked for comparison in attributive position. A comparative deictic adverb is postposed to the adjective as if it were a predicate, and the object of the comparison can be specified as a locatively marked prepositional modifier of the noun phrase (cf. 2.1.1.2.6): | True

text: Morphology 547 (2833) Aumai aka se fao tai ffula atu i fao konei. bring please a nail quite thick Dxs at nail those ‘Can you bring me a thicker nail than these (nails)?’ Attributive adjectives can also be marked for superlative comparison, and the same strategies are employed as those associated with predicative contexts (cf. 1.8.7). An intensifying adverb is postposed to the adjective, and a standard of comparison can be expressed as a locatively marked prepositional modifier of the noun phrase: (2834) A Vaitupu ko te fenua lasi eiloa i fenua o Tuuvalu. Cnt Vaitupu Foc the island big indeed at island of Tuvalu ‘Vaitupu is the largest island of Tuvalu.’ No distinction is made between superlative comparisons that take as standard of comparison other entities and comparisons that take as standard the same entity at another location or another time. Only adjectives that modify nouns corresponding to the subject of equivalent predicative adjectives can be marked for comparison. Comparative constructions with other adjectives yield pragmatically unacceptable results. 2.1.4.5. Degrees of quality Degrees of quality are marked on predicative adjectives in the same fashion as any other verb. Attributive adjectives can also be marked for degrees of quality with the same intensifying and downtoning adverbs as are used with predicates. Following is an example of attributive adjectives modified by intensifiers: (2835) Se tamaliki poto kkii. a child intelligent very ‘[He’s] a very intelligent child.’ (2836) ne pati tonu kkisi eiloa some word right dead indeed ‘dead-right words indeed’ Although the superabundance adverb too ‘too’ is most idiomatic with predicates, it is not ungrammatical as a modifier of attributive adjectives: (2837) Te tuulaga teenaa se tuulaga too faigataa moo te llei o tou olaga. the status that a status too difficult Ben the good of your life ‘Where you find yourself is too difficult a position for it to be of any good to your life.’ Adverbial downtoners of all types can modify attributive adjectives freely: (2838) Se mataaupu tai faigataa tena mea ne avaka. a matter quite difficult his thing Pst bring+Dxs ‘What he brought up is quite a difficult matter.’ Degree of quality presumes gradability, and therefore adjectives that denote notions that are not readily gradable cannot be modified by adverbials denoting degree of quality. In this category fall verbal adjectives like muamua ‘first’ and numerals, as well as all nominal adjectives. However, these adjectives can be modified by the all-purpose intensifier eiloa and its allomorphs. | True

text: 548 Morphology 2.1.4.6. Verbal morphology of predicative adjectives Predicative adjectives are indistinguishable from regular verbs, as shown in 1.2.1.1.2 and in the above sections. Thus their morphology resembles that of a verb in every respect. 2.1.5. Prepositions and case markers As discussed in 1.16.5, prepositions are difficult to distinguish from case markers. The following discussion therefore focuses on both categories. There are no postpositions. 2.1.5.1. Inventory of prepositions and case markers Like other Polynesian languages, Tuvaluan has a comparatively small inventory of forms that function as prepositions and case markers. For this reason, and because most grammatical and semantic functions are encoded with prepositions and case markers, each form has a broad range of functions, some of which are clearly related to one another, while others are more loosely connected. The functions of all forms are discussed at length in 2.1.1 and the extent to which they constitute a well defined morphosyntactic class is discussed in 1.16.5. The following lists and cross-references the various functions associated with each form. This description is necessarily brief, and reference should be made to the relevant discussion for a fuller account of the exact nature and range of each function. Furthermore, the categorization provided here should not be taken to imply that each category is syntactically or semantically distinct. Again, cases where this question is relevant are discussed in the appropriate section. The following overview covers morphologically simple prepositions, and only treats overt forms, to the exclusion of ‘zero’ prepositional elements. Allomorphs, where they exist, are not listed here. Forms that result from compounding or derivation are discussed in 2.2.6. (a) Case marker nee The least multifunctional of all case markers, nee functions primarily as the ergative case marker (2.1.1.2.2(a), (b), and (e)), as well as the marker of pseudoergative case (2.1.3.1.3(d)). (b) Case marker a This case marker denotes either the absolutive case (2.1.1.2.1.1 and 2.1.1.2.4) or contrastiveness (1.11.2.1.7), and often both at once. It is optional in most instances, although it becomes obligatory or strongly preferred under certain circumstances, particularly with the third-person singular pronoun or the interrogative word ai ‘who?’, and with nouns that lack an overt article (cf. 2.1.1.2.1.1 and 2.1.2.6.1). (c) Case marker ko This case marker marks constituent focus (1.11.2.1.4) and subjects or predicates of copular constructions (1.2.1.1.1(a) and 2.1.1.2.3). It also appears with object complements (2.1.1.2.11) and qualification (2.1.1.4.31), and may mark a single noun phrase or nominalized verb to emphasize the entire sentence (1.11.1.3.2–3). It is often found in answers to yes-no questions (1.11.3). (d) Preposition i The primary function of i is to mark location at rest in space or time (2.1.1.5.1(a) and 2.1.1.6.1), as well as nonlocal, local, and temporal source | True

Preposition-noun agreement Prepositions do not systematically agree for any grammatical category with their objects. However, the three most basic prepositions, namely i (location), ki (direction), and mai (source), regardless of their grammatical or semantic function, are obligatorily suffixed with a morpheme -aa or its allomorph -a when their object falls into one of several categories. The long form of the suffix is used when the following word consists of two morae or less, and the short form is used elsewhere. The suffix is required when the object of the preposition is a proper name with a human referent, as illustrated in all examples provided so far. The suffix is generally not used when the object of the preposition is a proper noun with a nonhuman referent or a proper noun which is not a name. However, when a place name refers to an entity of political import, and when this import is foregrounded in the situation denoted by the sentence, the suffix must be used. Such is the case, for example, when the place name refers to a nation or a government with volitional power, which thus acquires anthropomorphic qualities: (2839) Falani ne takavale ia ai i ttaua teenaa? America ‘So America spoke to Britain [and asked them] to leave America.’ The appropriate interrogative word in these contexts is the proper interrogative word ai ‘who?’, as illustrated in and discussed in 2.1.2.6.1. The suffix is obligatory with many pronouns (cf. 2.1.5.3) and with the interrogative word ai ‘who?’, whether or not they refer to human or nonhuman entities (cf. 2.1.2.6.1). The suffix is also obligatory when the object of the preposition is the name of a month (cf. 2.1.1.6.1). text: 552 Morphology 2.1.6.1. Numerals used in counting Numbers from 0 to 10 used in counting read as follows: (2845) 0 leai 6 ono 1 tasi 7 fitu 2 lua 8 valu 3 tolu 9 iva 4 faa 10 sefulu, toa 5 lima The numerals leai and sefulu are borrowings from Samoan. The numeral toa is the original native Tuvaluan term for 10. While sefulu can be used in counting, in attributive positions, and in forming numerals between 11 and 19 and multiples of 10, toa can only be used in counting objects either unit by unit, or in pairs (e.g., lua, faa, ono, valu, toa). Before the introduction of sefulu, a reflex of the Proto-Polynesian *hagafulu (e.g., agafulu) was probably in use as an attributive numeral, as the forms agafulu and -gafulu are found in the specialized numeral system (cf. 2.1.6.3). Multiples of 10 are formed by juxtaposing the multiplier and sefulu ‘ten’: (2846) 30 tolu sefulu 50 lima sefulu 40 faa sefulu 90 iva sefulu Multiples of 100 are formed by juxtaposing the multiplier and the word for 100, selau, a borrowing from Samoan: (2847) 100 selau 300 tolu selau 200 lua selau 900 iva selau In a similar fashion, multiples of 1000 are formed by apposing the multiplier to afe ‘thousand’, also a borrowing from Samoan: (2848) 1000 afe 3000 tolu afe 2000 lua afe 9000 iva afe There are no terms for higher numerals, even though such terms are found in certain Polynesian languages such as Tongan and Nukuoro, and in many Micronesian languages (Harrison and Jackson 1984). The word kiu ‘plenty, many’ derives from a Proto-Nuclear-Polynesian form *kiu that can be reconstructed as a high numeral whose exact value differs from daughter language to daughter language, but it does not have a numerical meaning in Tuvaluan. Occasionally, the word miliona ‘million’, a borrowing from English, is used; its syntactic and morphological usage is identical to that of selau and afe. Units following tens may be simply apposed to the tens, or, more formally, introduced with the conjunction ma or ma le, which are used exclusively with numerals. One multiple of 10, namely 20, can take on either the regular form lua sefulu or the form luafulu when followed by a unit: (2849) 12 sefulu lua, sefulu ma lua, or sefulu ma le lua 24 luafulu lua, luafulu ma lua, or luafulu ma le lua, lua sefulu lua, lua sefulu ma lua, or lua sefulu ma le lua 76 fitu sefulu ono, fitu sefulu ma ono, or fitu sefulu ma le ono 231 lua selau tolu sefulu tasi, lua selau tolu sefulu ma tasi, or lua selau tolu sefulu ma le tasi 1989 afe iva selau valu sefulu iva 26945 lua sefulu (or luafulu) one afe iva selau faa sefulu lima | True

For most speakers (but not all), the analytic method cannot be used if 1 appears as something other than a unit in a numeral expression. text: 554 Morphology predicative and attributive positions. As predicates, numerals are indistinguishable from predicative adjectives (cf. 2.1.4). As attributes, numerals may be either preposed or postposed to the nouns they modify. In postposed position, they share many features with relativized predicates; in preposed position, they lose most of their verbal characteristics. In addition, some numerals can be used as adverbial modifiers of verbs. The following discussion of the structure of numerals, which focuses primarily on ordinary numerals (i.e., numerals whose morphology is discussed in 2.1.6.1), also applies to most specialized numerals (cf. 2.1.6.3), as the latter can also be used either attributively, in either preposed or postposed position, or predicatively. 2.1.6.2.1. Predicative cardinal numerals As predicates, numerals can be marked for any tense, aspect, or mood category, and may be modified by any appropriate modifier: (2857) Vaitupu e lua ana ituuala. Vaitupu Nps two its village-side ‘Vaitupu [has] two villages sides.’ (2858) Koo iva nei ttou paala. Inc nine now our-3-i kingfish ‘We[’ve caught] nine kingfish so far.‘ Like ordinary predicates, numerals can appear in all types of subordinate clause: (2859) Taumafai [kee afe au taalaa [e maua]]. try Sbj thousand your dollar Nps get ‘Try to earn one thousand dollars.’ Numerals used predicatively may undergo or govern any syntactic process commonly associated with verbs. In particular, they may be nominalized, which is the way in which ordinal constructions are formed (cf. 2.1.6.4). When a predicative numeral is part of a measurement, the unit of measure usually forms a verbal compound with the numeral, in which the unit comes last: (2860) E iva pauna te mmafa o te atu teenei. Nps nine pound the weight of the bonito this ‘This bonito weighs nine pounds.’ If the numeral in a measurement is 1, the unit is marked with the singular definite article te (or its allomorph t- or a singular definite possessive pronoun): (2861) Koo tasi nei toku tausaga i konei. Inc one now my year at here ‘I’ve been here a year.’ 2.1.6.2.2. The first category are numerals between 1 and 9 that are modified by toko (cf. 2.1.6.5.1(a)), which, when used adverbially, denote the number of individuals involved in the event denoted by the verb: (2885) Maaua e mmoe toko lua fua i konei. we-2-e Nps sleep Num two only in here ‘We sleep here, just the two of us.’ (1886) A taatou kaa ssala ttou mea inu taki toko tasi. Cnt we-3-i Fut look-for our-3-i thing drink each Num one ‘We’ll each look for our own drinks.’ The numeral tasi ‘one’ with no modifiers can be used adverbially to mean ‘together, as one’: (2887) Taatou e olo tasi! we-3-i Nps go together ‘Let’s [all] go together!’ As an adverbial modifier of the verb kai ‘eat’, tasi can take on a special and culturally important meaning. The term kai tasi may be applied to two or more persons to denote the fact that they are related to each other in such a way that they still own land in common (cf. Specialized numerals Tuvaluan has a relatively complex system of specialized numerals, used to count animals, objects, and concepts of particular importance in Tuvaluan society and culture. Native speakers recognize these numerals as a noteworthy area of language; they are the subject of prescriptive discussions and are seen as an area of language worth investigating. Yet there are idiolectal and dialectal variations in the form and use of these numerals, particularly for the less common forms and in the formation of complex expressions. Most of the data presented in this section were elicited on Nukulaelae atoll, and differences in details may be encountered in other dialects of Tuvaluan. Specialized numerals are used in both cardinal and ordinal expressions, both in counting and as attributes, and may be proposed or postposed like ordinary numerals (cf. 2.1.6.2.3). Most are obligatory and in common usage in everyday speech, and the system is by no means a prescriptively preserved system no longer in common use. However, some forms (e.g., those associated with humans, bonitos, reef fish, and coconuts) are more widely known and used than others (e.g., those associated with birds, crabs, coconut-frond blinds, and footsteps). text: 560 Morphology modifier toko used in counting humans is treated in both this section and in 2.1.6.5.1(a) because its use with numerals higher than ten is in variation with specialized forms for humans. In general, specialized numerals have idiosyncratic forms. One category of objects may thus be counted like a second category within a certain number range, and like a third category within another number range. For example, bonitos and bigeye tunas are counted by suffixing ordinary numerals with -gafua in the range of 3 to 9, as are coconuts and birds. But the numeral referring to 20 tunas or bigeye bonitos is tekau, which is not used for any other object; and when counting tens of such fish between 30 and 90, the adverb tino is preposed to ordinary numerals (e.g., tino tolu ‘thirty (bonitos or bigeye tunas)’), a method also used to count people and birds, but not coconuts (cf. tolugapulupu ‘thirty (coconuts)’). Similarly, when counting bonitos in most idiolects, a different form is used for the unit part of the numerals 12 and 22 (lua v. teaoa). Finally, certain specialized numerals may be combined with ordinary numerals to form complex numerals, while others can only be combined with other specialized numerals. The form of specialized numerals presents a number of morphological (and hence orthographic) problems. Which forms are to be considered bound morphemes, and which are free morphemes? The restricted use of most specialized numeral forms does not allow many of the substitutions and permutations which one uses to answer this question in ordinary circumstances. For the purpose of determining which morphemes are to be written as affixes and which are to be written as separate words, I have used the following rule of thumb: if a specialized numeral modifier can modify the interrogative word fia ‘how many’ (cf. 2.1.2.6.4(a)), this modifier is considered to be a free morpheme and is written as a separate word. For example, tino ‘multiplicand by ten [for humans]’ and mata ‘multiplicand by ten [for reef fish]’ can modify fia and are thus considered to be independent words: (2890) Koo tino fia taatou? Inc ten how-many? we-3-i ‘How many tens of us are there?’ (2891) Mata fia au kanase? ten how-many? your mullet ‘How many tens of mullets did you catch?’ In contrast, -gapulupulu ‘multiplicand by ten [for coconuts]’ cannot modify fia, and thus it is written as a suffix. text: Morphology 569 2.1.6.4. Ordinal numerals The same forms are used for cardinal and ordinal numerals. Both ordinary and specialized forms can be used ordinally, although specialized forms are rarely encountered as ordinal numerals in natural discourse. There are two ways of constructing ordinal structures. See also 2.1.6.5.1(e) for the discussion of another ordinal-like construction. 2.1.6.4.1. Nominalized numeral predicates as ordinal numerals Ordinal numerals can be formed by nominalizing predicative numerals. The numeral retains any adverb that may modify it as a predicate, and the construction has all the characteristics of ordinary nominalized constructions (cf. 2.1.1.3.4 and 2.1.3.5). The quantified noun can be left unmarked for case, although it is more commonly marked for inalienable possession with the possessive marker o, as are subject arguments of many nominalized intransitive verbs: (2930) Ko te tolu teenei o aso o ttou maafutaga. Foc the third this of day of our-3-i gathering ‘This is the third day that we have gathered together.’ (2931) Koo faanau te toko lima o laa tama. Inc born the Num five of their-2 child ‘Their fifth child was just born.’ Nominalized ordinal numerals function like ordinary noun phrases. They can be marked for any case category and may fulfil any grammatical function commonly associated with noun phrases. 2.1.6.4.2. Ordinal numerals marked with the preposition i The second ordinal numeral construction is a nominalized form of the numeral modified by the locative preposition i (cf. 2.1.1.5.1). The resulting prepositional phrase modifies the noun being quantified: (2932) te tino i te toko tolu i te unu mua the person at the Num three in the row front ‘the third person in the front row’ This construction derives from a postposed attributive cardinal-numeral construction (cf. 2.1.6.2.2). For example, the ordinal phrase in the above example derives from the following postposed attributive cardinal phrase: (2933) tino (e) toko tolu person Nps Num three ‘three people’ Ordinal-numeral structures marked with i do not differ in meaning from ordinal- numeral structures described in 2.1.6.4.1. Other derivatives of numerals and related forms Discussed here are modifiers of numerals that are not part of a specialized numeral system (cf. 2.1.6.3) and lexemes frequently associated with numerals. Other modifiers and affixes are discussed in 2.1.6.6. One preposed numeral modifier, hoko ‘exactly, even’, is found in the Nanumea and Nanumaga dialects of Northern Tuvaluan, but does not have an equivalent in the Southern dialects. 2.1.6.5.1. Free modifiers of numerals (a) Classifier-like toko for humans As described in 2.1.6.3(a), the preposed classifier-like morpheme toko is obligatorily preposed to ordinary numerals when they refer to humans. It appears in both cardinal- and ordinal-numeral expressions, and with both preposed and postposed numerals. The following illustrates its use with an ordinal numeral: (2936) te toeaina i te toko lua i te feituu ki tai the old-man at the Num two at the side to lagoon ‘the second old man towards the lagoon’ It is optional with verbs like uke ‘many’, timomo ‘few’, and fia ‘how many’ (cf. 2.1.2.6.4(a)). When toko modifies a cardinal number in a postposed attributive construction, the numeral morpheme e, which is ordinarily obligatory, becomes optional (cf. 2.1.6.2.1). When marked with toko, the numeral tasi ‘one’ may acquire the meaning of ‘by oneself, independent(ly)’. Toko tasi can be used as either a regular numeral or an adverb, and can refer to humans and nonhumans. Ordinary numerals between 2 and 9 preposed with toko may be used as independent nouns in an idiomatic expression roughly translatable as ‘these/those N’. Most structure-altering morphological processes in the language have been described elsewhere in the grammar. The following discussion cross-references these discussions and describes morphological processes not covered elsewhere. It is important to distinguish true derivational morphological processes, which are productive and whose effect on meaning is predictable, from homophony, which can be of two major types. First, two words can be homophonous because they derive synchronically from the same root, even though one word is not derivable from the other through a productive morphological process. Such is the case of ttogi ‘pay’ and ‘price’, since the relationship between the meaning of the verb and noun forms does not conform to any pattern at play elsewhere in the lexicon. Second, ‘chance’ homophony describes sets of genuinely unrelated words that are nevertheless identical in form. An illustration is laa ‘sail’, laa ‘sun’, laa ‘their-2, they [clitic]’, laa ‘letter L’, laa ‘musical note A’, laa ‘downtoning adverb’. Chance homophony is common because the language has a restricted phonemic inventory and a highly constraining phonotactic structure. One can also include in this category forms that may have been historically related but can no longer be analysed as such. For example, it is possible that motu ‘islet’ and motu ‘broken, discontinuous’ were related to one another in some manner at some stage in the history of the language, since islets are often talked about as pieces of land ‘broken up’ by the sea. Further problems are encountered in distinguishing derivational morphology from compounding morphology. As traditionally defined, derivational morphology produces new words by affixing bound morphemes to existing roots (and perhaps modifying the internal form of existing roots), while compounding morphology produces new words by juxtaposing free lexemes either linearly or hierarchically. The distinction thus assumes that one can easily decide whether a particular morpheme is bound or free. In Tuvaluan, this decision is not always simple. Take for example the morpheme gaati, which means ‘coconut meat lining the inside wall of the nut’ when used as a free morpheme. When preposed to certain lexemes, it can also mean ‘empty X’ where X is the meaning of the lexeme, as in gaati vakalele ‘empty airplane’, gaati pookesi ‘empty box’, or metaphorically ‘worthless’ (e.g., gaati taaofi ‘worthless opinion’). There is a clear metaphorical connection between the meaning of gaati as a free lexeme and in compounds, but it is unclear whether the two meanings are sufficiently different that two separate words should be posited, one free and one bound, or whether they retain enough semantic similarity to posit a single lexeme with two different meanings. In the first instance, the formation of compounds with gaati is part of derivational morphology, while it is a compounding process in the second instance. In the following discussion, I take a conservative approach, and discuss only processes that are unproblematically derivational in nature, thus relegating compounding processes like those with gaati to a study of the lexicon. In 2.2.6.3, I overview one compounding process that affects the internal structure of the compounded elements, one compounding process that affects the morphological classification of the compound, and one related aspect of word morphology, namely collocationally restricted modifiers. 2.2.1. Nouns from other categories 2.2.1.1. Nouns from nouns There are no productive derivational processes that create nouns from other nouns. Among unproductive processes is a prefix gaa-, which can be attached to a closed set of words, namely uta ‘land, bush’, tai ‘sea, lagoon’, loto ‘village’ (in its primary meaning, ‘centre’), mua ‘public arena’ (in its primary meaning, ‘front’, and metaphorically ‘front part of a village, where power resides’), and muli ‘private arena’ (in its primary meaning, ‘backside’). The prefixed words fall into two semantic categories: gaauta, gaatai, and gaaloto all mean ‘in the direction of X, around X’, where X is the meaning of the unprefixed form; and gaamua and gaa-muli are strictly speaking nouns but are rarely used unless prefixed with faka- ‘in the manner of (cf. 2.2.2.1.3), which transforms the words into adverbs or verbs with the specialized meaning of ‘(act) for the interest of the community’ and ‘(act) for one’s own or one’s family’s interest’. Deverbal nouns Many verbs have cognate nouns, to which they are identical in form, and which they resemble in behaviour, particularly in nominalized form: pule ‘rule’ and pule ‘boss, ruler’, kini ‘strike’ and kini ‘coconut-midrib broom’, kapu ‘catch by surrounding’ and kapu ‘handful’. However, cognate nouns and nominalized verbs differ from one another in several respects, as discussed in 2.1.3.5(a). Furthermore, because the relationship between the meaning of verbs and cognate nouns is generally idiosyncratic and unpredictable, a derivation process is probably not at play. 2.2.1.2.2. Nominalizing suffix -(C)aga A suffix of form -(C)aga appears in the form of some nouns. This suffix is a reflex of a morpheme which can be reconstructed as a productive nominalizing suffix of the same form in Proto-Polynesian. The suffix has a noun-deriving, semantically idiosyncratic function in contemporary Tuvaluan, and it is found in no more than a dozen lexical items. As shown in the following sample, the meaning of the suffixed form (in the left-hand column) is not predictable from that of the root form (right- hand column) to which it is related: (3043) afusaga ‘steam, vapour’ aafu ‘misty’ folomaga ‘palate’ folo ‘swallow’ inumaga ‘casual bush refreshment’ inu ‘drink’ liitaga ‘bandage’ lii ‘bind’ saitaga ‘tied bundle’ ssai ‘tie’ taamaga ‘torch-fishing party’ taa ‘drive fish’ taomaga ‘canoe cover’ ttao ‘cover’ tauaga ‘coconut-cream wringer’ tau ‘wring out’ The consonant found in these suffixed forms is identical in form and distribution to the root-dependent consonant found in the -(C)ia and -(C)aki suffixes (cf. 2.1.3.1.2(f) and 2.1.3.6.9 respectively). As shown in 2.1.3.1.2(f), when the same root form can take more than one of these three suffixes, the consonant is identical in all cases. There is one exception to this pattern, namely the noun telekaga ‘rush of women bearing baskets of food coming to meet a returning fishing party’, which, if indeed it is derived from tele ‘run’, exhibits a consonant k which is not attested in either suffixes -(C)ia or -(C)aki (however, it may derive from an abbreviated form of the deictic adverb aka ‘up’). The above suffixed forms should be distinguished from suffixed words borrowed from Samoan, such as aofaga ‘plan’, fonotaga ‘conference’, nofoaga ‘seat’, taalosaga ‘prayer’, tuupulaga ‘generation’, tuulaga ‘pulpit’, tuusaga ‘share, contribution’. Verbs from other categories 2.2.2.1. Verbs from nouns 2.2.2.1.1. Nouns functioning as verbs As discussed in 1.16.1, many words that are nouns in their most basic form can occur as verbs without undergoing any change in their morphological structure. However, this remark is not true of all nouns in the lexicon, and members of certain semantic fields are much more prone to morphological boundary-crossing than others. In the following, I identify these semantic fields and describe the semantic relationships between the noun and verb forms. The broadest and least well-defined category of nouns that can be used as verbs denotes objects which can be viewed as instruments in a broad sense (including settings, tools, metaphors, conduits, etc.): (3044) [said of someone who comes and helps herself to food in our larder] Tou fafine naa koo sitoa ki ttou sefe! your woman that Inc store with our-3-i larder ‘That woman thinks that our larder is [her private] store!’ (3045) Maatou e oofisa i loto. we-3-e Nps office at middle ‘We have our office inside.’ Also broadly defined are nouns that refer to an entity that can be viewed as a major attribute of the referent of the verb: (3046) A Fiiti e mauga? Cnt Fiji Nps mountain ‘Is Fiji mountainous?’ Certain nouns that denote instrumental-like or qualifying notions are particularly frequent as verbs. These include pogai ‘reason’ and uiga ‘meaning’ which, as verbs, mean ‘motivate, have as reason’, ala ‘road, way’, meaning ‘come to (be, have, etc.)’ as a verb, and igoa ‘name’, which means ‘call (by a name), so-called’ (cf 2.1.1.4.31): (3047) Teenaa te aogaa o te mea teelaa e igoa ki te tusi laauga. that the use of the thing that Nps name to the book sermon ‘This is why the so-called ‘sermon books’ are useful.’ To this list can be added two nouns in a different semantic domain, namely muna and pati ‘word’, which are commonly used to introduce reported speech (cf. text: 594 Morphology ‘go by X, ride a X’. Certain nouns denoting temporal notions are often encountered as verbs. These include any temporal expression whose referent coincides with a festival or comparable event, and the resulting verb denotes ‘spend X’, where X refers to the temporal entity as well as, in most cases, the relevant festival. For example, of the days of the week, Aso saa ‘Sunday’ (or its casual speech variant Assaa) can be used as a verb: (3049) Maatou ne Assaa i Oolataga. we-3-e Pst Sunday at Olataga ‘We spent Sunday at Olataga [islet].’ The names of other days of the week cannot be used as such. Names of months which can be used as verbs are Mee ‘May’ and Oketopa ‘October’, both of which refer to religious holidays. Interestingly, Teesema ‘December’ cannot be a verb, perhaps because Kilisimaasi ‘Christmas-time’ and aso llasi ‘end-of-year holidays’ (literally ‘big days’) fulfil the role it would play. Other temporal terms which may function as verbs include senitenali ‘centenary’ and iuupelii ‘jubilee’. 2.2.2.1.2. -a ‘abundance of’ This relatively unproductive suffix is attached to nouns to indicate the abundance of the referent of the noun to which it is suffixed: gakoa ‘fatty’ from gako ‘fat’, galua ‘(of the sea) rough’ from galu ‘wave’, gaogaoa ‘littered with rubbish’, perhaps related historically to gao ‘footprint’, kaumanaa ‘cloudy’ from kaumana ‘cloud’, tonaa ‘ulcerous, full of ulcers’ from tona ‘ulcer’, lafaa ‘afflicted with ringworm’ from lafa ‘ringworm’. In a few forms, the suffix appears as -aa, e.g., ligoligoaa ‘peaceful’, related to taligoligo, a collocationally restricted modifier of uu ‘sheltered’ (cf. 2.2.6.3.4), and logoaa ‘noisy’ from logo ‘hear’ (the latter being derived from a verb rather than a noun). 2.2.2.1.3. faka- ‘cause to have, in the manner of’ The multifunctional prefix faka-, whose morphology and primary function are discussed in 2.1.3.1.3(a), may be prefixed to a noun meaning ‘X’ to derive a verb meaning ‘cause to have X’ or ‘cause to be X’, e.g., fakasuka ‘sweeten’ from suka ‘sugar’, fakasausau ‘perfume’ from sausau ‘perfume’, and fakafui ‘tie (coconuts) in bunches of ten’ from fui ‘bunch of ten tied coconuts’. Only some nouns can take the prefix, and no clear semantic patterns seem to dictate which nouns do or do not. However, nouns that can be prefixed tend to denote objects that are applied to something else, or to describe features that result from the action denoted by the verb. Furthermore, faka- can be prefixed to a noun denoting a category (of person, usually) and the result is either a verb, verbal adjective, or adverb meaning ‘in the manner of (an) X, à la X’, where X is the meaning of the original noun. Nonpersonal proper nouns (and the interrogative word associated with such nouns) are frequent in this frame: (3050) Ne talo faka-Lotuma. some taro in-manner-of+Rotuma ‘[It’s] taro à la Rotuma.’ (3051) Pati fakaaa pati konaa? word in-manner-of+what? word those ‘What language is this?’ | True

text: Morphology 595 (3052) Koo faka-Saamoa ana aamioga. Inc in-manner-of+Samoa his behaviour ‘[He] is behaving like a Samoan.’ As remarked in 1.2.1.3.1.1, faka-prefixed adverbs and verbs are frequently interchangeable, and thus an alternative of the last example reads as follows: (3053) Koo aamioga faka-Saamoa. Inc behave in-manner-of+Samoa Two faka-prefixed island names have acquired a special metaphorical meaning: faka-Nuui ‘take French leave’ (i.e., without saying goodbye) and faka-Nanumaga ‘each keep what one gathers without redistributing or sharing’ (e.g., on a fishing expedition, the implication being that participants are stingy or inappropriately competitive). With place names, faka- can also mean ‘via, by way of’. The result is usually an adverb, but it can also function as a verb: (3054) Te Niivaga e vau faka-Niulakita. the Nivaga Nps come via+Niulakita ‘The M.V.Nivaga is coming via Niulakita.’ (3055) Te Niivaga koo faka-Niulakita mai tena malaga. the Nivaga Nps via+Niulakita Dxs its journey Prefixed to certain kinship terms (cf. 5.1.1.1), faka- creates both nouns (e.g., fakatuagaene ‘cousin of opposite gender’ from tuagaene ‘sibling of opposite gender’) and verbs denoting ‘related as an X’: (3056) Au e fakatuagaene ki ei. I Nps in-manner-of+sibling to Anp ‘I am her cousin.’ For a discussion of the quirky behaviour of fakafa(a)fine ‘act feminine’ and fakata(a)gata ‘act masculine’, see 2.1.1.8.3. Finally, faka- can turn certain nouns denoting institutions or abstract concepts into verbs, verbal adjectives, and adverbs, but requires that a definite singular article te appear before the noun. The result can roughly translate as ‘pertain(ing) to X’, where X is the meaning of the noun. Examples are faka-te- maaloo ‘pertain to the government’, faka-te-fono-pule ‘pertain to the Island Council’, faka-te-maneapa ‘pertain to the maneaba’ (i.e., the Council of Elders, customs and traditions), faka-te-lalolagi ‘pertain to the sacred’ (cf. lalolagi ‘heaven’), in opposition to faka-te-foitino ‘pertain to the body’. With a few nouns, the article is optional, with no precise effect on meaning, e.g., fakafenua or faka-te-fenua ‘pertain to the island community’; none of the previous examples can appear without an article. 2.2.2.1.4. mau ‘constantly, plentiful’ This morpheme can be preposed to verbs and nouns alike to derive verbs that denote the prolonged nature of a situation, or the continuous presence or abundance of something. Cnt the knife this Nps constant indeed at the dull ‘This knife continues to be as dull as ever (no matter how much one sharpens it).’ 2.2.2.2. Verbs from verbs Relevant to this discussion is the unproductive prefix ma- ‘capable of’ discussed in 2.1.3.4.7. 2.2.2.2.1. Approximative faka- As shown in 2.1.3.1.3(a), the primary function of faka- is to form causative verbs, a function which can be viewed as a derivational process. In addition, faka- can be prefixed to verb roots and results in giving an approximative meaning to the word (‘sort of, as if’). From gasuke ‘move’, for example, can be derived fakagasuke ‘sort of move’, from tipa ‘take a step’ fakatipa ‘(look) as if one is taking a step’, and from ppusa ‘blister(ed)’ fakappusa ‘on its way to blistering, look blistered’. Only verbs that can take the causative faka- can be prefixed with this other meaning of faka-, which suggests that the two functions of the prefix may be related. The prefix faka- is also involved in deriving verbs in its multiplicative function with numerals (cf. 2.1.6.5.2(a)). 2.2.2.2.2. -goofie ‘readily’ and -gataa ‘not readily’ The two suffixes -goofie and -gataa denote respectively the ease and difficulty with which a situation is brought about, or the high and low incidence or frequency of a situation. They may be attached to a wide variety of forms, although they are not productive enough to be suffixed to borrowings. They may be suffixed to intransitive verbs: (3060) Ko ia loo koo konaagoofie. Foc he indeed Inc drunk+readily ‘He gets very easily drunk.’ (3061) Seeai se tamaliki e kaugataa peelaa! Neg a child Nps partake+not-readily thus ‘She’s the most disobedient of children!’ It may also be affixed to transitive verbs; however, the result is an intransitive verb, which takes as its argument the direct object of the transitive verb from which the verb is derived: (3062) Koe naa koo mateagataa i ou gatu konaa. you that Inc recognize+not-readily in your clothing those ‘You are difficult to recognize in those clothes.’ | True

text: Morphology 597 The two suffixes thus follow an ergative-absolutive pattern, in which subjects of intransitive verbs and direct objects form a unified category in opposition to subjects of transitive verbs. The noun phrase that functions as the subject of a transitive verb and as the experiencer of the suffixed form of the verb may be expressed as a locatively marked oblique modifier of the suffixed verb: (3063) Te kao teenei koo inugataa i au. the sour-toddy this Inc drink+not-readily at I ‘That sour toddy is nearly undrinkable to me.’ Some verbs acquire a specialized meaning when suffixed with either suffix. Such is the case of kau ‘partake (in a group activity)’, which, when suffixed with -goofie or -gataa, means ‘obedient’ and ‘disobedient’ respectively (e.g., (3061)). The unsuffixed and suffixed forms are closer in meaning in Tuvaluan than in English, in that work is almost always communal in Tuvaluan society (and hence involves ‘partaking’) and because ‘obedience’ is mostly equated with one’s willingness to perform tasks for the community. The form -gataa only can be suffixed directly onto the unproductive past suffix ana- (cf. 2.1.1.6.4), and the result, anagataa, means ‘long lasting’. Suffixing the polysemic verb fai ‘do, make’ gives rise to the forms faigoofie and faigataa, with the general meaning of ‘easy’ and ‘difficult’ respectively which can govern raising (cf. 1.1.2.7). All forms in -gataa undergo subject-verb agreement controlled by the subject as with other noncausative agreeing verbs. Agreement is marked by applying partial internal reduplication to the suffix, which becomes -gaattaa. The verb root remains unchanged, even if it has an agreement form (cf. 2.1.3.6.1). Thus inugataa ‘difficult to drink’, which is derived from inu ‘drink’ (plural form, iinu), takes on an agreement form inugaattaa. In contrast, -goofie does not have a plural form, and blocks subject- verb agreement. Thus forms suffixed with -goofie are invariable. The suffix -gataa is roughly equivalent in meaning to some uses of a preposed verb-modifying adverb fui ‘not readily, slow in, difficult to’: (3064) Te ika teelaa e fui maua i koga konei. the fish that Nps not-readily get at place these ‘That fish is rarely caught in these areas.’ This adverb does not affect the valency of the verb. 2.2.2.2.3. taka- ‘around, all over’ This relatively unproductive prefix can be attached to certain verbal roots to denote circular movement or the indiscriminate repetition of the situation, not unlike metaphorical uses of ‘around’ in English. For example, takatipa ‘stagger around’ is derived from tipa ‘take a step’, takatuutuu ‘stand around’ from tuu ‘stand’, and takafiatoa ‘go around acting defiantly’ from fia ‘pretend to be’ (cf. 2.1.3.4.15) and toa ‘courageous, warlike, defiant’. When it is prefixed to verbs that already denote circular movement, taka- denotes repetition, emphasis, or both, as in takammio ‘twist around’ from mmio ‘twist’, and takannimo ‘completely dizzy’, from nnimo ‘dizzy’. The prefix also appears with roots that are not attested in unprefixed form in the contemporary language, e.g., takafili ‘roll over’ (cf. Proto-Polynesian *fili ‘turn, roll’), takapili ‘move around, (of the wind) shift direction’, and takalialia ‘have aversion, disgusted’ (cf. fakalialia ‘demented’). Miscellaneous bound morphemes Mention should be made of an unproductive set of prefixes that may have been involved historically in the derivation of certain verbs from other verbs. These morphemes are recognizable as the first element in certain words, and can take on the forms ga-, pa-, or to-. Some prefixed forms are the stative equivalent of the unprefixed form, which suggests that these prefixes may have been allomorphs of the stativizing ma- (cf. 2.1.3.1.2(e)) at some point in the history of the language. Possible examples include: galue ‘shake, oscillate’ from lue ‘shake’, galulu ‘tremble’ (cf. luuluu ‘shake’); gaofe ‘bent’ from ofe ‘bend, force’; pakini (also makini) ‘fast’, perhaps related to kini ‘strike’; palele ‘run out’, perhaps related to lele ‘run’; patoo ‘produce crashing sound’, perhaps related to too ‘fall’, tafiti ‘wrestle’, perhaps related to fiti ‘struggle’; tafuli ‘hurry along’, perhaps related to fuli ‘chase’; and tatoo ‘slope down’, perhaps related to too ‘fall’. 2.2.2.3–4. Verbs from adjectives and adverbs Verbal adjectives behave like regular verbs with respect to derivational morphology. Verbs are not generally derived from adverbs, although the observations made in 1.2.1.3.1.1 regarding the propensity for adverbial notions to be expressed as verbs are of relevance here. 2.2.2.5. Verbs from interjections The multifunctional prefix faka- can be attached to a conventionalized rendition of many interjections to denote ‘produce the interjection X’. By ‘conventionalized rendition’ I mean that the interjection is phonological and suprasegmentally regularized, i.e., its form is made to conform to the phonological structure of words if it does not already do so, alternative forms are usually conflated into one standard form, and it is stripped of exclamatory intonation. Thus io ‘all right, yes’ produces fakaioio ‘to keep on agreeing by saying “io”’, while a whistle gives rise to fakasii ‘produce a whistle’: (3065) Seki fakataalofa mai ki au. Neg utter-interjection+hello Dxs to I ‘[She] never said hello to me.’ (3066) E fakasii mai kee fanatu koe. Nps utter-interjection+Itj Dxs Sbj go you ‘[He] is whistling (hither) [to you] for you to come over.’ 2.2.3. Adjectives from other categories For the derivation of nominal adjectives from nouns and that of verbal adjectives from verbs, see 1.16.4. Adjectives cannot be derived from adverbs. 2.2.4.
