Fagaua Nps oriented in-manner-of+long ‘Fagaua [Islet] runs north to south.’ (3068) Tuu aka au i te ono valu o gaalue faka-pelesitene. stand then I in the six eight Cmp work in-manner-of+president ‘I then stepped up in ’68 and worked as president.’ See also 2.1.1.6.1 for examples of faka-prefixed temporal adverbs. Two unproductive prefixes generate temporal adverbs, namely maa-, denoting the future (cf. 2.1.1.6.3), and ana-, denoting the past (cf. 2.1.1.6.4). 2.2.5. Other possibilities No other possibilities are identifiable. 2.2.6. Compounding Sections 2.2.6.1 and 2.2.6.2 are concerned with prepositions, while 2.2.6.3 covers compound morphology. 2.2.6.1. Complex prepositions Complex prepositions form a heterogeneous class, loosely defined by the fact that they take noun phrases as objects, they are syntagmatically incompatible with other prepositions, and they are formed by compounding simple prepositions or case markers with lexical elements. The following discussion covers all prepositions considered to be complex or derived in this grammar; other compounds in the language could also be considered to be complex prepositions by another analyst. 2.2.6.1.1. Two prepositions The only prepositions that can occur in sequence are the two prepositions denoting nonlocal or local source, mai and i ‘from’ (cf. 2.1.1.4.2 and 2.1.1.5.1). The compound mai i does not differ in meaning from either mai or i, although it tends to be more characteristic of careful language. For examples of its use in various contexts, see 2.1.1.4.2 and 2.1.1.5.1. 2.2.6.1.2. Nominal formations Complex local prepositions are made up of three elements. The first is a preposition, which may be i for location at rest, ki for direction, and mai for source (see 2.1.1.5.1 for a more detailed characterization). The second is an unmarked noun in the plural, from an inventory of so-called ‘local nouns’ provided in 2.1.1.5(c), or the particle loo, which denotes object of comparison (cf. 2.1.1.2.6). The third is either the locative preposition i or the inalienable possessive preposition o; no difference in meaning is attached to the use of one or the other, although syntactic differences emerge in certain contexts (cf. 1.2.1.1.3). Sentences and phrases with complex prepositions are provided in 2.1.1.5(c) and throughout section 2.1.1.5. | True

text: 600 Morphology Arguments for treating local nouns, i.e., the middle component of complex prepositions, as plural are provided in 2.1.1.8.2. The particle loo (cf. 2.1.1.2.6) is the only morpheme sandwiched between two prepositions that is not found elsewhere as an independent word. Local nouns may be modified by noun modifiers like ordinary nouns, although only monolexemic modifiers are allowed, and only those with a more ‘grammatical’ meaning: (3069) Te niu koo too ki loto tonu o te kema. the coconut Inc fall to middle right of the trough ‘A coconut fell right in the middle of the trough.’ The first two elements of complex prepositions, i.e., the first preposition and the local noun, also often occur as full prepositional phrases without a modifier. Such instances can simply be analysed by treating the local noun as the object of the preposition: (3070) Koo nnofo katoa taagata i lalo. Inc stay all men at below ‘All the men are sitting down [on the floor].’ Among the local nouns, luga ‘top, up’ occupies a special place because it can appear whenever no other local noun appears, in variation with simple prepositions. Thus the following two sentences have the same meaning: (3071) Koo tteke te fenua ki luga i te faiga teenaa. Inc oppose the island-community to top at the way that ‘The island community is opposed to doing it that way.’ (3072) Koo tteke te fenua ki te faiga teenaa. Inc oppose the island-community to the way that Complex prepositions with luga can even replace nonlocative uses of simple prepositions, including case functions such as direct-object or middle-object marking: (3073) Ne lasi kkii te fesoasoani ne maua mai luga ia koulua. Pst great very the help Pst get from top at you-2 ‘I received a lot of help from the two of you.’ The difference between simple and complex prepositions with luga when no upward location is denoted is stylistic. Complex prepositions with luga are more flowery and formal, and they are slightly more polite in reference to either the topic of discourse or the interlocutor. A couple of preposition-like compounds resemble the complex prepositions described here. These are of the form (i) te vaa o ‘between’ and (i) te feituu o ‘next to’: (3074) i te vaa o maaua mo toku taina at the gap of we-3-e and my sibling ‘between my brother and me’ (3075) ki te feituu o te sai puaka to the side of the pen pig ‘(to) next to the pig pen’ These compounds differ from other complex prepositions in two respects: the local noun is not in the plural; and no variation exists between i and o as the last element | True

Strings with feituu and vaa should therefore not be analysed as complex prepositions, but rather as ordinary prepositional phrases with feituu and vaa as objects of prepositions modified by possessive phrases. 2.2.6.1.3. Verbal formations Several preposition-like compounds discussed elsewhere can be considered to be verbal formations. They include peenei mo ‘thus’ and others in this series (cf. 1.9.1(a)); ttusa mo ‘equal to, amounting to’ (cf. 2.1.1.2.8(b)); uiga moo or uiga ki ‘about, concerning’ and comparable forms (cf. 2.1.1.4.15); aunoa mo ‘without’ and related forms (cf. 1.4.7(d)); igoa ki ‘by the name of, so-called’ (cf. 2.1.1.4.31) and related forms; oko ki (cf. 2.1.1.6.6–7); and keaattea mo (cf. 2.1.1.5.4). 2.2.6.2. Simple derived prepositions The only simple preposition-like morpheme that could be analysed as a simple derived preposition is tau ‘concerning, regarding’ (cf. 2.1.1.4.15(b)). Derived from the verb tau ‘befit’, tau is directly apposed to its object, which lacks an article. 2.2.6.3. Compound morphology Whether Tuvaluan has compounds is a complex question, because at first blush most candidates resemble regular head-modifier structures. For example, the string fulu mata ‘eyebrow’ could be taken as a compound, although in many respects fulu ‘hair’ behaves like the head of a noun phrase and mata ‘eye area’ as a nominal adjective, and the morphological behaviour and structure of the string appear to be no different from the morphological behaviour and structure of other strings made up of a noun modified by a nominal adjective. Thus, according to this analysis, fulu mata would deserve special consideration in a bilingual dictionary because its translation into a foreign language such as English is not straightforwardly retrievable from the structure of the Tuvaluan compound; however, but it would not require special consideration in a monolingual dictionary. Deciding whether a string constitutes a compound or an ordinary head and modifier depends first on the extent to which the elements undergo formal changes, second on the extent to which the string behaves like a single unit, and third on the extent to which the meaning of the string is retrievable from the meaning of its elements. The third criterion is the least reliable, both in Tuvaluan and crosslinguistically. It works well in extreme cases, i.e., when the meaning of the compound is very different or very similar to the sum of the meaning of its parts, but does not work well in most cases, such as that of fulu mata ‘eyebrow’, as arguments could be presented in support of either analysis. The relevance of the first criterion to Tuvaluan morphology is limited by the fact that, for the most part, no morphological changes occur in the formation of what may turn out to be compounds (but see 2.2.6.3.2 for an exception). The second criterion is the most useful. The string fulu mata, it turns out, behaves like a single morphosyntactic unit, rather than a noun-modifier string, in several respects. In 1.2.5.3, I mention that a noun can only have one nominal adjective, one verbal adjective, or one of both, and two verbal adjectives if one of them is a colour term. In these respects, fulu mata behaves exactly like an ordinary noun: (3076) fulu mata lapa ‘plastic eyebrow’ (lapa ‘plastic’) fulu mata loi ‘false eyebrow’ (loi ‘false’) fulu mata uusi loi ‘dark-coloured false eyebrows’ (uusi ‘dark’) | True

text: 602 Morphology Furthermore, the word mata cannot be modified independently of fulu with the intensifier eiloa, for example, which can otherwise modify nominal adjectives (cf. 2.1.4.5). Thus mata is in fact not a regular nominal adjective, and fulu mata must be treated as a compound. Compounds are generally made up of two components, although compounds made up of three words are also encountered: (3077) fale tali maaloo ‘guest house’ (fale ‘house’, tali ‘receive (a guest)’, maaloo ‘guest’) mea puke leo ‘tape recorder’ (mea ‘thing’, puke ‘grab, record’, leo ‘voice’) paa ttaki atu ‘bonito-trawling lure’ (paa ‘lure’, ttaki ‘trawl’, atu ‘bonito’) tino fai koloa ‘trader’ (tino ‘person’, fai ‘have, do’, koloa ‘goods’) Most three-words compounds can be analysed as follows: the first component is a noun, the second a verbal adjective, and the third an incorporated direct object. Occasionally other structures are encountered, but they can always be analysed as nested binary structures of a recognizable type: (3078) [faamasino [fono manafa]] ‘land-court judge’ (faamasino ‘judge’, fono ‘court’, manafa ‘land’) [tau [lima lua]] ‘ambidextrous’ (tau ‘(be)fit’, lima ‘hand’, lua ‘two’) Compounds of all sizes are generally nouns, although a few are verbs. Their first element is generally a verb and their second element either a verb or an adverb: (3079) taku tonu ‘promise, swear’ (taku ‘name, mention’, tonu ‘right’) taku ssee ‘accuse falsely’ (ssee ‘wrong’) Verbal compounds must be distinguished from verbs with incorporated direct objects (cf. 2.1.3.6.12) and serial-verb constructions (cf. 2.1.3.7). Furthermore, some compound-like verbs are borrowings from Samoan (e.g., talitonu ‘believe’, from Samoan tali ‘accept’ and tonu ‘true’), and should not be analysed as compounds. Several compounding patterns are noteworthy for different reasons. One, discussed in 2.2.6.3.1, consists of pairs of nominal lexemes, the first of which denotes a generic quality. A second pattern, discussed in 2.2.6.3.2, is a relatively productive pattern of noun compounding in which the form of the first compounding element is suffixed with a linking bound morpheme. Another, covered in 2.2.6.3.3, generates verbs and verbal adjectives from noun-verb pairs. Lastly, section 2.2.6.3.4 is concerned with collocational restrictions between certain verbs and adverbs. . 2.2.6.3.1. Noun-noun pairing with productive first element Among the more systematic patterns of noun compounding emerges a pairing mechanism involving two nominal lexemes, the first of which has a generic meaning that refers commonly to a shape or other qualitative or quantitative feature. The resulting compound denotes a unit of the referent of the second noun, a component of it, or a specific manifestation of it. Noun compounds with linker -a- The morpheme -a- functions as linking device between pairs of lexemes of different types. The first element of such pairs can sometimes function as an independent lexeme in other contexts without -a- and sometimes not, and the second element is always attested elsewhere as an independent morpheme. The compound functions as a noun, although with certain first elements it has peculiar characteristics, which are described elsewhere (cf. 1.15.2). I write the linker as an interfix because it clearly functions as a suffix to the first element of the compound (for example, stress assignment treats -a- as an integral part of the first element), but the suffixed first part cannot occur without the second part of the compound. The following is an exhaustive listing of/h/forms in the Nukulaelae dialect (the glosses are only approximative, and the words in parentheses are the corresponding forms in the other Southern dialects): (3094) hee ‘where?’ (fea) hee ‘not’ (see) heeai ‘not exist’ (seeai) heki ‘not yet’ (seki) haa ‘don’t’ (saa) he ‘a’ (se) hai ‘do, make’ (fai) haa ‘group’ (saa) hano ‘go’ (fano) hoki ‘again, also’ (foki) hua ‘just, only’ (fua) When it functions as a verb meaning ‘return’, the form foki does not appear with an/h/in the Nukulaelae dialect. Restrictions on vowels All five vowels and their geminate counterparts may occur in word-final, word- initial, and word-medial positions. All vowels can also occur in sequence and all possible sequences of two vowels are attested. Three-vowel clusters are less frequent and not all possibilities are attested with equal frequency. If a morphological process outputs a string of more than two identical vowels, the string is reduced to two vocalic morae. Strings of more than two identical vocalic morae occur most frequently across morpheme boundaries as shown in (3096), which gives the word followed by its morphological structure and then a gloss. (3096) fakaaattea faka+aattea ‘away, strange’ fakaaakoga faka+aakoga ‘school (someone)’ Phonetically, these strings are either broken up by a rearticulating of the vowel at the morpheme boundary or, more commonly in fast speech, reduced to a regular geminated vowel. 3.3.1.4–6. Liquids, nasals, and fricatives When geminated, the articulation of the liquid/l/, the nasals/m n g/, and the fricatives/f v s/is held for a slightly longer period of time than the articulation of the corresponding ungeminated segments. In the Nukulaelae dialect, geminated/ h/does not occur, and the geminated/l/cannot be realized as a tap, unlike its ungeminated equivalent (cf. 3.1.2.1.4). 3.3.1.7. Plosives Geminated plosives/p t k/are heavily aspirated. 3.3.2. Stress 3.3.2.1. Significance of stress Stress is a significant feature, but it is predictable and thus not phonemic. 3.3.2.2. Phonetic correlates of stress Stressed vowels are realized with greater intensity, on a higher pitch, and for a longer duration than unstressed vowels. These correlates are most noticeable for primary stress. Stress has no phonetic effect on consonants. 3.3.2.3. Stress levels One can distinguish primary, secondary, and tertiary levels of stress. They have the same basic phonetic effects on segments, with decreasing intensity. In fast speech, the phonetic distinction between tertiarily stressed segments and unstressed segments is not perceptible to the naked ear. 3.3.2.4. Position of stress Stress position is regular, and its assignment applies uniformly to all words and compounds. Stress assignment can be described most economically by making reference to the moraic structure of the word, and by treating geminated vowels as two morae. | True

text: 614 Phonology Words of one mora, which are all grammatical morphemes (cf. 3.2.4), do not carry stress. In words of two or more morae, primary stress generally falls on the penultimate mora: (3097) ave [1ave] ‘send’ tele [1tele] ‘run’ maeva [ma1eva] ‘in flight’ maafatia [ma?fa1tia] ‘sorrowful’ laallala [la?1l?ala] ‘(of hair) dishevelled’ When the penultimate mora is part of a geminated vowel, stress is distributed evenly over the entire vowel: (3098) taa [1ta?] ‘beat’ kkii [1k?i?] ‘very’ uatee [ua1te?] ‘noisy’ patoo [pa1to?] ‘emit booming sound’ maamaa [ma?1ma?] ‘cheap, light’ When an ungeminated high vowel either precedes or follows a nonhigh vowel that receives primary stress with no intervening consonant between the two vowels, the high vowel is realized as a glide: (3099) ssai [1s?ay] ‘bind’ auee [a1we?] interjection of approval poi [1poy] ‘startled’ fesuiaki [fesuy1aki] ‘switch around’ tauemu [taw1emu] ‘ridiculed’ When the penultimate-stress rule assigns stress to a ungeminated high vowel which is immediately preceded by a nonhigh vowel (with no consonant intervening between them), the stress shifts to the preceding nonhigh vowel. In addition, the high vowel is realized phonetically as a glide, as predicted by the rule stated above: (3100) faiva [1fayva] ‘fishing method’ taua [1tawa] ‘fight’ fetaui [fe1tawi] ‘meet’ avaifo [a1vayfo] ‘send down’ peleue [pel1ewe] ‘coat’ Secondary stress is assigned to words of four or more morae. It falls on the second mora preceding the mora that receives primary stress: (3101) fakapaa [2faka1pa?] ‘explode’ finagalo [2fina1?alo] ‘(God’s) will’ kapakkau [2kapa1k?aw] ‘wing’ maafaufau [ma?2faw1faw] ‘mind’ menetia [2mene1tia] ‘manager’ When the mora that receives secondary stress is part of a geminated vowel, secondary stress is distributed over the entire vowel, as in the case of primary stress: (3102) puupuu [2pu?1pu?] ‘hollow’ taakato [2ta?1kato] ‘lie down’ peenaa [2pe?1na?] ‘thus’ maakkeke [2ma?1k?eke] ‘hard (plural)’ fooliki [2fo?1liki] ‘small’ | True

text: Phonology 615 Tertiary stress is assigned to the mora preceding the mora that receives primary stress, as long as this mora does not already receive primary or secondary stress by virtue of forming a geminated segment with a primarily or secondarily stressed mora: (3103) nekeneke [2ne3ke1neke] ‘type of dish’ matolu [3ma1tolu] ‘thick’ uttanu [3u1t?anu] ‘germinated coconut’ Unstressed vowels are often phonetically reduced, e.g., shortened, devoiced, and realized as glides. 3.3.3. Pitch and tone Neither pitch nor tone is significant. 3.3.4. Intonation Intonation varies greatly across dialects. In fact, Southern Tuvaluan dialects are most readily distinguished from one another by their distinctive intonation patterns. However, all Southern dialects share certain general patterns. Noncontrastive declarative sentences do not have a clearly identifiable intonation nucleus. Rather, the pitch is relatively level over most of the sentence, and descends gradually over the last few morae of the sentence, with a possible short burst over the last stressed mora: 3104) (3105) (3106) (3107) (3108) Contrastive declarative sentences generally exhibit an intonational nucleus over the contrastive phrase or word: In questions of all types, the contour rises at the end of the clause: In interrogative-word questions with nonfinal interrogative words, the interrogative word usually receives a secondary intonational nucleus: | True

text: 616 Phonology 3.4–5 SEGMENTAL AND SUPRASEGMENTAL MORPHOPHONOLOGY As in other Polynesian languages, very few processes affect the segmental or suprasegmental morphophonology. Suprasegmental morphophonology is restricted to a few limited cases affecting gemination; stress is constant under morphological processes and intonation has no morphophonological effects. 3.4.1. Segment alternation 3.4.1.1–2. Assimilation and dissimilation There is no process of assimilatory or dissimilatory morphophonology. 3.4.1.3. Other alternations between segments The nominalizing suffix -Vga, whose morphology and semantics are discussed in 2.1.3.5(b), may affect segment gemination in a number of ways. When the suffix is attached to a verb ending in a geminated vowel, the suffix takes the form -ga and it has no effect on the root, as shown in (3109) which gives the suffixed form followed by root and then a gloss. (3109) siiga sii ‘fly-fish’ peega pee ‘swell’ mmaaga mmaa ‘clean’ ffooga ffoo ‘massage’ tuuga tuu ‘stand’ When the root ends in a ungeminated vowel, suffixing has the effect of geminating the last vowel of the root: (3110) ppisiiga ppisi ‘splash’ mateega mate ‘die’ ppalaaga ppala ‘rot’ ppono ppono ‘close’ vvoluuga vvolu ‘red-faced’ In fast speech, the resulting geminate is sometimes degeminated. Thus ppisiiga sometimes surfaces as ppisiga. In addition, in verb roots in which the consonant preceding the stressed vowel is geminated, this segment is sometimes degeminated, although this may only occur if the root-final vowel is geminated (either through suffixation or from the phonological shape of the root). Thus ppisiiga has a third fast-speech allo-form, pisiiga; the fourth logical possibility, *pisiga, is not attested. Many degeminated suffixed forms are homophonous or nearly homophonous with forms which have been relexicalized and must be distinguished from nominalized forms of the verb (although the meanings of the relexicalized form and of the verb are always related). Occasionally, the phonological shape of the relexicalized form differs slightly in idiosyncratic ways from that of the nominalized form. Compare the first column of (3111) which gives relexicalized forms with the second column giving the respective nominalized forms: (3111) olaga ‘life’ olaaga ‘live’ pakiaga ‘wound’ pakiaaga ‘wounded’ faiga ‘deed’ faiiga ‘do, make’ | True

text: Phonology 617 kkaiga ‘festive meal’ kaiiga ‘eat’ fanauga ‘litter’ faanauuga ‘give birth’ okaga ‘husk pile’ okaaga ‘husk’ sainaga ‘contract’ sainaaga ‘sign’ moega ‘bedding’ moeega ‘sleep’ To this category one must also add many forms in -ga which have been borrowed from Samoan, which should be distinguished from both nominalized and relexicalized autochthonous forms (cf. 2.1.3.5). If neither the stressed vowel of the verb root nor the vowel that precedes it is already geminated, the gemination effect of -Vga is optionally transferred to the stressed vowel. When this takes place, if the consonant preceding the stressed vowel is a geminate, it must be degeminated. Thus the following alternative suffixed pairs (first and second column) are attested (excluding fast-speech alternatives); root and gloss are also given (third and fourth columns): (3112) umiitiga umitiiga umiti ‘crave’ saaliga ssaliiga ssali ‘flow’ fepaakiga fepakiiga fepaki ‘clash’ peelega peleega pele ‘beloved’ kaakega kakeega kake ‘climb’ saakaga sakaaga saka ‘dance’ ootaga otaaga ota ‘eat raw’ eeloga elooga elo ‘stink’ poonoga pponooga ppono ‘close’ fuusuga ffusuuga ffusu ‘fight’ This process cannot take place if the antepenultimate vowel is a geminate; thus fooliki ‘small, young’ does not have a suffixed form *fooliikiga. The process is also blocked if the stressed vowel is already geminated, since vowels cannot have triple length within morpheme boundaries. Forms which have undergone gemination transfer are often relexicalized in more or less idiosyncratic ways. For example, while it is acceptable to use saaliga as the nominalized form of ssali ‘flow’, the form has the secondary meaning of ‘crack in the reef through which sea water flows at high speed at ebbing tide’, which the form ssaliiga does not have; peelega is usually given the meaning of ‘CARE package’ (from pele ‘favourite’); and saakaga means ‘choreography’ (from saka ‘dance’). These relexicalizations do not exclude interpretations of the form as a nominalized form (although the relexicalized meaning is more primary), and relexicalization has not taken place for all forms. It should be noted that gemination transfer in nominalized forms is very common in Samoan, a language from which Tuvaluan has borrowed heavily. Many nominal borrowings from Samoan thus exhibit transferred gemination; examples are laauga ‘speech, oratory’ (cf. Samoan lau ‘call out’), puulega ‘authority’ (cf. Samoan pule ‘rule’), and tiinoga ‘prayer’ (cf. Samoan tino ‘openly expressed’). Because many of these borrowed forms exist only in suffixed form in Tuvaluan, the transferred gemination they exhibit should be distinguished from the process described above. Two other minor morphological processes have an effect on gemination. One is the gemination reassignment in certain demonstrative phrases (cf. 2.1.2.5(c)) and the other is gemination reassignment and restrictions with the verbal suffix -(C)ia (cf. 2.1.3.1.2(f)). | True

text: 618 Phonology 3.4.2. Metathesis Unlike certain languages of Eastern Oceania (see Besnier 1987 for an example), Tuvaluan does not exhibit synchronically productive metathesis. A few lexemes have undergone metathesis-like processes at some stage in the development of the language, affecting either consonants or vowels. In some cases, diachronic metathesis has taken place in some dialects but not in others. Examples are Southern Tuvaluan kaipea ‘crab species’ (Northern Tuvaluan paikea, from *paqikea), Southern Tuvaluan mmala ‘charcoal’ (Northern Tuvaluan malala, from *malala), and Niutao dialect ole ‘stink’ (other dialects elo, from *qelo). Such historical developments are not unusual in Polynesian languages. 3.4.3. Coalescence and split The only process of coalescence is that which follows the deletion of unstressed vowels in the formation of geminated consonants, as described in 3.4.4.1. 3.4.4. Deletion and insertion The only productive process of deletion or insertion is the deletion of vowels that carry tertiary stress in certain environments. 3.4.4.1. Deletion processes When two CV sequences in the base form of a word are identical and positioned so that the second sequence receives primary stress, the vowel of the first sequence is obligatorily deleted and the resulting cluster of two identical consonants is realized as a geminated consonant (cf. 3.3.1.4–7). The following gives the base form followed by the form following deletion and then a gloss: (3113) *vavae vvae ‘divide’ *mamao mmao ‘far’ *totolo ttolo ‘crawl’ *fakakaa fakkaa ‘light (a fire)’ *ananafi annafi ‘yesterday’ What I call ‘base form’ is both a synchronic abstraction and a diachronic reconstruction. Synchronic evidence for the structure of the base form comes from a number of synchronic sources. First, vowel deletion is optional in two Northern dialects, Nanumaga and Niutao, and in conservative idiolects in Nanumea, and thus the base form is identical to some attestations of the word in those dialects. Second, in many cases the environment of vowel deletion results from reduplication or from word formation processes; for example, *vavae in the above is a reduplicated form of the root *vae, and *fakakaa derives from the causative faka-and the root kaa ‘burn’. The domain of vowel deletion is the entire word, and a morpheme boundary can occur between the two CV sequences. This is illustrated by the last two examples in the above. Deletion has taken place diachronically in a few words in which the deleted vowel is not identical to the stressed vowel: (3114) uttanu ‘germinated coconut’, from *uto ‘kernel’ and *tanu ‘buried’ pakkili ‘skin’, from *paka ‘bark’ and *kili ‘skin’ mattea ‘filled with pus’, from *mata ‘face’ and *tea ‘pale’ | True

text: Phonology 619 Deletion can also take place across word boundaries in one particular case in which the stress structure does not necessarily correspond to the pattern described in the above. This is the case of the singular definite article te when it precedes a word beginning with/t/(cf. 2.1.1.8.6). In most borrowings from Samoan, deletion may apply in fast speech, as is shown in (3115), which gives the original form followed by the form after deletion and then a gloss: (3115) vavae vvae ‘wick’ susuga ssuga ‘honourable’ salalau sallau ‘broadcast’ Some borrowings from Samoan cannot undergo deletion, as is the case of faavavau ‘eternity’. Whether deletion can apply or not in borrowings from Samoan appears to be lexically determined. 3.4.4.2. Insertion processes There is no clear case of insertion, although internal partial reduplication (cf. 3.4.5.2.2) can be analysed as such a process. 3.4.5. Reduplication Reduplication is a ubiquitous feature of the language, used for many different semantic purposes. It comes in two forms: full reduplication and partial reduplication. 3.4.5.1. Full reduplication Full reduplication can only apply to bimoraic roots. It consists in the doubling of the root, the result being a single word; the following gives the reduplicated form followed by the root and then a gloss: (3116) teletele tele ‘run’ peipei pei ‘throw’ inuinu inu ‘drink’ mapumapu mapu ‘experience difficulty breathing’ In its most productive form, full reduplication yields forms whose meaning is an iterative or repetitive version of the meaning of the root. Full reduplication applies productively only to verbs, although many nouns are the result of diachronic full reduplication. Fully reduplicated forms are not always derived from a synchronically attest- able nonreduplicated form whose meaning is predictable from the meaning of the reduplicated form. The following examples illustrate the fact that the root from which the fully reduplicated form is derived only exists in partially reduplicated form, that the reduplicated form may belong to a different morphological class from the nonreduplicated form, or that its meaning may differ slightly from that of the fully reduplicated form: (3117) vinivini ‘crow repeatedly’ vvini ‘crow’ magamaga ‘fish tail’ maga ‘branch’ vaavaa ‘spaced apart’ vaa ‘gap’ Clearly, full reduplication is an historical as well as synchronic process. | True

text: 620 Phonology Full reduplication must be distinguished from repetition. The former is a morphophonological process, while the latter is better characterized as a discourse process. Full reduplication of the verb fano ‘go’ yields the form fanofano, and repetition outputs the string fano fano. These two processes are distinguished in several ways (even though their outputs are frequently identical phonetically). First, fully reduplicated forms are assigned stress as one lexeme, while repeated lexemes are assigned stress independently of one another. Second, full reduplication can only apply once, and thus can yield only two segmentally identical strings, while repetition can apply iteratively. Strings of up to eight repeated forms of certain verbs (e.g. nofo ‘stay’, fano ‘go’, inu ‘drink’) are not uncommon. Third, only bimoraic roots can undergo full reduplication (thus inuinu ‘drink iteratively’ is grammatical, but *matakumataku ‘iteratively afraid’ isn’t), while repetition is not thus constrained. The constraint on full reduplication refers to the phonotactic structure of roots, and not lexemes; thus full reduplication may apply to a bimorphemic root which only exists as a lexical item in partially reduplicated form; for example, the simplest lexical manifestation of the root *losi ‘accuse falsely’ is the partially reduplicated form llosi, which can reduplicate fully as losilosi. Fourth, fully reduplicated forms can undergo certain morphological processes, like partial internal reduplication to mark agreement (cf. 2.1.3.6.1) as single lexemes (e.g., the plural form inuiinu ‘drink’), while repeated forms undergo agreement separately. Reduplicated forms are written as one word throughout this grammar, while repeated forms are written as separate words. For examples of the use of both full reduplication and repetition for the purpose of marking various imperfective aspectual categories, see 2.1.3.3.2.1(c) and (g). 3.4.5.2. Partial reduplication Partial reduplication is ubiquitous and can have a variety of common functions, most notably the marking of number agreement in verbs that allow such marking (cf. 2.1.3.6). The following discussion distinguishes between reduplication in which the reduplicated element can be treated as a prefix or suffix (‘external’ reduplication) and reduplication in which the reduplicated element must be treated as an infix (‘internal’ reduplication). The distinction is only relevant to words whose unreduplicated form has more than three morae. 3.4.5.2.1. External partial reduplication In bimoraic words, external reduplication affects the stressed mora and the preceding consonant, if there is one, by prefixing a copy of the string to the word. When the target is of the shape CV, the result then undergoes obligatory deletion of the tertiarily stressed vowel (cf. 3.4.4.1): (3118) oola ola ‘alive’ aasi (*asi) ‘show’ ttula tula ‘(of one’s head) bald’ ffati (*fati) ‘break’ kkano (*kano) ‘flesh’ As illustrated by several of the above examples, the nonreduplicated root is not necessarily attested in contemporary Tuvaluan. In words of three or more morae, external reduplication affects the last two morae of the word and the consonants that precede each mora by suffixing a copy of the string to the word: | True

text: Phonology 621 (3119) takatokato takato ‘lie down’ uateetee uatee ‘noisy’ masakisaki masaki ‘sick’ foolikiliki fooliki ‘small’ taaofiofi taaofi ‘stop’ Stress assignment treats the result as a single word, providing evidence for the monolexemic status of the reduplicated form. 3.4.5.2.2. Internal partial reduplication Internal reduplication concerns words of three or more morae. It affects the vowel preceding the stressed mora, as well as the consonant immediately preceding the stressed mora if there is one or, if there isn’t one, the stressed vowel itself. Several cases need to be considered in turn. When the stressed vowel of a three-mora word is immediately preceded by a consonant, internal reduplication geminates both this consonant and the vowel that precedes it, but does so by treating each segment independently: (3120) siinnaa sinaa ‘(of hair) white’ toonnaa tonaa ‘affected by yaws’ foollau folau ‘travel by sea’ paakkia pakia ‘wounded’ taakkato takato ‘lie down’ maattilo matilo ‘sparkle’ When the stressed vowel of a three-mora word is not immediately preceded by a consonant, internal reduplication geminates both the stressed vowel and the preceding vowel independently: (3121) laaooa laoa ‘choke’ maaeeva maeva ‘in flight’ gaaoofe gaofe ‘crooked’ Two three-mora nouns, tagata ‘man’ and fafine ‘woman’, have special plural forms, taagata ‘men’ and faafine ‘women’ (cf. 2.1.1.8.3). These forms constitute exceptions to the above rule, in that the internal reduplication applies only to the antepenultimate vowel, and not to the consonant preceding the stressed vowel. In contrast, the homophonous adjectival forms of these two words, tagata ‘male’ and fafine ‘female’, internally reduplicate regularly as taaggata and faaffine respectively. Words of four or more morae exhibit a different, and simpler, pattern under internal reduplication. In such words, only the consonant immediately preceding the stressed vowel is reduplicated, or, if there is no such consonant, the stressed vowel itself is reduplicated: (3122) kaillao kailao ‘whoop’ maukolloa maukoloa ‘wealthy in goods’ foolliki fooliki ‘small’ uattee uatee ‘noisy’ fakaeeke fakaeke ‘support on something elevated’ As illustrated by the occurrence of both the externally reduplicated form uateetee (cf. 3.4.5.2.1) and uattee (above), the same word can be a candidate for either external and internal reduplication. | True

However, in words of three morae, if one target segment is geminated and the other ungeminated, reduplication can apply to the ungeminated segment. text: Ideophones and interjections 4.1. IDEOPHONES As in most Oceanic languages, there are no ideophones in Tuvaluan. Some words, particularly those referring to sound production, are clearly onomatopoeic: ggolo ‘snore’, guuguu ‘dumb, hum’, ggulu ‘growl, rumble’, kaa ‘bark’, kii ‘squeal’, kuuku- kukuu ‘crow, cock-a-doodle-doo’, miaau or giaau ‘meow’, pakee ‘crack’, and patoo ‘produce a crashing sound’. Onomatopoeia that do not refer to sounds include ppou ‘stink’ (iconic of the sound one makes when smelling a stench) and tuli ‘Pacific golden plover, Pluvialis dominicus’.38 However, these terms are not ideophones according to current working definitions of ideophones as words whose phonological configuration denotes systematically some property of their referent, such as smell, colour, or position (Schachter 1985:21). 4.2. INTERJECTIONS The internal structure of most interjections follows regular phonological and morphological patterns. However, interjections are frequently uttered with intonational contours that are peculiar to them. For example, in the Nukulaelae dialect, the vowels in taapaa ee, exclamation of surprise, are often prolonged for an unusual period of time, particularly the first one, which is also commonly lowered, and the intonation contour begins in the lowest range of the speaker’s voice and ends with a falsetto. Some interjections or the peculiar intonation contours associated with them in particular dialects function as well-known dialectal shibboleths and are the subject of much inter-island teasing. The interjections listed here can only occur as interjections. The following list is representative but probably not exhaustive: (3123) auee, aauee, uee approval, used in formal contexts display (cf. 1.1.1.2.4.2) ee with a name, vocative (cf. 2.1.1.4.28), also sudden recall, surprise ei mild pain, sudden realization that one is mistaken eiauee, oiauee sorrow, pain, particularly in wailing eeia return to a normal state of affairs ia discourse conjunct (cf. 2.1.9(a)) Chapter 4 38 The name tuli resembles the plover’s song. The proverb Koo tagi te tuli ki tena igoa ‘the plover is singing his own name’ is invoked in reference to someone singing his or her own praises inappropriately. | True

A form that does not conform to regular phonological or morphological patterns in the language is aua in the Nanumaga dialect of Northern Tuvaluan (see the footnote at the end of 1.4(c)). In addition, kisimu ‘(to a dog) fetch, attack’ (see the following list), is often realized with its last segment either voiceless or absent. Similarly, the internal/i/in saagikeepoi (see the following list) is often voiceless or absent. Among vocalizations that can be considered interjections figures (k)uuuiii uttered in falsetto voice, used to call someone out of sight in the bush; it resembles a bird song and thus can be used without alarming birds on bird hunts. A sustained nasal mmm generally marks agreement, and can occur on a variety of intonation contours, usually descending. A sustained sibilant sss, which is sometimes palatalized, can be used to attract someone’s attention, even if the intended recipient is close by. It is frequently heard in reported speech. A sustained teeee, with a lowered and centralized vowel, or taaaa, is an expression of disapproval or disgust often uttered with creaky or breathy voice. text: Lexicon 5.1. STRUCTURED SEMANTIC FIELD S 5.1.1. Kinship terminology The notion of ‘being related’ is most generally expressed with the word kaaiga ‘family’, which can function as a noun or as a noun-derived verb. The term kano ‘blood relation’, etymologically related to kkano ‘flesh’, is also used as either a noun or a noun-derived verb. Alternatively, toto ‘blood’ and tino ‘body’ can have the metaphorical meaning of ‘blood relation, related by blood’. The three terms kano, toto, and tino refer only to blood relations to the exclusion of adoptive and affinal relations. The term kaaiga is more encompassing. The kinship term inventory is relatively small, and each kinship term covers a broad range of referents. In the basic system, the most important semantic parameters are generation and gender relative to ego (i.e., whether the referent is of the same gender as ego or not). The seniority parameter, of importance to the kinship terminology of other Polynesian societies, is not relevant in Tuvaluan. Terms for siblings are their own converse, and so are several other terms. There are few terms for affines. All kinship terms and their affixed and modified forms can be used as nouns or verbs. Following is a sample of uses of the term taina ‘sibling of same gender as ego’ and its modified forms, beginning with an example of a nominal use of the term: (3125) A Peetaia ko toku taina. Cnt Petaia Foc my sibling ‘Petaia is my brother.’ (3126) Maaua mo Peetaia e taina tonu. we-2-e and Petaia Nps sibling true ‘Petaia and I are brothers.’ (3127) Maaua e fakataina mo Peetaia. we-2-e Nps in-manner-of+sibling and Petaia ‘Petaia and I are cousins [i.e., classificatory brothers].’ (3128) Au e taina kiaa Peetaia. we-2-e sibling to Petaia ‘I am a brother to Petaia.’ For a discussion of kinship terms in possessive constructions, see 2.1.1.4.6. See also 2.1.6.5.1(b) for examples of the use of the preposed numeral modifier tua, which refers to degrees of kinship remoteness. Chapter 5 | True

text: Lexicon 627 5.1.1.1. By blood Terms referring to blood kin categories can be modified in one of several ways. First, all terms referring to generations between –2 and +2 can be modified with the attributive adjective tonu ‘true, real’ to distinguish canonical referents from collateral ones. For example, the term maatua can be applied to any female relative of the generation above ego, but one’s maatua tonu can only refer to one’s mother. (See 5.1.1.4–6 for another meaning of tonu with kinship terms.) The presence of the optional modifier tonu always implies that a contrast is being drawn, although this contrast need not be explicit. (See also 5.1.1 for terms for ‘kin’ that can only refer to blood relations.) Second, the morpheme faka- ‘in the manner of’ (cf. 2.2.2.1.3) is optionally prefixed to terms for blood kin categories of the same generation as ego’s, of one generation above or below ego’s, or two generations above ego’s (i.e., tupuna ‘grandparent’, but not mokopuna ‘grandchild’), to denote specifically collateral kin categories, but not affinal or adoptive categories. Thus all of ego’s maatua ‘mother’ who are related to ego by blood but are not ego’s genetrix are ego’s fakamaatua. As with the modifier tonu, optional prefixation with faka- connotes that a categorical distinction is being drawn. Third, four basic terms are not marked for gender: tama ‘child’, tupuna ‘grandparent’, mokopuna ‘grandchild’, and tuaatina, only with the meaning of ‘sister’s child’. These terms (and most frequently the first three) can be modified with the noun-derived attributive adjectives fafine ‘woman’ and tagata ‘man’ if specifying gender is important to the discourse context.42 5.1.1.1.1. Same generation as ego Two basic terms refer to siblings and classificatory siblings. They are distinguished in terms of whether ego and the referent are of the same gender or not:43 (3129) taina ‘sibling of same gender as ego’ • for female ego: Z (sister), MZD, MBD, FZD, FBD (first cousins), MMZDD, MMZSD, MMBDD, MMBSD, MFZSD, MFZSD, MFBDD, MFBSD, MMZDD, FMZSD, FMBDD, FMBSD, FFZDD, FFZSD, FFBDD, FFBSD (second cousins), etc. • for male ego: B (brother), MZS, MBS, FZS, FBS (first cousins), MMZDS, MMZSS, MMBDS, MMBSS, MFZDS, MFZSS, MFBDS, MFBSS, MMZDS, FMZSS, FMBDS, FMBSS, FFZDS, FFZSS, FFBDS, FFBSS (second cousins), etc. (3130) tuagaane (or more archaically tuagaene) ‘sibling of different gender from ego’ • for female ego: B (brother), MZS, MBS, FZS, FBS (first cousins), MMZDS, MMZSS, MMBDS, MMBSS, MFZDS, MFZSS, MFBDS, MFBSS, MMZDS, FMZSS, FMBDS, FMBSS, FFZDS, FFZSS, FFBDS, FFBSS (second cousins), etc. 42 That these adjectives are derived from the nouns fafine and tagata rather than from the homophonous verbs meaning ‘female’ and ‘male’ respectively is supported by the fact that they cannot be used predicatively, and that they pluralise as faafine and taagata respectively, rather than as faaffine and taaggata (cf. 2.1.1.8.3). 43 Kinship terms are described with the conventional abbreviations of kinship studies: M=mother; F=father, Z=sister, B=brother, D=daughter, S=son, W=wife, H=husband, with FM=father’s mother, MBD=mother’s brother’s daughter, and so forth. | True

text: 628 Lexicon • for male ego: Z (sister), MZD, MBD, FZD, FBD (first cousins), MMZDD, MMZSD, MMBDD, MMBSD, MFZSD, MFZSD, MFBDD, MFBSD, MMZDD, FMZSD, FMBDD, FMBSD, FFZDD, FFZSD, FFBDD, FFBSD (second cousins), etc. The above is the simplest sibling term inventory one finds in Polynesia. In particular, the system makes no reference to seniority, a parameter of common relevance in Polynesian sibling terms, and of much greater importance in most Polynesian kinship systems than in Tuvaluan society. The term tuagaane (and its archaic form tuagaene) may be modified with either of the attributive adjectives mmalu ‘respectful’ and tapu ‘forbidden, sacred’ to restrict the reference of siblings to whom avoidance taboos (fakammalu) apply, i.e., usually first and second cousins, and sometimes third cousins. These categories can also be referred to with the derived term fakatuagaane, but this term does not have the same connotations as tuagaane mmalu or tuagaane tapu. The modifier mmalu can be loosely translated as ‘respectful’, where ‘respect’ is demonstrated through avoidance. Pairs of tuagaane mmalu are expected to avoid being in one another’s presence, addressing one another, and talking about one another.44 Most important, tuagaane mmalu cannot get married to one another (incest being a topic of great concern in Tuvaluan society), hence the alternative modifier, tapu ‘forbidden’. The responsibility for ensuring that this avoidance is maintained falls in large part upon women; men are expected to ‘protect’ (tausi, a Samoan borrowing) their sisters’ and classificatory sisters’ reputation by fending off any party who might take sexual advantage of them, and beating the hell out of them if they get pregnant before marriage. Third parties are also expected to avoid talking to someone about her or his tuagaane mmalu, particularly in a joking or lewd manner, although the relationship is nowadays often the subject of a great deal of mild teasing, mostly in private contexts. The adjective tapu is used in a related sense with maasaga ‘twin’; a maasaga tapu is a twin (or pair of twins) of different gender. There is no Southern Tuvaluan reflex of Proto-Polynesian *taqokete ‘man’s elder brother’. The term taina, a reflex of *tahina ‘man’s younger brother’, has been extended to refer to this category. One does find an irregular reflex of this term in the Niutao dialect, taakete, where it is an affectionate term for ‘[one’s] child’, similar in affective connotation to the Southern Tuvaluan toe (cf. 5.1.1.1.3). 5.1.1.1.2. One generation above ego Three basic terms can be identified: (3131) maatua ‘mother’ M (mother), MZ, MMZD, MMBD, MFZD, MFBD, FZ, FMZD, FMBD, FFZD, FFBD (aunt), etc. (3132) tamana ‘father’ F (father), FB, FMZS, FMBS, FFZS, FFBS (paternal uncle), etc. (3133) tuaatina ‘mother’s brother’ MB (maternal uncle), MMZS, MMBS, MFZS, MFBS, etc. 44 The canonical illustration of avoidance behaviour, which Tuvaluans invariably provide in elicitation contexts, is the expectation that individuals, particularly women, step off a path and look for a different route to their destination if they see their tuagaane mmalu coming in the opposite direction. | True

text: Lexicon 629 The term tuaatina is the same as for ‘sister’s child’ (cf. 5.1.1.1.3), and denotes a particularly important relationship normatively characterized by a strong affective bond. There is no reflex of Proto-Polynesian *masakitaya ‘father’s sister’, a term whose reflexes in certain Polynesian languages like Tongan denote an important category for reasons of power and rank. 5.1.1.1.3. One generation below ego Two terms can be identified, one of which applies to either female or male ego (although it has a different range of referents in either case), while the other is only relevant to male ego: (3134) tama ‘child’ • for both female and male ego: D (daughter), S (son), BD, BS, MZSD, MZSS, MBSD, MBSS, FZSD, FZSS, FBSD, FBSS (niece or nephew), etc. • for female ego only: ZD, ZS, MZDD, MZDS, MBDD, MBDS, FZDD, FZDS, FBDD, FBDS (niece or nephew), etc. (3135) tuaatina ‘sister’s child’ for male ego only: ZD, ZS, MZDD, MZDS, MBDD, MBDS, FZDD, FZDS, FBDD, FBDS (niece or nephew), etc. The term tuaatina is the same as for ‘mother’s brother’ (cf. 5.1.1.1.2). It is its own converse for male ego, but not for female ego. A few additional terms are of relevance, although they do not belong to the basic kinship terminology. The term faanau, a Samoan borrowing, refers to one’s children as a whole. The term toe is often used to refer to ‘child’, and has positive affective connotations. (It is homophonous with and perhaps historically related to a verb meaning ‘remain’ and an adverb and preposed adjective meaning ‘last, again’.) The terms toekimuli ‘last-born child’ (etymologically ‘child to the back’), toekimua (etymologically ‘child to the front’), uluaki (etymologically related to ulu ‘head’), and the Samoan borrowing ulumatua ‘first-born child’ may also be used instead of tama, although more rarely so than toe. These terms also mark the referent for seniority, in contrast to other terms for ‘child’. There is no Southern Tuvaluan reflex of Proto-Polynesian *qila(a)mutu ‘man’s sister’s child’, as tuaatina (which can only be reconstructed with the meaning of ‘mother’s brother’) has been extended to cover this category. Elsewhere in Polynesia, this category is of great social importance. However, in Northern Tuvaluan, one finds an archaic term laamutu, which refers to a man’s female cousin’s child. 5.1.1.1.4. Other generations All members of the second generation above ego’s can be referred to with the same term: (3136) tupuna ‘grandparent’ MM, FM (grandmother), MF, FF (grandfather), MMZ, MFZ, FMZ, FFZ (great-aunt), MMB, MFB, FMB, FFB (great-uncle), etc. Similarly, all members of the second generation below ego’s are referred to with the same term: (3137) mokopuna ‘grandchild’ DD, SD (granddaughter), DS, SS (grandson), ZDD, ZSD, BDD, BSD (great-niece), ZDS, ZSS, BDS, BSS (great-nephew), etc. | True

text: 630 Lexicon The meanings of both terms can also be extended to refer to members of the generations prior to the second generation above ego’s and after the second generation below ego’s respectively. Members of generations above one’s tupuna’s generations can also be referred to either individually or collectively as tupuga or tuupuga ‘ascendant, ascendance, great-grandparent’. There are several terms for members of the generation below the second generation below ego’s (i.e., great- grandchild and below). These terms are relatively infrequent except to refer to one’s descendants as a whole, and they are probably of Northern Tuvaluan origin, although they have been integrated into the Southern Tuvaluan vocabulary. These terms read as follows: (3138) mokopuu ‘member of –3 generation’ mokomoko ‘member of –4 generation’ moko ‘member of –5 generation’ The three terms are etymologically related to mokopuna ‘grandchild’ (-na in the latter is a fossilized third-person singular possessive suffix, also found in several other kinship terms). One’s descent as a whole is referred to with the term fakasologa, literally ‘ordered listing’. 5.1.1.2. By partial blood There is no basic term for individuals related to ego through partial blood. Partial- blood kinship with siblings with whom ego shares only one blood parent can be specified by modifying the sibling term with the Samoan borrowing nofoaaulu ‘half [sibling]’, a term which can also be used as a predicate. 5.1.1.3. By marriage There are few terms for kin by marriage, a fact which is undoubtedly related to the lack of importance placed on affinal kin ties in Tuvaluan society. The basic term for ‘spouse’ is aavaga, which is neither specified nor specifiable for gender. This term is reputedly a borrowing from Samoan, although one only finds a form a¯vaga with the meaning of ‘elope’ in Samoan (Milner 1966:37). An obsolete term loko appears to have referred to a man’s wife only, although some native speakers attribute to the term a meaning that encompassed both a spouse and affinal relatives of the same generation as ego, for both male and female egos. The most important term for affinal relatives other than ego’s spouse is the following: (3139) maa ‘spouse’s sibling of same gender as ego, or spouse of the canonical sibling of different gender from ego’ • for female ego: BW, HZ (sister-in-law) • for male ego: ZH, WB (brother-in-law) The term is not applied to collateral siblings of one’s spouse or to more distant relatives of one’s sibling’s spouse. The social relations to which it refers are characterized by circumspection and restraint, particularly among men, a characteristic which is clearly linked to the brother-sister avoidance patterns described in 5.1.1.1.1. Men who are maa to one another are related through the tuagaane tapu, and therefore they must control their behaviour in each other’s presence and maintain a certain level of (mostly negative) politeness towards one another. | True

text: Lexicon 631 Terms for siblings-in-law who are not one’s maa are the same as one’s sibling of the same gender, but they can refer to individuals of either gender, in contrast to the primary meaning of the terms (cf. 5.1.1.1.1): (3140) taina ‘spouse’s sibling of same gender as ego’s spouse, or spouse thereof • for female ego: HB (brother-in-law), HBW (brother-in-law’s spouse) • for male ego: WZ (sister-in-law), WZH (sister-in-law’s spouse) The fact that the same term is used for one’s sibling of same gender on the one hand, and one’s spouse’s same-gender siblings and spouses thereof on the other is clearly motivated by social similarities between these categories. In contrast to one’s maa and tuagaane, one’s taina can all be treated casually. This is particularly true of the siblings of one’s spouse of the same gender as one’s spouse, who are potential marriage partners after the death of one’s spouse. Ego refers to his or her parents-in-law as maatua ‘mother’ and tamana ‘father’, and to his or her spouse’s siblings’ child as tama ‘child’. There is no lexicalized way of distinguishing these affinal referents from blood relatives that are denoted by the same terms (cf. 5.1.1.1). One archaic term for in-laws is generally attributed to the Nukulaelae dialect and Northern Tuvaluan dialects. The Nukulaelae form is fugaona while the Northern form is fugaono. The exact referential scope of the term is the subject of some disagreement among speakers, although most agree that the term refers to at least one’s daughter-in-law in the Nukulaelae dialect and to at least one’s daughter- or son-in-law in the Northern dialects, in addition to perhaps other affinal relatives. The term is not in common use. There are no terms for ego’s wife’s brother’s wife and ego’s husband’s sister’s husband (i.e., spouse of one’s maa). There are no terms either for collateral siblings and other relatives of one’s spouse. Kinship terms with affinal referents cannot be modified with any of the modifiers described in 5.1.1.1. 5.1.1.4–6. By adoption, fosterage, and affiliation Several types of adoption and fosterage are recognized in Tuvaluan society, all of which supplement rather than replace blood kin ties. Adoption of all types is very frequent, as in many other Polynesian societies, and plays an important role as an adaptation strategy to often scant resources such as land, since the creation of adoptive ties coupled with the maintenance of blood ties can increase an individual’s access to land resources (Brady 1976, Koch 1963). There are several ways of referring to adoptions that involve the creation of fictive parent-child ties. The verb puke ‘take’ is the most common term. The terms tausi ‘keep, take care’ and faagai ‘feed’ usually connote a fostering relationship, often temporary, usually not legalized. All three terms are transitive verbs and take as subject an expression referring to the parent and as direct object a reference to the child: (3141) Maalia ne puke nee Moapi. Malia Pst take Erg Moapi ‘Moapi adopted Malia.’ The same three terms can also modify tama ‘child’ attributively (e.g., tama faagai ‘foster child’). Often an individual past child-bearing age adopts a young child, thus creating a fictive grandparent-grandchild relationship, which is referred to in the same manner. text: 632 Lexicon the English borrowing saina ‘sign, signature’, which can only be used predicatively (e.g., tama saina ‘legally adopted child’). Fictive kin ties can also be established between age mates. Individuals of the same or opposite gender can decide to become adoptive siblings; even though the procedure is not legalizable and hence has no impact on land ownership, it can lead to serious patterns of reciprocity and sometimes to coresidence. Particularly when coresidence occurs, relatives of either party can treat the fictive sibling as a child, sibling, grandchild, etc., and call him or her as such in everyday interactions. These ties are referred to predicatively with the verb ssai ‘bind’, which can take a sibling term as direct object or a comitatively marked modifier referring to a person: (3142) Laaua mo Sokomani ne ssai nee laaua telaa taina. they-2 and Sokomani Pst bind Erg they-2 their-2 sibling ‘He and Sokomani took one another as brothers.’ The term ssai is also used in reference to friendship ties (ssai taugaasoa ‘become bond friends’) and romantic ties (ssai faamau ‘become sweethearts’). The term can also modify sibling terms attributively; ego’s taina ssai and tuagaane ssai are ego’s fictive sibling of same gender as ego and different gender as ego respectively. All adoptive ties can also be referred to with the verb fai ‘do, make’. The same term can also be used attributively with tama ‘child’ instead of puke, tausi, or faagai, with taina ‘sibling of same gender’ and tuagaane ‘sibling of opposite gender’ instead of ssai, and with maatua ‘mother’ and tamana ‘father’. With the last two terms, fai is the only attributive modifier that can refer to an adoptive tie. All terms contrast with the predicative or attributive kinship-term modifier tonu which, in addition to its other meaning (cf. 5.1.1.1), can mean ‘nonadoptive’ in contrast to ‘adoptive’. Thus ego’s maatua fai ‘adoptive mother’ contrasts with ego’s maatua tonu ‘blood mother’. In addition, the use of tonu in comparative or metaphorical contexts can also help distinguish permanent and legalized adoptive relationships from more informal adoption and fosterage. Following are two utterances from written wills that illustrate the typical use of tonu in reference to adoptive ties (the will from which the second extract is taken was dictated from a deathbed, hence the third- person references): (3143) Lemuelu ne puke nee au o ttaku peelaa ko taku tama tonu. Lemuelu Pst adopt Erg I Cmp call thus Foc my child real ‘I adopted Lemuelu legally (i.e., so that he came to be considered my blood child).’ [lit.: ‘I took Lemuelu to call like my real child.’] (3144) See toe ttaku peelaa ne tama fakaaattea, a koo ttusa eeloa Neg again call thus some child different but Inc equal indeed mo ana tama ttonu. with his child real ‘[They] shall not be considered [lit.: called] children of different [parents], but shall be treated the same as his blood children.’ Finally, faatamaa, a borrowing from Samoan fa’atama¯ ‘treat like a father’ (Milner 1966:239) refers to a temporary, informal foster father; the term is associated in particular with temporary fictive kin ties established between secondary-school children away from their home island and male heads of local families that take in these children for the duration of their schooling. No equivalent term exists for a foster mother. | True

text: Lexicon 633 5.1.1.7. Terms for pairs of kin The compounding element tau is preposed to certain kinship terms to denote pairs of relatives related through the particular relationship denoted by the kinship term. For example, the expression tau maatua, formed with maatua ‘mother’, refers to a mother-and-son pair or mother-and-daughter pair. The individuals involved may be of any age, and the relationship may be either by blood or adoption of any type. The term is not applied in its literal sense to relatives who are not tonu ‘true’, e.g., to a pair comprised of an aunt and niece or of a mother-in-law and son-in-law (see further on for special terms referring to collateral relationships). The word tau is historically related to numerous other terms denoting plurality or related notions in Polynesian languages: in Tuvaluan, it appears as a numeral modifier for coconuts tied up in bunches (cf. 2.1.6.5.1(c)) and as an adverb denoting habitual or continuous aspect (cf. 2.1.3.3.2.1(c)-(d)). Kinship terms that can form compounds with tau are terms that denote relationships normally characterized by strong affective bonds and mutual alofa ‘empathy’, although the particular behaviour differs from one type of relationship to the next. One finds the following inventory of forms: (3145) tau tamana ‘father and child’ tau maatua ‘mother and child’ tau tuaatina ‘mother’s brother and sister’s child’ tau tupuna ‘grandparent and grandchild’ tau aavaga ‘husband and wife, married couple’ tau tuagaane or tau tuagaene ‘brother and sister’ tau taaina ‘pair of siblings of same gender’ In the last compound, the kin term taina takes on a special plural form taaina found only in this environment. This noun is one of the few nouns with an inflected plural form (cf. 2.1.1.8.3). As should be clear from the above exhaustive list, terms for pairs of kin of different generations take as the unmarked term that which refers to the higher generation. Absent from the inventory are terms referring to pairs of in-laws. In addition, most compounds with tau can be further prefixed with faka- (cf. 5.1.1.1) to denote pairs of kin which are not in a basic kin relationship. For example, fakataumaatua denotes a pair of individuals, one of whom is the other’s fakamaatua ‘collateral mother’ (e.g., a mother’s sister). Note that faka- precedes tau in these compounds. The only term referring to a pair of kindred that cannot be prefixed with faka- is tau aavaga ‘husband and wife’, which is predictable since there is no collateral spouse category. All terms for pairs of kin are nouns in their most common manifestation: (3146) A ko te tau maatua teenaa koo olo ki fea? Cnt Foc the pair-of mother that Inc go to where? ‘And where is that mother-and-child pair off to?’ They can also be used as verbs as long as their subject refers to both members of the related pair: (3147) Maaua mo Kiitiona e fakatautaaina. we-2-e and Kitiona Nps in-manner-of+pair+sibling ‘Kitiona and I are cousins.’ For a discussion of number agreement with demonstratives and verbs controlled by compounds with tau, see 2.1.2.5.4 and 2.1.3.6.5(b) respectively. | True

text: 634 Lexicon 5.1.2. Colour terminology Colour terms are verbal adjectives. They can thus be used as predicates or attributes: (3148) Tena sulu e kkena. his loincloth Nps white ‘His loincloth is white.’ (3149) tena sulu kkena his loincloth white ‘his white loincloth’ However, colour terms are unusual among verbal adjectives because there is a strong preference to use them as modifiers of the noun lanu ‘colour, tint’, with which they form a verbal noun-adjective compound (cf. 2.2.6.3.3), particularly in predicate frames. Thus, while the above examples are grammatical, the following are considerably more common and preferred: (3150) Tena sulu e lanu kkena. his loincloth Nps colour white ‘His loincloth is white.’ (3151) tena sulu lanu kkena his loincloth colour white ‘his white loincloth’ The noun lanu in noun-adjective compounds can also be modified by descriptors other than colour terms, particularly plant names, to create nonbasic colour terms (‘colour of X, X-colour(ed)’). Thus the colour term inventory can be expanded with conventionalized nonbasic colour terms discussed in 5.1.2.2, or with nonconventionalized descriptors created on the spur of the moment. With descriptors other than colour terms, lanu is obligatory. Colour terms are subject to some dialectal variation. Variations within the Southern dialects are noted in the following discussion. K.Chambers (1978) provides a description of colour terms in the Nanumea dialect, although phonemic gemination is not indicated consistently in that work. 5.1.2.1. Basic colour terms Four basic colour terms can be identified, using criteria for basicness provided in Berlin and Kay (1969:5–7) and subsequent refinements: (3152) kkena ‘white’, including light shades of any colour; also ‘(of a person) light-complexioned’ uli ‘black’, including dark shades of any colour, particularly dark grey; also ‘(of a person) dark-complexioned, suntanned’ kkula ‘red’, including shades of purple and deep orange, but not in reference to red hair; also ‘(of a person) sunburnt’ ssega (Funafuti, Vaitupu, and Nukufetau dialects) or ssama (Nukulaelae dialect) ‘yellow’; also ‘(afflicted by) hepatitis’ Another term for ‘yellow’ in the Vaitupu dialect is the nonbasic term ffelo (cf. 5.1.2.2.1). The three terms for ‘yellow’, ssega, ssama, and ffelo, are understood and occasionally used throughout Southern Tuvalu. With basic terms for the colours black, white, red, and yellow, Tuvaluan is a Stage IIIb language in Berlin and Kay’s universal hierarchy of basic colour terms (Berlin and Kay 1969:69–70). | True

text: Lexicon 635 5.1.2.2. Nonbasic colour terms Nonbasic colour terms fall into several categories: derived terms, i.e., monolexical terms that are derived from or identical to a non-colour term and that refer to the typical colour of the referent of the related or identical term (5.1.2.2.1); compound terms (5.1.2.2.2); borrowed terms (5.1.2.2.3); and terms that are restricted to a limited range of referents (5.1.2.2.4). Modifiers of colour terms are treated in 5.1.1.2.5. 5.1.2.2.1. Derived terms The following derived colour terms can be used in all frames regularly associated with colour terms, e.g., with lanu ‘colour’ optional but preferred: (3153) llega ‘deep yellow, reddish orange’, from lega ‘egg yolk’ (cf. Proto- Polynesian *rega ‘turmeric’) ffelo (Vaitupu dialect) ‘yellow’ (cf. felo ‘Malay custard apple, Ficus tinctoria’) Under this category fall descriptors of marking patterns, whose referents are not considered colours in other societies, but which behave exactly like colour terms in Tuvaluan. For example, they can modify the noun lanu ‘colour’ and frequently form verbal noun-adjective compounds with it: (3154) pulepule ‘spotted, chequered, with a pattern of two or more colours’ (probably from pule ‘cowrie (shell), Cypraeidae species’, whose shell is spotted) selesele ‘striped’ (cf. sele ‘cut in strips’) tasi ‘solid’ (literally, ‘one, same’) tuuttutu ‘with polka-dots’ (probably duplicated form of tutu ‘cauterise’) valevale ‘multicolour, polychrome’ (literally ‘any old way, variously’) 5.1.2.2.2. Compound terms Compound terms are always noun-adjective compounds whose nominal element is lanu ‘colour’. In contrast to basic and derived colour terms, this noun is obligatory for this class of colour terms. text: 636 Lexicon 5.1.2.2.3. Borrowed terms Many English colour terms are known and used, even by people with limited proficiency in English. The extent to which the terms are adapted to the phonological structure of Tuvaluan depends largely on the relative fluency of the speaker in English; thus bilingual speakers often use the term green, thereby engaging in one- word code-switching, while speaking Tuvaluan, while monolingual speakers of Tuvaluan use the phonologically adapted version of the term, kulini. Following are the most common borrowed terms in phonologically adapted form: (3156) kaakii ‘khaki, beige’ kaasimia ‘light purple, mauve’ (from cashmere) kookoo ‘brown’ (from cocoa) kulei ‘grey’ kulini ‘green’ oolenisi ‘orange’ palauni ‘brown’ piniki ‘pink’ puluu ‘blue’ violeti ‘purple, violet’ All borrowed terms can be used in noun-adjective compounds with lanu ‘colour’ (e.g., lanu kulini ‘green’). 5.1.2.2.4. Semantically restricted terms A number of forms can only refer to the colour of a restricted range of objects. Some refer to colour only in conjunction with other qualities. Many of these terms are generally not used in noun-adjective compounds with lanu: (3157) kkelo ‘(of hair) blond, red’ (cf. kelo ‘albino, blond-haired person’) meamea ‘(of sunburnt skin) red’ mmelo ‘(of one’s face) red from exposure or intense emotion’ (cf. melo ‘purplish’, in animal names) uusi ‘(of hair) dark, thick, and shining, (of vegetation) lush and dark’ ssina ‘(of the sand, a flower, hair, etc.) white’ ssulu ‘(of a ripe fruit, the moon, or drying leaves) brightly coloured, usually bright yellow or bright brown’ ttea ‘(of a person) pale because of illness or intense emotion, (of a colour, a coloured garment, etc.) faded’ vvolu ‘(of one’s face) red from exposure or intense emotion’ One verb, lleu, refers to the appearance of a ripe pandanus nut, commonly identified by the bright orange-red colour of its segments. While not a colour term in the strict sense of the word, it is always defined in terms of colour. A number of forms appear with some regularity in compound animal names and a few other compound terms. One, uli ‘black, dark’ (e.g., lavia uli ‘parrot fish species’, matuku uli ‘blue heron, Demigretta sacra’, aaseu tafa uli ‘trevally species’, literally ‘dark-flanked trevally’), is identical in form to the basic colour ‘black’. Colour term modifiers Colour terms can be modified by a number of words. The intensifier kkii can modify basic or nonbasic terms denoting warm colours to denote brightness (e.g., kkula kkii ‘bright red’) and terms denoting cool colour to denote darkness (e.g., puluu kkii ‘deep blue’). The adjective maalosi and mmafa, literally ‘healthy, strong’ and ‘heavy’, both mean ‘deep, dark’ with colour terms (e.g., palauni mmafa ‘dark brown’, puluu maalosi ‘deep blue’). The term kkefu, which means ‘blurred’ in its literal sense, combines with uli ‘black, dark’ in a compound uli kkefu ‘(dark) grey’, or sometimes just appears as kkefu. Lightness is denoted by either maamaa ‘light’ or mmaa ‘clean, clear’ (e.g., kkula mmaa ‘light red’). A number of collocationally restricted modifiers (cf. 2.2.6.3.4) can only modify specific colour terms and no other word in the language: (3158) kkula paauli ‘deep red’ kkula mmii ‘bright red’ (or the reduplicated form miimmimi) uli patoi(toi), uli tamumu, uli tokitoki ‘jet black’ uusi palailai ‘(of hair, vegetation) deep dark’ vvolu tokitoki, vvolu tukituki, vvolu patoi(toi) ‘(of complexion) very flushed’ The collocational patterns associated with these modifiers are highly idiosyncratic. text: 640 Lexicon ‘protein food (usually fish, but also meat or eggs) intended to be eaten raw’. The term meakkai can refer generally to ‘food’, or more specifically to ‘starch food’, prototypically swamp taro, taro, sweet potato, or breadfruit. This pattern of polysemy is common throughout the Pacific, where starch food is considered fundamental to a meal, and hence is equated with food in its unmarked form, while protein and vegetable food are garnish. 5.1.4.1. Cooking terminology Several terms can denote the act of cooking in its general form, the most unmarked of which is fakappaku ‘cook (any style)’, the causative form of ppaku ‘cooked’ (also ‘(of food or one’s flesh) burnt’). The latter term is the antonym of mmata ‘raw, uncooked, undercooked’, and has a now obsolete synonym, mmoso. The latter term only refers to cooked food, in contrast to the polysemic ppaku. The polysemic verb fai ‘do, make’ can also be used as a transitive verb or with an incorporated object, most commonly meakkai ‘food’. Lastly, the borrowing kuuka means ‘cook in Western fashion’, where ‘Western fashion’ can refer to a method (e.g., in a pan over the kerosene stove) or a style (e.g., in a stew). Of relevance is the term fakagaalue ‘prepare (protein food) as a stew or a casserole’, the causative form of gaalue ‘work’, which refers to cooking in a Western fashion. Basic terms for cooking methods read as follows: (3159) lala ‘cook against a flame, toast, singe’, also ‘heat up’ (not necessarily food) saka ‘boil’ ssunu ‘grill, char’ taataa ‘roast over hot stones, a hot iron-sheet, or an open fire, barbecue’ tao ‘bake in an earth oven or a European-style oven’ ttunu ‘cook in a container over an open fire’ These terms can be modified with adverbs or prepositional phrases to denote other methods, e.g., ttunu ki te afusaga ‘steam’ (cf. afusaga ‘vapour’; the prepositional phrase is an instrumental). text: Lexicon 641 Basic cooking terms probably denote methods that were in use in pre-contact days (i.e., prior to the mid-nineteenth century). Baking, which stands out as a particularly basic and probably ancient method, was and is done in an underground oven (umu) similar to those found throughout Polynesia, created by heating stones in an open fire in a pit in the ground, placing the food wrapped in leaves over the stones, covering the food wrappings with protective mats, woven leaves, or canvas, and burying the entire oven. The oven is uncovered (pusa) after a period of one or several hours, during which the food has cooked slowly à l’étouffade. While the umu is only prepared on festive occasions or once a week in more Westernized areas of Polynesia, it remains part of everyday cooking on the Outer Islands. Nonbasic cooking terms can be productively formed with the polysemic prefix faka-, in its canonical causative sense (cf. 2.1.3.1.3), or in the sense of ‘cause to be, cause to have’ and ‘in the manner of, à la’ (cf. 2.2.2.1.3). The resulting form can function as a verb or an adverb. The meaning of some forms is predictable from that of the root, while in some cases the root is not recognizable as a contemporary lexeme. The following is a representative sample (roots are provided in brackets if identifiable): (3160) fakkale ‘curry’ (kale ‘curry powder’) fakalolo ‘cook with coconut cream’ (lolo ‘coconut cream’) faka-Lotuma ‘à la Rotuma, i.e., prepare (flour or mashed swamp taro) by mixing it with coconut toddy and coconut cream’ (Lotuma ‘Rotuma’) fakamaasima ‘salt (fish) and dry in the sun’ (maasima ‘salt’) fakatolo ‘mash cooked starch food (usually swamp taro, breadfruit, or sweet potato) with coconut cream’ fakasega ‘mix grated coconut or germinated coconut kernels with caramelized toddy’ In a number of terms borrowed from Samoan, one can recognize the prefix faa-, from fa’a- the Samoan version of the Tuvaluan prefix faka-: (3161) faalifu ‘mix (cooked starch food) with coconut cream’ faaula ‘caramelize (coconut toddy, sugar, etc.)’, or sometimes the native form fakkula, literally ‘cause to be red’ faausi ‘bake in an underground oven (starch food cut up in fist-size cubes and dipped in coconut cream with toddy)’ A number of other terms exist that have very specialized meanings. Their meaning as cooking terms is often extended from a more basic and general meaning; for example, kkumi ‘cook (shark or ray meat) by dipping the baked meat in salt water, squeezing the water out, and drying it in the sun’ literally means ‘squeeze, throttle’. 5.1.4.2. Eating terminology The most basic verb referring to the act of ingesting food is kai ‘eat’. The act of eating other types of food raw can be described as kai mmata (mmata ‘raw’), not ota. The phrase ota mmata refers to the ingestion of meat or fish normatively not eaten raw, such as pork. text: The Cambridge Introduction to Shakespeare’s Comedies Why did theatre audiences laugh in Shakespeare’s day and why do they still laugh now? What did Shakespeare do with the conventions of comedy that he inherited, so that his plays continue to amuse and move audiences? text: Chapter 1 Introduction: comedy as idea and practice Laughter Laughter is universal; we all need to laugh, and many different events can bring it about. Throughout the sixteenth century there were signiﬁcant discussions of the role of laughter in relation to the ‘decorum’ – or proper conduct – of daily life, especially among the gentry and nobility, who were considered the patterns of Renaissance behaviour. Here is one such discussion: He is a living creature that can laugh: because this laughing is perceived only in man, and (in manner) always is a token of a certain jocundness and merry mood that he feeleth inwardly in his mind, which by nature is drawn to pleasantness and coveteth quietness and refreshing, for which cause we can see men have invented many matters, as sports, games and pastimes, and so many sundry sorts of open shows . . . And although all kind of jests move a man to laugh, yet do they also in this laughter make diverse effects. For some have in them a certain cleanness and modest pleasantness. Other bite sometime privily, otherwhile openly. Other have in them a certain wantonness. Other make one laugh as soon as he heareth them. Other the more a man thinketh upon them. Other in laughing make a man blush withal. Other stir a man somewhat to anger. But in all kinds a man must consider the disposition of the minds of the hearers. Baldassare Castiglione, The Book of the Courtier, tr. Thomas Hoby (1561), Book 2 What is the relation between laughter and comedy? It will be the business of this book to tease out the distinction, to look at the ways in which Shakespeare, writing in the 1590s and the ﬁrst decade of the 1600s, combined laughter- causing moments with a form of dramatic story-telling that has a long and ancient history. Whatever happens along the way in a dramatic comedy, the ending will offer an image of happiness – for at least some of the characters whose fortunes we have followed. One constant, however, is the practice of clowning: the contribution of actors whose job it is to amuse the audience – hopefully, to make them laugh – at various points in the play. When Castiglione speaks of ‘the disposition of the minds of the hearers’ he is reminding us of the most vital aspect of comedy: its audience. His list of ‘jests’ acknowledges that things strike us as funny in different ways at different times. Yet in writing a comedy, the playwright must provide the opportunity for clowns to do their work. To begin, then, with a question: what is the funniest Shakespeare scene you (the reader) can recall in performance, either profes- sional or amateur? Most people, without having to think much, will enthu- siastically offer the performance of the play ‘Pyramus and Thisbe’ in the last act of A Midsummer Night’s Dream. After this, three other comic models often come to mind: Malvolio’s letter scene and cross-gartered appearance before Olivia (Twelfth Night); Beatrice and Benedick’s volley of sarcastic put-downs and their ‘overhearing’ scenes (Much Ado About Nothing); and – my personal favourite – the one-sided conversations between Lance and his oblivious dog in Two Gentlemen of Verona. What is it about these scenes (and their analogues) that almost infallibly produces laughter when played on a stage? (though it may very well not do so in silent reading). Then there are the eloquent hero and heroine, each of whom has a dithyrambic death scene, Thisbe’s ending the play with such self-believing passion (Flute never steps out of role to explain it) that it often silences the patronising on stage audience and wrings a tear.
